PRIORITIES RESOLUTION

Preamble

DSA meets at its fall 2003 national convention at a time of right-wing dominance in United States domestic and foreign policy. The Bush administration’s doctrine of “pre-emptive” wars involves unilateral United States intervention around the globe in an arrogant and violent manner not witnessed since the Vietnam War and the covert/proxy wars of the 70’s and 80’s. In addition, Bush’s tax give-away to the rich and radical expansion of military spending has created a structural deficit that will place downward pressure on public spending for generations to come. The Bush administration has cynically used the ‘war on terrorism’ to justify an assault on already weakened civil rights and civil liberties, and to justify a massive increase in military spending and a gutting of funding for even its own public policy initiatives, such as “The Global War on AIDS” and “The Leave No Child Behind” educational act. There is no doubt that this is the most reactionary administration in at least a century, especially given its control of all three branches of government. Moreover right wing administrations are less constrained and more vicious during a second term than in their first since they no longer have to be concerned with reelection.

The danger posed by a second term is real. A re-election of the rogue Bush regime would further a unilateral foreign policy that threatens global peace and threaten the destruction of our already minimalist public sector, particularly Medicare, Social Security, and public education. But, the reelection of this President is not certain. There is wide spread popular concern about the economy and foreign policy that has surfaced in the polls and is evident in the strength of the anti-war candidates for the Democratic nomination. The Bush administration’s foreign policy overreach has given rise to a quagmire in Iraq and its failure to aid state budgets has accentuated the costs of the economic downturn. The uneven economic ‘recovery’ has benefited only the affluent, while placing tremendous social welfare burdens on state and local governments.

Thus, the challenge facing the broad democratic left – which includes DSA – is to defeat the Bush administration in the 2004 elections, while also strengthening a coalition of progressive forces that would pressure whatever administration that replaces the Bush regime to implement more humane and democratic foreign and domestic policies. We have no illusion about the centrist character of most of the feasible alternatives to Bush; but politicians necessarily respond to popular pressure from below. How many social gains can be derived from Bush’s defeat will depend on how much the labor, civil rights, environmental, and feminist movements strengthen themselves through this popular resistance to Bush. As socialists, our participation in an anti-Bush campaign will not be simply as builders of someone else’s election. We will proceed with an eye to promoting campaign strategies that can help grow the many social movements we support.

The outcome of the 2004 elections will be the single biggest factor determining the shape of political work in the near future, but regardless of the outcome, we commit ourselves to continue our challenge to America’s low-wage economy and its structural underpinnings.

In engaging in the political and organizational priorities, this convention reiterates the 2001 convention’s commitment that all of DSA’s politics will be guided by a demand for social and economic justice for all. In pursuit of justice, multi-racial coalition building and an anti-racist politics must be an ongoing, integral part of all our projects and activism. We must also consistently look for opportunities to work side-by-side with activists in communities of color.

To move forward towards the goals mentioned above, DSA adopts the following four main priorities at this convention:

I. To participate actively in a Dump Bush movement. This includes :

1) encouraging DSA members to participate actively in the primary campaign of the candidate of their choice;

2) organizing DSA members who are delegates to the convention, providing testimony at platform hearings on our issues, organizing DSA events at the Democratic National Convention and elsewhere, and working to unify the efforts of progressive delegates at the convention;

3) building a sufficiently strong left coalition that it can pressure the campaign to engage in genuine grass-roots mobilizations and put heat on any new administration to adopt the most progressive policies possible.

II. To strengthen DSA’s organizational capacities. DSA must engage in more internal and public education as to the relevance of democratic socialist vision and program for building a more humane world as an alternative to capitalism in the twenty-first century. In particular, the organization must reinvigorate its tradition of educating young people to this politics, particularly – but not exclusively – by rebuilding a DSA/YDS presence on college and university campuses.

III. We must build upon the increased organizational focus and coordinated activism that the “Low Wage Justice” campaign, initiated at the 2001 DSA convention, has brought to the organization. The DSA NPC and national office will continue to provide resources and information to aid locals in living wage campaigns, immigrant justice activism, single payer advocacy, and labor support work.

The national leadership and staff will also work to bring together religious, labor, student, environmental and community activists to build a national campaign to achieve justice for Wal-Mart workers as well as reforms in Wal-Mart’s business practices. We cannot envision victory in our efforts against the low-wage economy without achieving significant and lasting change at Wal-Mart.

IV. With our international connections we will work to develop a project around a public dialogue between progressive elected officials in the United States and other countries. The dialogue would attempt to develop several points.

1) The importance of a genuine multilateral approach to international crises and the need for international leadership on human rights and peace issues from outside the United States.

2) Opposition to American jingoism, anti-Europe bashing, simplistic unilateralist or phony multilateral foreign policy programs, and contempt for international law. Educating the public as to the superior structure of the economic and social welfare systems of other advanced industrial nations.

3) International solidarity to meet human needs and further popular aspirations while opposing corporate-driven globalization.

This convention commits the national staff and NPC to :

Strengthening the relationship between YDS and DSA

The locals and the national will endeavor to provide whatever aid will help YDS re-establish a presence on college campuses (and high schools) around the nation.

Improving the effectiveness of our communication and outreach

We must continue to improve the editorial quality and timeliness of Democratic Left, the DSA web site, and the organization’s listserve.

Regular coverage of local activities shall continue to be part of the mission of Democratic Left and the website.

We must continue to implement the 2001 Convention Resolution on Internet Enabling DSA, including providing an internet discussion list and making minutes available. We should routinely collect email addresses.

In order to expand the pool of members, activists, and contributors (and thus increase our staff and resource capacity), DSA will attempt to return to its practice of mailing 50-100,000 pieces of direct mail recruitment letters each year.

Conferences

This convention also endorses continuing the practice of substituting regional activist conferences for a single, non-convention-year, national activist conference.

Regional conferences and National Conventions should devote more time to democratic discussion and decision-making.

Development Committees

To enhance the relationship between the national office and leadership and our local activists, the NPC will appoint a Local Development Committee consisting of NPC and non-NPC members. This committee will maintain regular communication between locals and organizing committees and the national organization; revise and update a Local Development Plan and work on carrying it out; make recommendations to the national organization in the interest of the health of locals; stimulate discussion about the concerns expressed by locals and the regional activist conferences; and research best practices of DSA locals and how they might learn to do better, and disseminate this information.

Similarly, the NPC will, if possible, appoint an At-Large Development Committee concerned with at-large members.

RESOLUTION ON THE OCCUPATION OF IRAQ

The prosecution of the War in Iraq and the subsequent occupation of Iraq completely validate the objections raised by those who opposed this war. Only the speedy restoration of Iraqi sovereignty to an independent and legitimate Iraqi government can end this quagmire.

To facilitate this, Democratic Socialists of America calls for the immediate withdrawal of the U.S.-British “coalition” forces from Iraq and simultaneous transfer of administration of Iraq to the United Nations, including the appointment of a UN High Commissioner. A UN-controlled peacekeeping force should maintain security during the period of UN administration while an Iraqi force is being developed and sovereignty is restored.

The Bush administration has failed to provide for even the most minimal needs of the Iraqi population. While corporations such as Halliburton and Bechtel are profiteering from no-bid contracts, U.S. citizens are paying for an old-fashioned colonial occupation in which U.S. troops—assigned to state-building duties for which they have no training—are being routinely killed. Iraqi civilians, too, are being killed in armed attacks by U.S. soldiers, by insurgents, and by common criminals taking advantage of the breakdown in social order. The Iraqi people are also suffering and dying due to their lack of sufficient clean water, electricity, and medical care. Its infrastructure destroyed, Iraq is being ravaged, and ethno-nationalist and reactionary Islamist forces are on the rise. DSA condemns the wholesale privatization of the Iraqi economy carried out unilaterally by the U.S. occupying forces. Only a sovereign and democratic Iraqi government can implement legitimate structural and economic reforms. DSA supports the efforts of organizations such as U.S. Labor Against the War that seek to protect workers’ rights and support an independent trade union movement in Iraq.

The Bush administration called for the creation of a UN-endorsed multilateral military force to join the U.S. occupation force in Iraq, to be commanded by an American and accountable to the Pentagon’s strategic control. As Phyllis Bennis of the Institute for Policy Studies noted, the plan did “not envision Washington even sharing authority and decision-making with the UN itself or with the governments sending international contingents, let alone ending its occupation and turning over full authority to the UN to oversee a rapid return to Iraqi independence.” We reject the administration’s arrogance.

We further demand that the U.S. and British meet their moral and legal responsibilities under international law by providing for the humanitarian costs of their unilateral intervention. Washington and London must pay the continuing costs of Iraq's reconstruction, including much of the cost of UN humanitarian and peacekeeping deployments. The Bush administration must immediately make public a realistic estimate for the cost of reconstruction in Iraq and turn over funds to UN authority, beginning with the $87 billion dollars allegedly appropriated for reconstruction (but the majority of which is aimed at supporting the military costs of United States occupation). Reconstruction funds would be far cheaper than the costs incurred by continuing the inhumane and counter-productive United States unilateral occupation of Iraq.

RESOLUTIONS ON ELECTORAL POLITICS

RESOLUTION REGARDING DSA ORGANIZING AROUND THE DEMOCRATIC NATIONAL CONVENTION

Whereas the Democratic Party will be holding it's 2004 Presidential nominating convention in Boston, and,

Whereas we as socialists seek to support our allies in the labor, racial and ethnic minority, feminist and peace movements within the Democratic Party, and,

Whereas it is important that socialists seek to influence the debate within the Democratic Party and articulate a democratic socialist vision for American politics, and,

Whereas it is vital that Democratic Socialists of America increase it's visibility and provide public forums for socialist ideas, and,

Whereas the Boston local is one of the largest local organizations in DSA,

Therefore be it resolved that the national organization of DSA and the Boston local shall jointly organize a public socialist event at or concurrent with the Democratic Party’s national convention in Boston in July of 2004.

RESOLUTION ON POLITICS

WHEREAS, DSA does not automatically assume that a Democratic President, even with a Democratic House and Senate, or any lesser Democratic officeholder at any level, will automatically be a progressive, or move in a progressive direction;

THEREFORE, be it resolved that DSA recognizes that left pressure will still need to be applied when Democrats are elected or re-elected at any level; and

THEREFORE, DSA will actively work to apply such pressure through itself and through left and progressive coalitions, at the national, state and local level, through all agencies available – progressive and grassroots organizations, trade unions and Jobs with Justice chapters, organizations of women and minorities, educational forums, and, just as important, through demonstrations and protests in the streets.

RESOLUTION ON ELECTORAL REFORM

DSA reaffirms its support for constitutional and electoral reforms to create a more democratic and representative political system in the United States, including:

Public funding for electoral campaigns.

Equitable access of candidates to mass media and the elimination of privately purchased campaign ads.

Limits on the size of individual campaign contributions and on total campaign spending.

The abolition of corporate PACs.

Same-day voter registration, and 24-hour voting on weekends or a national holiday for Election Day.

The elimination of the undemocratic Electoral College.

Experiments with proportional representation, electoral “fusion," and single-transferable ballot and "instant runoff" voting, so that people may vote for what they believe in without fearing that their votes will be wasted.

Equitable financing and provision of crucial public goods: not only standardized, high-quality machinery but also a voter-verifiable permanent audit trail. Any voting technology should allow preferential voting, including instant runoff and proportional representation.

Restoration of full voting rights to convicted felons.

DSA supports efforts to defend the right to vote, and we condemn the racist programs of the Republican Party and others to deny ballot access to minority voters, such as in Florida in 2000.

RESOLUTION ON MISSION STATEMENT

The NPC shall initiate an organization-wide discussion aimed at the development of a mission statement. Until such time as wider discussions within the organization – including at the planned regional activist conferences – may result in a better formulation, the following shall serve as DSA’s working mission statement:

Democratic socialists fight for a world in which all people participate democratically in the governing of the economic, political and cultural institutions and relationships that shape their lives. In the near term, this means that democratic socialists struggle for reforms that shift power and resources away from corporate elites and put them in the hands of ordinary people. The mission of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is to participate in establishing democratic socialism as a political force in the United States and the world by training and mobilizing socialist activists; by educating the public about the democratic socialist values of equality, liberty and solidarity; and by helping to build progressive coalitions to win victories that move the United States towards greater democracy.

RESOLUTION ON CORPORATIONS

The pernicious doctrine designating corporations as artificial persons has given them a degree of power exceeding that of natural persons. We should examine and pursue, in coalition with groups such as Programs on Corporations, Law and Democracy (POCLAD) and Alliance for Democracy, ways to reduce and eventually limit this power by defining persons only as living individuals.

[PDF page 1] 2011 Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) National Convention Priorities Resolution **************************** I. DSA’s Activist Agenda: Building Movements for Economic Justice DSA will participate in social movements and protest activity that demand jobs for all and the expansion of public funding of basic human needs through the restoration of progressive income and corporate taxation, and ending the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and cuts to unnecessary military hardware spending. DSA will deepen its already significant presence, around the nation, within the Occupy Wall Street movement, as we welcome it as a major form of resistance to corporate power and the neoliberal ∗political class who accommodate it. Every DSA local and YDS chapter will decide which struggles to join depending upon their groups’ capacity, existing activist commitments, and their analysis of local political conditions and opportunities. In general, DSA locals should work in one or more of the following priority areas: a. Grassroots opposition to any long-term “budget compromise” that fails to sustain vital social programs; b. Coalitions fighting for full employment and a massive public jobs program; c. Movements fighting to prevent further disastrous cutbacks in state and local budgets, particularly to public higher education; and d. Movements fighting corporate America’s attack on the labor movement and the rights of working people, both at home and abroad, and the role the destruction of labor rights has played in causing the current global economic crisis. II. Public Educational Initiatives for Economic Justice a. The NPC has developed an ambitious “Economic Justice through Economic Education Project” that aims to “train the trainers” (grassroots activists, including DSAers) to critique neoliberal ideology and put forth a progressive, socialist-feminist alternative economic policy. b. The 50th Anniversary of The Other America Project. The convention also endorses the NPC’s efforts to create a significant educational and political project around the 50th Anniversary of The Other America and Michael Harrington’s role in initiating the War on Poverty. ∗ Neoliberalism is a worldview that favors the private sector over government and a policy agenda that supports privatization, deregulation, tax cuts, and union-busting. 1

[PDF page 2] c. DSA locals will continue to advocate and engage in educational work in regard to the structural problems of a capitalist economy and the potential for a full transition to a democratic socialist economy. III. Electoral Work in 2012 and beyond DSA locals do more social movement work and educational activities than concerted electoral work. But where they engage in electoral action, they mostly work to elect progressive Democrats (and sometimes independents) who come out of and represent grassroots struggles for social justice. We also recognize that it is crucial to work to re-elect the most progressive voices in Congress. Thus, in our PAC activity we will work to aid the re-election efforts of Senator Bernard Sanders (I-VT) and Congressman John Conyers (D-MI). IV. Building Organizational Capacity One Brick at A Time a. The DSA national office, NPC, and local activists will prioritize strengthening existing DSA locals and YDS chapters and building new ones. b. To expand our organizing capacity and achieve such growth, the DSA NPC will strengthen its Local Development and Program Committee (and recruit non-NPC members to their ranks) as well as the various DSA commissions. c. DSA and YDS will make a concerted effort to promote the movement of YDS activists into existing DSA locals or YDS graduates starting new DSA locals. d. DSA and YDS will organize DSA and YDS contingents at key national and regional gatherings of progressives. e. The NPC and national staff will organize a DSA Membership Drive to conclude at the 2013 national convention. f. DSA and YDS will act to develop their on-line capabilities, including by updating the DSA website and improving the use of social networking. g. Finally, this convention recognizes the need to integrate fundraising and budgeting into every level of DSA’s work, including DSA local and YDS chapters. *************************** Preamble: Building a Socialist Presence within Social Movements The politics of the United States has too long been characterized by a highly racialized body politic and the existence of a center and a Right, but no effective Left. As a result, amidst the greatest economic downturn since the Great Depression, the Obama administration counsels a “moderate” form of fiscal austerity as its alternative to even more inhumane Republican proposals for slashing social programs which support those who need them the most – the elderly 2

[PDF page 3] and children. Over the summer of 2011, President Obama appeared to be running for re-election as “the only adult in the room” willing to make “the painful sacrifices” to restore “long-term fiscal balance.” But his “responsible” program of extensive budget cuts and insufficient tax increases on the rich and corporations will leave tens of millions of Americans unemployed and severely weaken Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security. Perhaps realizing belatedly that his re-election chances will be heavily tied to the employment picture over the next twelve months, the administration in September 2011 advanced a modest stimulus program to be paid for by tax hikes on the rich. But the Republicans will resist even these modest efforts to revive a flagging economy -- proposals that may well be too little too late. Fortunately, the emergence of an international “Occupy Wall Street” movement signals that masses of ordinary people understand that there is no solution to this crisis without greater democratic control over the economy. President Obama’s unwillingness to take on the “Wall Street Consensus” means that he has failed to use his bully pulpit to educate Americans that the economic crisis results not from excessive social spending, but from economic deregulation, the “casino” nature of a finance- driven economy, wasteful military spending, and thirty years of regressive tax giveaways to the rich and corporate America. An electorate faced with a choice between a moderate who prioritizes “fiscal responsibility” and a conservative Republican may well opt for the more aggressive budget slasher. Nevertheless, ordinary Americans care about jobs, affordable housing, and real living standards more than they do budget deficits. What we do know is that the powers that be in Washington, D.C., will not respond adequately to mass unemployment and widespread foreclosures until there is a much greater degree of protest against this economic misery. DSA has long played a role as a “leaven” within the broader Left; our stronger locals engage in effective grassroots activism while bringing to the social movements a systemic analysis of the role of class, race, and gender oppression under capitalism. Over the last two years DSA has continued renewing and revitalizing itself to meet the challenge of making the socialist tradition relevant to 21st-century America. Membership has grown steadily for several years; new DSA locals and YDS chapters have been created; a new young National Director has begun work. The ability of many DSA locals and YDS chapters to play an immediate role in the Occupy Wall Street movement demonstrates a significant growth in our organizational capacity – a capacity that we must continue to build. While DSA recognizes that many progressive Democrats in federal and state office represent the trade union, Black, Latino, feminist and other progressive constituencies, we have no illusion as to the corporate piper who calls the tune of political elites. DSA understands that neither moral imperatives nor a correct analysis of our economic woes will cause politicians to enact the policies we need. Thus, over the next two years, DSA at both the national and local level will prioritize an educational and activist program that will build the protest politics that alone can move American politics to the left. To do this, the 2011 convention also recommends that DSA continue to take concrete steps to revitalize and strengthen our activist capacity, both in DSA and in YDS. I. DSA’s Activist Agenda: Building Movements for Economic Justice 3

[PDF page 4] Thus, the 2011 DSA national convention resolves that DSA’s number one political priority over the next two years be to deepen popular struggles against the neoliberal politics of “fiscal austerity.” This two-party consensus manifested itself in the reactionary “budget compromise” of the summer of 2011 and in the likely proposals of the Congressional Super Committee (which will prioritize slashing vital social programs over cutting the military budget and restoring progressive income and corporate taxation to the pre-Reagan era). To counter this neo-liberal consensus DSA will prioritize: Participating in social movements and protest activity that demand jobs for all and the expansion of public funding of basic human needs through the restoration of progressive income and corporate taxation, and ending the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and cuts to unnecessary military hardware. DSA locals and YDS chapters, aided by educational materials and strategic guidance from the NPC and National Office, will endeavor to be “present in every struggle” that pushes for national and state policies that prioritize jobs and human needs. We place a particular priority on working within the Occupy Wall Street movement and broadening its social base by working to build coalitions between it and the labor movement, feminist organizations, progressive electoral organizations, and community groups active in the inner city and other communities of color. DSA, nationally and locally, will work to bring “socialist value-added” to the campaigns outlined below by emphasizing that the current crisis results from a thirty-year class war by corporate elites against the rights of working people around the globe. On a global scale, the inability of working people to buy the very goods their enhanced productivity produces led to the indebtedness and fiscal and trade imbalances that caused the Great Recession. The disastrous results of this global class war, initiated by elites obsessed with driving up short-term corporate profit margins, can only be reversed if working people rebuild their own institutions and political capacity, both at home and abroad. Working people can only truly govern their destiny when they achieve democratic control of the wealth their labor (paid and unpaid) creates – by building a democratic socialist society. Every DSA local and YDS chapter will decide which struggles to join depending upon their groups’ capacity, existing activist commitments, and their analysis of local political conditions and opportunities. In general, DSA locals should work in one or more of the following priority areas: a. complete_text: [PDF page 1] DSA Endorses Occupy Wall Street Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) endorses the Occupy Wall Street movement and its demand for justice. We join the demonstrators in taking a stand against corporate power and neoliberal politicians. These protests have been condemned in the press as class warfare, but in the words of a protestor on Wall Street, “they only call it class warfare when we fight back.” It was class war under the Carter administration when the government deregulated the airline, trucking, rail, communications and finance industries in favor of capitalists over workers and consumers. It was class war when Ronald Reagan fired over 11,000 striking air traffic controllers and signaled the beginning of an era of relentless union busting by employers. It was class war under the Reagan administration when the government dramatically cut taxes on the rich and raised them on the poor, while slashing Social Security survivor and disability benefits. It was class war under the Clinton administration when the government repealed the Glass-Steagall Act, legalized over-the-counter derivatives trading, crippled cash assistance to single parents with infant children, raised taxes on Social Security benefits and engineered the pro-business North American Free Trade Agreement. It was class war under the George W. Bush administration when the government further cut taxes on the rich, engineered unnecessary foreign war while ignoring domestic need, and bailed out the very banks that caused the financial crisis with trillions of dollars of taxpayers' money. It was class war under the Obama administration when the government extended the Bush tax cuts, bailed out the banks without any strings attached, failed to end foreclosures, and drastically slashed funding for essential federal programs. It was class warfare when the Supreme Court decided to lift all restrictions on corporate involvement in political campaigns. We must draw on the great traditions of resistance in our history - the Patriots, the Abolitionists, the Suffragists, Industrial Unionism, the Civil Rights Movement, and the feminist and LGBTQ movements - and engage our creative imagination in forming a movement for the 2010s. We must bear witness, but we must moreover build power that can challenge the commanding heights of capitalism and can succeed in changing laws in the people's favor. We must make demands on the state, and we must win. In the spirit of solidarity, we encourage the movement to demand: • A public jobs program • The nationalization of failed banks • Medicare for all • The forgiveness of student debt • An end to foreclosures • Substantial investment in clean energy • A fair & progressive, income & corporate tax structure • A tax on all speculative financial transactions We can fund these vital public policies if we reverse the Bush and Reagan tax cuts for the top two per cent, restore effective corporate taxation, and end wasteful military spending. And we can only reverse the decline in working people's standard of living if we restore the democratic right of working people to unionize. This is the crossroads of our age. Before us lie two divergent paths. One leads to further domination of capital and the descent of our society into a world of “have-nots” dominated by a handful of “have-lots,” a world where the government values bombs over books, where the poor pay more taxes than the rich, where environmental destruction continues to accelerate, and where racist, patriarchal and homophobic structures grow stronger. The other path leads towards greater freedom and democracy, guided by the vision of a democratic society. We must refuse to continue down the established road of increasing injustice and instead choose the difficult trek towards liberation. As Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. said, we are facing a choice between ”chaos or community,” and we must choose community. The Democratic Socialists of America enthusiastically support the Occupy Wall Street movement. Together, all the democratic forces of the 99% can remake our society, and remodel it in keeping with our age-old values of liberty, equality and solidarity. Let us show them that "we the people" are still a force to be reckoned with!

The newly-elected National Political Committee with National Director Maria Svart and Deputy Director David Duhalde. (Peg Strobel, NPC member, not in photo) Photo Credit: Reid Jenkins

By Barbara Joye

DSA and YDS delegates from across the country set the organization’s course for the coming years, shared skills and insights in numerous workshops and joined in song during a three-day convention Nov. 13-15 at a retreat center in rural Pennsylvania. The attendees agreed that the “Bernie moment,” which has enabled DSA’s accelerated growth in recent months – reflected in increased attendance compared to previous conventions, justifies optimism about the future of democratic socialism in the U.S. and of DSA in particular.

[Maria Svart delivering her National Director’s report (left) and Group Photo (right)]

“It was the best DSA convention I’ve been to!” said veteran National Political Committee member David Green from Detroit DSA. He was re-elected together with seven other incumbents, who were joined by six new members. Six members are now under the age of 32, continuing the transfer of leadership to a new generation, which has been underway in recent years and was also reflected in a significant contingent of YDS members and recent YDS “graduates” attending the convention.

Most previous conventions were held in major metropolitan areas and included an evening of public speeches and entertainment, but this one focused more on internal matters. Notably, the delegates voted to approve a new, detailed strategy document, culminating a two-year period of dialogue and debate, which included numerous conference calls and a “virtual” discussion that brought together some 100 members last May. The document will be edited for style, posted on the website and distributed to members, followed by a much shorter version for use in outreach. (The previous document outlining our strategy was updated in the late 1990s.)

[Intersectionality plenary with Michele Rossi, Natalie Midiri, and Jack Suria Linares (left) and Young Democratic Socialists meeting (right)]

The convention also passed the customary “priorities resolution,” which guides the national staff in its use of the organization’s limited financial and personnel resources. The priorities included 1) building DSA and increasing public awareness of democratic socialism through grassroots work for Bernie Sanders (but independent of his official campaign); 2) implementing the approaches to organizing laid out in the strategy document; 3) increasing DSA involvement in local anti-racist coalitions; 4) electoral work to defeat the Right while building the Left and a stronger DSA; and 5) rethinking our organizing practices and structures to facilitate our longer-range strategy. The priorities resolution will be posted on the DSA website, along with resolutions supporting local work to promote public banks, use of social media to build DSA and support Internet democracy, and a DSA Environmental Justice Network. [Update: See below for the priorities resolution.]

Two new working groups were established in addition to the one addressing the environment: one charged with reviewing DSA’s approach to international issues (including membership in the Socialist International), and a social media committee. Those interested in joining these groups should contact the national office.

The 2016-17 National Political Committee elected members are: Jared Abbott, Hope Adair, Theresa Alt, David Green, José Gutierrez, Elizabeth Henderson, Frank Llewellyn, Sean Monahan, Simone Morgen, Brandon Payton-Carrillo, Joe Schwartz, Peg Strobel and Russell Weiss-Irwin. The convention also voted to add two new honorary vice chairs: Deborah Meier and Bhaskar Sunkara.

Barbara Joye is a member of Metro Atlanta DSA.

National Political Committee (NPC) Priorities Resolution Passed at the 2015 DSA National Convention

Whereas national conventions set the main political and organizational priorities that govern national DSA work over the ensuing two years, particularly the time and resources of national staff and the elected national political leadership devoted to these tasks;

And whereas the campaign of democratic socialist Bernie Sanders for the Democratic Party presidential nomination provides a unique opportunity to enhance public knowledge of democratic socialism and to recruit for and strengthen DSA;

And whereas the completion of the new DSA strategy document provides the opportunity to educate our members and interested parties as to the role of a socialist organization in the United States – and to recruit to and build that organization,

Be It Resolved That:

National DSA resources and leadership and staff time will be primarily devoted to the following five areas:

1. Building DSA through the Sanders campaign

To accomplish that task, the NPC and national staff, working with the national DSA Sanders Committee, will help locals and future locals to

a. table and canvass with DSA materials related to the Sanders effort

b. engage in effective recruitment to DSA of people who sign up through DSA tabling and canvassing efforts

c. organize well-publicized DSA forums (or co-sponsored forums) on such topics as “Sanders and Building a Socialist Movement” and “Building a More Racially and Class-Diverse Sanders Campaign”

d. develop broad, multi-racial coalitions that can continue the work of the Sanders movement after the campaign is over. Such coalitions are essential to building a stronger U.S. left and a stronger socialist current within that left

In fulfilling these goals, DSA locals and activists will emphasize in their Sanders work the need to emerge from the campaign with a stronger socialist organization (DSA) and an increased socialist presence within U.S. politics. The Sanders campaign has raised public consciousness as to how unrestrained corporate power subverts democracy. DSA’s task is to increase public awareness of the democratic socialist alternative to capitalism

The national organization will provide training in the skills necessary for this work including training for one-on-one recruitment

The national organization will set local and YDS goals to ensure that work is not only done but also evaluated

The national organization will consider (weighing our limited resources) organizing activities inside and outside of the Democratic National Convention aimed at recruiting Sanders delegates to DSA and at recruiting activists in the streets who will be demanding that the Democrats advance a pro-labor economic and racial justice program

DSA will also work in the Sanders movement to broaden the racial, class, and gender base of the Sanders movement and to build local progressive coalitions and relationships with organizations and protest movements that last beyond the campaign

2. Building the Organization by Implementing Our Strategy

Over the next two years the national leadership and staff will aid our locals in expanding their activist core – and the skills of that core — so that the organization can begin to implement the strategy document at the local and state level

The National Office (NO) and NPC will work with each local and YDS chapter to develop a concrete plan to build a more visible and effective socialist organization in their localities. Locals should come up with a feasible set of tasks to increase their capacity do “mass work” or “coalition politics” while bringing a unique socialist perspective to the work. DSA locals will work to advance this socialist perspective through public and internal education and by injecting more demands for anti-corporate measures and non-reformist reforms into our coalition work.

When possible, the national organization will aid stronger locals in developing their own projects that are complementary to existing progressive projects so that we can maximize our own visibility as socialists (e.g., campaigns for public banks or for financial transaction taxes to finance expanded public goods or for living wage legislation)

This work will include developing study guide materials for reading and study groups to discuss the strategy document and the issues in socialist vision, analysis, and strategy raised therein

3. Increasing DSA Involvement in Local Anti-Racist Coalition Work

To build a stronger, more diverse Left—and ultimately a more diverse socialist organization—democratic socialists must increase their involvement in coalitions fighting for racial justice

The NPC and national staff will develop materials and training to aid our locals in engaging in more anti-racist coalition work. The national organization will also help locals to develop knowledge of their local political communities, as well as to enhance their organizing and political skills. Depending on local circumstances, anti-racist work may involve joining struggles against mass incarceration and police brutality; the fight to defend and expand voting rights; struggles for more equitable public education (e.g., campaigns to end “the school to prison pipeline”); and/or the fight for immigrant rights

4. Electoral Work in 2016: Defeating the Right, while Building the Left and a Stronger DSA

While building the socialist wing of a stronger Left, we also recognize the importance of defeating the increasingly successful right-wing campaign to control state and national governments at the executive, legislative, and judicial levels. Such control threatens basic labor, voting, immigrant, and reproductive rights

Thus, our electoral strategy will have two primary components: building a stronger socialist electoral presence in U.S politics, and defeating the right and center’s unconscionable attacks on the welfare state, labor rights, immigrant rights, and reproductive justice.

In the summer and fall of 2016 DSA locals will engage strategically in electoral work, depending on local circumstances. Where Democrats face serious challenges from the extreme right, locals may work to ensure electoral victory over Republicans. Where Democrats do not face such a threat our focus may be either on supporting left-wing Democratic candidates in primary challenges against centrist Democrats or in supporting independent socialist and other third-party candidates (often in non-partisan local races) if they serve to strengthen independent socialist electoral capacity

In either case, we will use these campaigns as opportunities to push substantive issues (such as raising the minimum wage, expanding basic democratic rights and participation, reversing climate change and increasing community oversight of police) as well as to build ties between diverse progressive constituencies that can be deepened after the election is over.

5. Rethinking our Organizing Practices and Structures

We will also evaluate how our organizing practices and organizational structures can be best adapted to facilitate our longer-range strategy.

Minutes of the 2025 DSA Nat’l Convention Approved for release by vote of the National Political Committee on October 1, 2025. The biennial National Convention of the Democratic Socialists of America was held from Friday, August 8, 2025 to Sunday, August 10, 2025 at McCormick Place in Chicago, IL, with Convention Planning Committee Co-chairs Laura W (Portland, OR) and Chris W (Seattle) presiding. The Convention was called to order at 9:00 am by Co-chair Laura W. The appointed Chair presiding over the first session was Alex M of Seattle. Friday, August 8, 2025 The DSA National Political Committee Co-chairs delivered opening remarks, with Ashik S (at-large) giving the first speech and Megan R (at-large) giving the second. The speeches from the Co-chairs reflected on the previous two years and their hopes for DSA in the next two years. The NPC Treasurer, John L (New Orleans) delivered a summary of the Budget and Finance Committee reports, which can be found under the Reports heading below. Credentials Subcommittee Co-chair Matt M of Pittsburgh delivered the Credentials Report, offering recommendations on challenges against delegations from Birmingham, AL; Los Angeles, CA; Delaware and the Queens, NY branch of NYC-DSA. The assembly accepted the recommendations on the challenges and the roster of delegates presented by the Credentials Committee by unanimous consent. CPC Co-chair Chris W moved adoption of the Convention Rules, noting the reduction of the threshold to remove items from the Consent Agenda from a majority vote to just 40 percent of delegates present and voting. Resolutions Subcommittee member Richard S from Baltimore moved an amendment to require masking while in the Convention Hall to prevent the spread of airborne disease. The amendment was rejected by a vote of 459 in the affirmative and 493 in the negative. The Convention Rules, unamended, were adopted by unanimous consent. Programming Subcommittee Co-chair Hayley BB (Portland) moved adoption of the Convention Agenda. The Chair ruled, upon advice of the Parliamentarian, that R06, One Member, One Vote for Federal Endorsements was contradicted by Article XIII of the DSA Bylaws and should be removed from General Orders as not being in good order. Ben D of Metro DC appealed from the decision of the Chair and gave a brief speech defending the resolution as consistent with customary practice in DSA, followed by the Chair’s rebuttal which focused on the language in the bylaws and his interpretation of the parliamentary authority. The ruling of the Chair was sustained by the Delegates, 669-501. Next, NPC Co-chair Ashik S moved an amendment to General Orders to promote CR03, CR07, CR09, and R24 much higher in the list while demoting R44 much lower in the list. Once stack was exhausted, the amendment was lost by a vote of 507 to 651. The Convention Agenda, including its unamended list of General Orders, was then adopted by unanimous consent. The Chair then moved adoption of the Consent Agenda as recommended by the CPC as the first Special Order of the day. With no objections or speeches against, the Consent Agenda was adopted by unanimous consent. The first General Order was CB03, Setting Fee Structures for the Organization’s Print Publications, moved by Faye W of San Francisco. The amendment would modernize the provisions of the bylaws governing DSA’s official publications, which were written based on the assumption of physical and not digital printing and distribution. With no objections or speeches against, the bylaws amendment was adopted by unanimous consent. Next, the assembly considered CB04, Fair Representation via STV Delegate Elections, moved by Ringo X of Worcester. The amendment would universalize Scottish Single Transferable Vote as the method that every chapter must use to elect delegates to the National Convention. After debate, the bylaws amendment was adopted by a vote of 711 in the affirmative and 412 in the negative. Around noon, the assembly heard the Convention’s keynote speech delivered by US Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan’s 12th Congressional District and member of Metro Detroit DSA. The speech denounced the genocide in Gaza and the collaboration of her colleagues in that crime, in the provision of weapons, logistical support, and diplomatic cover. The Representative emphasized the need for a clear political alternative that will not compromise on the fundamental humanity of the Palestinian people. The well-received speech was followed by a brief performance by the NYC-DSA choir. The Convention then recessed for lunch around 12:30 pm. After lunch and convention programming the delegates reconvened at 2:00 pm, with Brian W of Metro DC relieving Alex M of appointed Chair duties. Deliberation resumed with CB01, Democracy Commission Comprehensive Structural Reform Proposal, moved by Democracy Commission Steering Committee member Aaron B (at-large). The Democracy Commission was created by the 2023 Convention to bring proposals to the 2025 Convention, and its members were elected from the general membership by the delegates to the 2023 Convention. Their proposal consisted of 10 individual pieces offered as an omnibus, one of which had already been adopted on the Consent Agenda. Each one of the planks addressed different areas in DSA’s internal administration and democracy, from how membership is counted, to the size of the board of directors, and the definition of committees, commissions, and working groups, just to name a few elements of the omnibus. Delegate Zeke D of Seattle rose to demand division of the question on CB01, to consider CB01-6, Changes to the NPC, and CB01-9, Rechartering the Democracy Commission, pursuant to RONR 12th ed. 27:10. The Chair considered the division of the question on demand not well taken, claiming that the amendment period preceding the Convention was the appropriate time to suggest or reject changes to the constitutional and bylaws amendments in CB01 and the ruling was appealed. The ruling of the Chair that the question would not be divided on demand was sustained by a vote of 909 in the affirmative to 260 in the negative. The question before the assembly returned to CB01 undivided. After debate, and a call for the previous question that failed with 718 in the affirmative and 457 in the negative, the omnibus proposal was adopted by vote of 989 in the affirmative and 217 in the negative. CB02, One Member, One Vote for National Leadership, as amended by CB02-A01: Power to the Members: Deliberative Democracy for One Member One Vote on the Consent Agenda, was then moved by Carl R of Metro DC. The constitutional amendment would require the election of the NPC and select national leadership by secret ballot of all members in good standing. During debate, Delegate Richard S of Baltimore moved to vacate the Chair. After the Chair clarified that he would be relieved of duty after the vote on the main motion, the motion to vacate was withdrawn before it was seconded. Debate on CB02 continued, and a vote to extend debate failed with 672 in the affirmative and 455 in the negative. The main motion was lost by vote of 487 in the affirmative and 736 in the negative. Brian W was relieved of appointed Chair duties by Ian G of Milwaukee after the vote on CB02 was tabulated and announced. The next General Order was R27: Staff Relationship to Members in a Democratic Organization, moved by Programming Subcommittee Co-chair and former DSA staffer Hayley BB. The resolution would clarify the expectations around staff’s political activity inside DSA, and would establish that all records of the organization will be accessible to members of the NPC and their designees. After debate, the resolution was adopted by a vote of 683 to 494. Next was R44: Resolution on Staff, Contractors, and Budgeting, moved by David J of New York City. The resolution would place a cap on personnel expenses preventing the NPC from allocating more than 40 percent of the operating budget on compensation for staff or contractors. The question immediately moved to R44-A01, For a Member-Guided Budgeting Process, which was moved by Budget and Finance Committee Co-chair Shane K of Baltimore. The amendment focused on transparency and accountability in the budgeting process itself. After debate, the amendment to R44 was adopted by a vote of 627 to 492. A scheduled recess then interrupted consideration of R44 as amended. Before the Convention recessed at 6:00 pm, delegates heard announcements explaining the NPC Co-chair elections process and the speaker lottery for the Political Exchange on Saturday. The Co-chair election ran from 6:00 pm to 10:00 pm, and so did the entry period for the speaker lottery. The assembly reconvened at 6:30 pm with Griffin M of Metro DC relieving Ian G of appointed Chair duties. The question returned to R44 as amended by R44-A01. After debate, the main motion as amended failed narrowly, 583 to 594, the closest recorded margin of the Convention. The next order of business was R35, For Working-Class Member Leadership, moved by NPC member Alex P of New York City. The resolution instructs the NPC to provide stipends to members of the NPC Steering Committee and the Co-chairs of the Communications Committee and National Labor Commission. No specific amount was specified. The debate moved to amendment R35-A01, Stipend the NPC, which would restrict stipends to NPC members or YDSA National Coordinating Committee members at a maximum of $1000 per month. After debate, the amendment was rejected by a vote of 538-642. The question on the floor returned to R35, unamended, and after debate was exhausted the resolution was adopted by vote of 651-501. The next item in General Orders was CR05, National Electoral Commission Consensus Resolution, moved by Hayley BB of Portland. Constitution & Bylaws Amendments (CB) To be considered for debate at the Convention, proposed changes to the Constitution or Bylaws must have a minimum of 250 signatures of support from DSA members who are in good standing. Proposals meeting the signature requirement also become eligible for amendment prior to convention. Constitutional changes require a two-thirds (⅔) vote of the Convention to pass; Bylaws changes require a three-fifths (⅗) vote of the Convention to pass. Any member or group of DSA members in good standing may propose secondary amendments to the constitution or bylaws changes. CB01: Democracy Commission Comprehensive Structural Reform Proposal Submitted by Aaron B (Southeast MN), Connell H (River Valley), Ramsin C (Chicago), Allison K (New York City), Kristian H (North Texas). Qualified on Apr 23, 2025, with 519 signatures as of May 11, 2025. Status: Adopted Introduction DSA’s 2023 Convention voted to create the Democracy Commission, a body tasked with bringing proposals reforming DSA’s national structure to the 2025 Convention. The first stage of the commission involved researching the structures of other parties as well as DSA itself to determine what is needed to make our organization more democratic and effective. DSA’s inability to address structural concerns several conventions in a row signaled the need for organizational consensus, requiring a commission that was politically representative of tendencies within DSA. Convention delegates voted for the 21 members of the Commission in an election in October 2023, resulting in a commission with members of eight different caucuses as well as uncaucused DSA members. Based on our research and discussion, the Democracy Commission developed guiding principles for our work to have a shared understanding of our goals and priorities. The guiding principles can be read in full in our report to membership; the central points of the introduction are below: * The purpose of member democracy in DSA is to empower the working class to act collectively in its own self-interest towards the project of its emancipation. * Democracy means people have power individually and collectively and requires that democratically-made decisions be carried out by organizational leadership. Democracy thrives on direct, honest, and comradely debate conducted in open meetings with meaningful stakes, where analysis is developed to inform specific strategies. * Healthy organizational democracy depends on both formal structure and rules and organizational culture. Rules should encourage and incentivize healthy habits, instincts, and norms and not merely prescribe them. They should be flexible enough to work at times of membership expansion and of contraction. Proposals by the Democracy Commission should foster a sense of shared organizational identity in the organization and among members. They should encourage horizontal relationships between chapters as well as improve member connection to DSA national. * Deliberation within DSA should be meaningful and members should be encouraged to engage with the ideas and arguments. We should encourage reconsideration of positions as a norm. A healthy democratic organization can decide on, and evolve, its shared principles and a program. * Members should be transformed through their engagement with DSA, empowered to lead and change and engage in democracy in the organization and subsequently their local community. DSA’s democratic culture should train members to intervene in democratic debates in their unions, communities, and in moments of mass struggle, to democratize workers’ movements and organizations. Based on our guiding principles, the Commission has drafted a package of reforms that, together, will improve DSA's democratic and organizational function across the organization. Everything below won a super-majority vote of the Democracy Commission. Working from the Commission’s democratically-adopted guiding principles, every proposal went through revision, compromise, negotiation, and debate before approval. No commissioner got everything and no commissioner got nothing; the omnibus is contoured by our most fundamental agreements. Positive and negative input from Commissioners across tendencies shaped each plank; each plank is specially shaped to support the overall omnibus as a single unified reform. We believe these planks will fix some structural problems with DSA. But more importantly, taken together these proposals are a vision for our organization: coming together across political disagreements to create a healthier democratic culture and structure that reduces the distance between members, chapters, and national leadership; unifies us through deliberation and decision-making, not fiat; and empowers workers to take control of our political life, on the road to taking control of our world. Members must remain in good standing to participate in national committees. Associations Members may form Associations, which is a lightweight recognized status for groups of members who share a common interest, identity, or focus. Associations may be formed one of two ways: * Members may seek recognition from the NPC showing that 15+ members have been meeting for at least three months * Open commissions that are being dechartered for inactivity may be converted into associations by the NPC if 15+ members of the group request it The NPC may exercise oversight of associations if necessary, but associations will not have liaising assignments or other ongoing use of NPC or staff time. Associations will be given a section of the DSA Forums. They cannot submit budget requests to the national organization. Associations with no proof of activity or discussion in their forum section for 6 months will be closed. Associations may not create websites, social media, pamphlets, or any other such outwardly facing materials construed as representing DSA or official opinions of the organization. Chartering, Renewal, and Dechartering All working bodies must be chartered by a vote of the NPC or Convention. All resolutions establishing a working body should specify the intended duration of their work, which may be in perpetuity, and a working body will close after two years of operation if no duration is specified, unless reauthorized by the National Convention or NPC. The report will include each working body charter, a brief summary of funding and any other notable institutional resources provided, and level of activity. It will also list any working bodies dechartered during the term for any reason. The NPC will vote on recommendations for the next term, whether to recharter, decharter, combine, or otherwise amend their status, and any amendments to their membership or structure. Members may propose amendments to these recommendations through the regular resolution process. Changes to membership and structure of working bodies will be proposed through this process. The report will be considered by the Convention, where delegates may amend recommendations on working bodies before voting on the package as a whole to approve the status of all working bodies for the next term. Despite otherwise being governed by rules governing amendments to resolutions proposed to the Convention, amendments to the working body report may be placed on the consent agenda and are eligible for secondary amendment. Records All working bodies must have a designated secretary responsible for maintaining minutes that reflect decisions made, including voting totals. Any votes conducted asynchronously (such as via Loomio, group chats, or other non-meeting motions) must be ratified at the next standing meeting of that body, using records maintained by the secretary. Any decision requiring action outside of a body’s official meetings must be automatically placed on the agenda for the next standing meeting of that body. Working bodies using asynchronous voting must establish a method and timeline for asynchronous voting, established as a standing rule by a two-thirds majority vote of the body. Working body records should be available to members in the DSA meeting minutes archive and policy library, updated at least quarterly, unless the NPC votes to make an exception for security reasons. All working body records must be made available to the NPC upon request. Any decision-making body that fails to maintain or provide its records may have its secretary replaced by the NPC or may be subject to dechartering by the NPC or the DSA National Convention. Status: Adopted Summary Once put into operation by the bylaws changes in CB01, this resolution establishes the chapter affiliation agreements for DSA. Along with expectations of chapters and national, this affiliation agreement establishes basic standards for DSA chapters. This includes a requirement for a minimum of one meeting per year with voting rights for all members in good standing, and a virtual discussion space for chapter members. Full text DSA National-Chapter Affiliation Agreement Preamble The purpose of this agreement is to ensure that the Democratic Socialists of America and its affiliated Chapters are working in partnership consistent with the organization’s democratic socialist principles, the policies of the organization, and in accordance with all applicable state and federal laws. While many of the practices addressed in this agreement are already commonplace within DSA, the intent of this agreement is to clearly define roles, responsibilities, and expectations for both DSA chapters and the National organization.

Section 1. Grant of Charter 1. Charter. DSA hereby grants CHAPTER a charter to be a local Chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, conditioned on the terms and conditions of this Agreement. CHAPTER agrees to abide by this Agreement and all DSA governance documents, rules, policies, and procedures relating to Chapters as adopted in this agreement. 2. Territory. CHAPTER shall represent DSA as DSA’s local affiliate in the boundaries defined in its charter (the “Territory”), in accordance with DSA’s mission and purposes as set forth in DSA’s Constitution and Bylaws, all national policies, and this Agreement. DSA agrees that CHAPTER shall be the sole and exclusive Chapter of DSA in the Territory during the term of this agreement. CHAPTER agrees that, except as approved in writing by the Officers of DSA, DSA shall be the sole and exclusive national association representing the interest of the chapter. 3. Authorized Activities. DSA specifically authorizes CHAPTER to conduct activities within the Territory consistent with furthering the principles and values of democratic socialism, including but not limited to meetings, political education programs, local campaigns, fundraising, and all such other activities as directed by the National Convention or the NPC. 4. Prohibited Activities. CHAPTER agrees to refrain from any and all such activities that conflict with DSA’s democratic socialist principles, that violate federal, state or local law, and/or that could incur liability or harm to DSA, including but not limited to supporting, by contributing funds or otherwise, for-profit corporations or law enforcement, using organizational funds to purchase weapons of any kind, or direct disbursement of funds to individuals without approval from the General Membership.

Section 2. Duties of DSA DSA’s obligations to CHAPTER under this Agreement shall include: 1. Provide up to date lists of members within the Territory to CHAPTER on a weekly basis; 2. Provide regular and ongoing organizing support, training, and mentorship from, but not limited to, DSA staff; 3. Provide access to DSA’s suite of national organizing and tech tools, currently including Action Network, Spoke, Zoom, HubDialer, and VAN; 4. Provide access to DSA’s national training library as well as technical support in utilizing tech and organizing tools through DSA; 5. Preside over any and all national expulsion and grievance appeals pursuant to the procedures laid out in Resolution 33 and DSA’s Non-Resolution 33 Expulsions Process; 6. Notify CHAPTER of the chapter’s delegate apportionment for any and all DSA National Conventions. 7. Distribute the dues share to incorporated chapters, and maintain the debit cards of unincorporated chapters. 1. Dues share is set to: * 30% of the average monthly dues contribution from the first 50 chapter members * 25% of the average monthly dues share from the next 51-200 members * 20% of the next 201 members and up

Section 3. Duties of the Chapter 1. Governing Documents. CHAPTER agrees that its governing documents are and shall remain consistent in all material respects with DSA’s governing documents, and that in any conflict between the two, the national requirement shall prevail. 2. Leadership Elections. CHAPTER shall report the results of elections for officers and executive committee members, and of officers or executive committee members that have resigned or been removed within 30 days of any elections, appointments or changes. 3. Programs and Activities. CHAPTER shall endeavor to organize programs and activities to advance democratic socialism in the Territory. 4. Regular Contact. Chapter shall maintain regular contact with DSA on a monthly basis, through either meetings with elected NPC members, Field Organizers, or by attending monthly District Calls. 5. Compliance with Laws. CHAPTER warrants that it is, and shall remain, in full compliance with all applicable laws, regulations, and other legal standards. 6. Compliance with DSA. CHAPTER agrees to conduct its activities in full compliance with all DSA policies, procedures, and regulations, including mandates of the National Convention and NPC. 7. Recordkeeping, Reporting, and Inspection. CHAPTER shall maintain all records related to its corporate and tax-exempt status and shall forward to DSA copies of its Articles of Incorporation, Bylaws, and tax exemption correspondence from the Internal Revenue Service, as well as any adverse notices, requests for information by law enforcement, or other correspondence received from any governmental agency (e.g., Internal Revenue Service, state Secretary of State, or corresponding agency). CHAPTER shall maintain reasonable records related to all of its programs, activities, and operations. CHAPTER shall annually submit to DSA a copy of its most recently filed Form 990, Return of Organization Exempt from Income Tax, as submitted to the Internal Revenue Service, within 30 days of such filing. If required to file, upon the written request of DSA and at DSA’s expense, CHAPTER will permit DSA or DSA’s designated agent(s) to review appropriate records of CHAPTER pertaining to its programs, activities, and operations. Alternatively, CHAPTER shall send to DSA copies of such records upon the request of DSA. 8. Incorporation and Tax Status. CHAPTER warrants and represents that it is an incorporated nonprofit corporation, shall incorporate as a nonprofit corporation under state law within 6 months of the Effective Date of this Agreement, and/or that it will utilize DSA’s umbrella tax status if granted explicit permission by DSA. Further, CHAPTER warrants that it shall at all times be in good standing with its state of incorporation and operate in a manner consistent with CHAPTER’s tax-exempt purposes. Section 4. Standards of Democracy Chapters further agree to uphold the following standards in their practice of democracy. 1. Members must be in good standing for 30 days to vote in elections for Chapter-wide leadership, to hold Chapter-wide office, or to vote in elections for delegates to national convention. 2. Shall incorporate the national member code of conduct; 3. Shall require the holding of at least one general decision-making meeting on an annual basis. A decision-making meeting is defined as a meeting or section of a meeting run under the current edition of Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised or other parliamentary procedure authorized by chapter bylaws. The meetings are open to all members in good standing of the chapter who may propose business in order for it to be debated and voted upon. Decisions made at these meetings are binding at the chapter level. A delegated convention may count as one decision-making meeting in a year, provided delegates are directly elected by members in good standing through a proportional method. 4. That there shall be no higher decision-making body than a time-bounded General Meeting or Convention open to all members in good standing; 5. Branch Meetings shall have the following requirements 1. The meeting or section of the meeting runs under the current edition of Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised or other parliamentary procedure authorized by chapter bylaws. 2. The meetings are open to all members in good standing of the given territory of a branch, who may propose business in order for it to be debated and voted upon. Should meet quarterly 6. Shall require publishing to its members the Chapter’s budget at least on an annual basis; 7. Shall require use of a national service or system for the handling of internal election of its officers and convention delegates; 8. Shall require use of a national model form for the keeping of general meeting minutes and filing or reporting of those minutes. 9. A means for members to notify the NPC or national office in cases of non-compliance with Chapters Agreements. 10. Shall require an officer-level position for member engagement and orientation and political education, which can be a single officer or multiple officers; 11. Every chapter of DSA is required to have a common digital platform to facilitate intra-chapter communication. This may be a Slack, Discord, forum, or other presence where individuals can communicate with other members directly. Section 5. Amending the Chapter Charter The contents of the charter may only be amended at the National DSA Convention. Compliance with any new contents of the charter only applies after a renewal of charter. Section 6. Charter Term and Renewal The charter granted by DSA to CHAPTER shall become effective on the Effective Date set forth above and shall remain in full force and effect for up to two years, or until revoked by DSA or by CHAPTER in accordance with the provisions of this Agreement. 1. Charter application. The application to renew a chapter charter shall include the following items 1. If you would like to add zip codes please list them here 2. Current Chapter code of conduct and HGO process 3. Certificate of good standing if chapter is incorporated 4. If you have a bank, where is it located and what is the current balance? 5. The last budget report to membership 6. Please list any Political Action Committees associated with the chapter. Do they have bank accounts? What are their balances? 7. Any disciplinary notices from state or city agencies within the last year. 8. Chapter email, address, and socials 9. The current bylaws of the chapter 10. The current roster of officers 11. The date of your last annual meeting / convention? 2. Two (2) Year Grace Period. Chapters have up to two years after convention to apply for a new charter. Failure to do so may mean the chapter is not in compliance and appropriate action will be taken as outlined here. 1. The NPC, or a delegated body will produce an omnibus approval block of charter renewals 2. The NPC, or a delegated body will have the power to pull individual charters that are deemed problematic to be voted on individually by the NPC-SC Section 7. Enforcement of Charter 1. Request for investigation and appeal: The National Political Committee can place in trusteeship (meaning direct administration) any Chapter found to be in violation of chapter agreement, for a period of 3, 6, or 12 months, based on the severity and duration of the violation. No Chapter may be placed in trusteeship except by vote of ⅔ of the entire membership of the NPC. The Steering Committee of the National Political Committee, or a delegate chosen for the purpose by the SC, may investigate Chapters suspected of non-compliance with the national Constitution and Bylaws, Chapter Agreements, or both. A report detailing the suspected non-compliance shall be provided to the SC and the Co-Chairs of the Chapter in question, with specific reference to the rules or provisions being violated and the date(s), nature and extent of the violations. The Chapter may provide a written response to the report no more than twenty-eight days after receipt of the report. If the SC, after the twenty-eight day response period, by majority vote finds that the Chapter is not in compliance, the Steering Committee may withhold dues from that Chapter. Should the Chapter not remediate the violation(s) within ninety days, the Steering Committee may by simple majority vote deny the Chapter access to organization-wide tools and data. Any decision imposing penalties on a Chapter must be communicated in writing to the Chapter’s Co-Chairs and members within five days of its adoption. A Chapter may, by written request of any of its elected officers or by petition of five (5) percent of its members, appeal any imposed penalty to the full NPC which may by simple majority of a quorate vote confirm, reduce, or repeal the penalty(ies). Such appeal must be heard and acted upon in no more than forty days, but no less than ten days, of receipt by the NPC. 2. Notice of Violation. DSA, through the NPC, shall be responsible for enforcing this Agreement and shall provide written Notice of Violations of this Agreement to CHAPTER with a minimum of (28) days to correct any breach of the Agreement. In the event that CHAPTER fails to correct any breach of the Agreement or to respond within the time period specified within the Notice, DSA through the NPC, may withhold resources to the chapter. If the breach of charter is still not correct after these actions, then the NPC may revoke CHAPTER’s Charter or establish Trusteeship over the Charter pursuant to the procedures specified in this Agreement. 3. Withholding resources. DSA, through the NPC, shall have the authority to limit or completely withhold the dues share or suspend the chapter’s access to Org Tools. 4. Trusteeship. DSA, through the NPC, shall have the authority to establish Trusteeship of CHAPTER if CHAPTER fails to comply with or respond to any Notice of Violation of this Agreement within the specified time period or in the event that half or more of the elected leadership of a chapter resigns. In the event that Trusteeship is established, the NPC or its designees shall act as Officers of CHAPTER until such time as new Officers may be democratically elected by the Membership but for a period no longer than 1 year. 5. Revocation of Charter. DSA, through the NPC, shall have the authority to revoke the charter of CHAPTER if CHAPTER fails to comply with or respond to any Notice of Violation of this Agreement within the specified time period. 6. Termination of Charter. CHAPTER may terminate this CHARTER and affiliation with DSA at any time. CHAPTER may initiate Termination of Charter through written notice of its intention to do so no less than thirty (30) days prior to the effective date of such termination. DSA reserves the right to all assets bearing DSA’s name and/or insignia and may request that they be surrendered by CHAPTER on the date of termination, including but not limited to email addresses, website domains, social media accounts, and publications.
