Qualified on May 4, 2025, with 304 signatures as of May 11, 2025. Status: Referred to NPC Summary Democratic socialism represents a distinct and meaningful political tradition. This resolution lays out some of its fundamental principles and aspirations to end capitalist and imperialist oppression and to bring the institutions of political, economic, and social life under popular and truly democratic control; the democratic socialist theory of change; and the broad coalitions of the democratic left, undergirded by mass working-class organization. Full text Whereas, democratic socialism represents a distinct and meaningful political tradition; Whereas, as a democratic socialist organization with a welcoming, open, mass, and nonsectarian character, DSA should define, in broad terms, what democratic socialism is so that millions of people can join the organization with confidence in its overall mission; therefore be it Resolved that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) affirms its identity as a democratic socialist organization along the following lines: 1. Democratic socialism is the movement to end capitalist and imperialist oppression and bring the institutions of political, economic, and social life under popular and truly democratic control; 2. This movement must activate a majority of the population and build popular capacity to govern the economy, civil society, and the State, and thus its aims must be achieved through democratic means. 3. The political basis of this movement will be a mass working class organization building a coalition of the democratic left based on labor, environmental, racial justice, feminist, queer, immigrant, peace, anti-imperialist, and faith organizations and people of democratic and progressive conscience. 4. This movement therefore orients toward bringing millions into action and building large working-class-based coalitions, rather than orienting its political appeal to the narrow swathe of the already radicalized. 5. The democratic socialist movement must be led by mass working-class organizations, but works to build political coalitions with other social groups on the basis of common interests and common values. 6. The fight against racism, sexism, anti-queer bigotry, national chauvinism, religious discrimination, and every form of social oppression is both morally righteous and essential to the political unification of the working class and the democratic left. 7. The democratic socialist movement is profoundly ecological, understands that environmental exploitation is inherent to capitalism, and therefore is fully dedicated to the global fight for a just transition to avert climate and ecological catastrophe. 8. Democratic socialists demand an end to anti-democratic, imperialist intervention by the US government in other countries, especially in the Global South, which has led to massive human and natural resource exploitation, the toppling of popular regimes, and even genocide around the world, and stand in solidarity with global left social movements and political parties fighting for self-determination, human rights, radical democracy and inclusive sustainable development. 9. Democratic socialists enter defensive alliances to stop the further political and electoral advance of fascism, while also simultaneously fighting to complete the work of the abolitionists, Reconstruction, the labor movement, the civil rights movement, and the peace movement to demolish the military-industrial complex, to move beyond economic exploitation and capitalism, and to transform the United States into a true political and economic democracy. 10. Specifically democratic socialist organizations with a welcoming, open, mass and nonsectarian character are required to cohere activists, facilitate popular education, and transmit a vision of a truly free, substantively equal, radically democratic post-capitalist society. Be it finally resolved, that DSA will work to orient current and future members to this conception of democratic socialism and communicate it to the general public in the US and abroad. Status: Adopted Summary Escalating fascist repression by the Trump Administration is the most urgent existential threat to the socialist movement in the current political moment. Recent years have shown that mass abolitionist organizing has been a key point of activation within the working class. In order for DSA to effectively lead in the fight against fascism, this resolution presents three strategic points: a national ‘Abolish ICE’ campaign; local abolitionist organizing; and strengthening organizational security. Full Text Whereas, Donald Trump and the Republican Party have made clear their intentions to conduct the "largest deportation operation in history,” criminalize political dissent and advocacy (including threats and campaigns to prosecute immigration lawyers, Black Lives Matter activists, climate organizers, and pro-Palestine protesters as “terrorists”), institute political purges using Schedule F, defund universities that refuse to crack down on Palestine solidarity protests, and a litany of other repressive actions that constitute a fascist agenda in the United States; Whereas, attacks on immigrant Palestinian solidarity activists like Mahmoud Khalil and Momodou Taal and immigrant rights advocates like Jeanette Vizguerra are the cornerstone of the fascist agenda to crush dissent and destroy any pretense of civil rights and a continuation of a legacy of repression of movements deemed hostile to US imperialism extending back to the Holy Land Five, Leonard Peltier, and beyond; Whereas, U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is part of a fascist strategy that unjustly treats immigrants as criminal threats to the nation and national identity, separates poor immigrant families, and perpetuates a culture of fear and oppression intended to chill dissent against the state; Whereas, the criminalization of immigrants and the expansion of ICE’s powers under both Democratic and Republican administrations have violated human rights and utilized illegal, repressive tactics including detention, deportation, and violence against immigrant communities; Whereas, at its height, the DREAMer movement and organizing for DACA pioneered a range of pressure tactics including high-profile hunger strikes, occupations, and protests to shut down detention centers; Whereas, racial capitalism is the primary motivator for the currently escalating fascism both in the United States and globally (e.g. the oppression of pro-Palestinian activism meant to protect imperial US interests in the Middle East, the proliferation of the for-profit prison industry as a means for elites to gain wealth from human misery, etc.); Whereas, per its 2021 political platform, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) supports abolishing the police, ICE, and the carceral state; Whereas, DSA recognizes that the fight against fascism and for the right to political expression is inseparable from the fight for immigrant justice, and that defending the rights of immigrants is a cornerstone of anti-fascist struggle; Whereas, mass abolitionist organizing against police brutality and state repression, such as the George Floyd uprising, the Stop Cop City movement, and the 'Sanctuary Campus' campaign led by YDSA and National Students for Justice in Palestine (NSJP) demonstrate that the abolitionist movement continues to be an inspiring source of popular consciousness and a point of activation against fascism within the working class; Whereas, as socialists, we know that the only way to overcome fascism and escalating state repression is decisive and coordinated collective mass action and militant organizing within the working class and labor, social, and student movements; Therefore, be it resolved, that DSA will develop a robust national priority ‘Abolish ICE’ 2025-2027 campaign directed to: 1. Develop national Know Your Rights (KYR) materials available in the eight most commonly spoken languages in the United States that (a) offer citizen and non-citizen members regularly updated guidance about their rights, (b) suggest best practices to maintain operational and personal security in the face of rising fascism, (c) are regularly updated by a team of legal professionals and organizers with insight into relational support and communications, including representatives from the most impacted groups, such as immigrants and activists, and (d) identify capitalism, imperialism, and illegal US-backed sanctions as the root causes of immigration from the global south; 2. Develop a shared resource hub housing trainings on local power mapping, direct action, and other organizing tasks that can also be distributed to chapters organizing around abolitionist demands; 3. Support chapters organizing around ‘sanctuary city’ and ‘sanctuary state’ demands by helping to draft language for legislative resolutions introduced by DSA-endorsed elected officials, and support the NSJP-YDSA ‘Sanctuary Campus’ national priority campaign; 4. Enumerate learnings from successful immigrants rights/defense coalition efforts (e.g. CIRC in Colorado) into resources for chapters navigating coalitional migrant defense organizing; 5. Develop a toolkit for chapters to build local migrant defense coalitions and recruit & train members for migrant defense organizing, including KYR trainings, ICE Watch, rapid response coordination, and legal defense work; 6. Participate in national and local coalitions centered around the demand of abolishing ICE; and 7. Publish an analysis of the campaign prior to the 2027 convention via DSA’s publications highlighting successes, failures, and future work. Be it further resolved, that the National Political Committee (NPC) will select an ‘Abolish ICE’ campaign Steering Committee comprising 11 members: six members elected from an open application process by Single Transferable Vote as well as one liaison each (for a total of five) from the IC Migrant Rights Working Group, YDSA National Coordinating Committee, National Abolition Working Group, National Electoral Commission, and Mutual Aid Working Group, with priority given to members with lived immigration experience and born outside the US; Be it further resolved, that DSA will, through the relevant national bodies, support chapters in building local and state-level campaigns around abolitionist demands, such as: 1. Fighting for ‘non-reformist’ reforms that challenge the core function of the state, such as ending cash bail, increasing court transparency, cutting police budgets, and eliminating mandatory minimums; 2. Recruiting and running the electoral campaigns of explicitly abolitionist cadre candidates in service of an abolitionist and socialist electoral project; 3. Building coalitions with local abolitionist organizations, such as racial justice, immigrants’ rights, prisoner solidarity, and labor groups; 4. Creating public directories of resources including aligned legal advocates, mutual aid, case management, and other relevant support for undocumented or detained Americans and their families; 5. Developing programs of solidarity with incarcerated individuals (including, but not limited to, political prisoners and immigration detainees) within local prisons or ICE detention facilities through means of letter writing, visitation, and direct material support. Be it further resolved, that DSA will, with the support of YDSA and input of non-citizen members solicited by the NPC, create the Collective Defense Fund for the purpose of providing as-needed disbursements to chapters, aligned organizations, and other individuals for legal service or cash bail costs, alternative housing for suspended student protestors or undocumented students, or any other services relevant to abolitionist organizing deemed valuable by the NPC; Be it further resolved, that communications to members regarding resources available to chapters through the Collective Defense Fund and Abolish ICE campaign shall be issued to membership quarterly through the DSA co-chair newsletter and national social media; Be it further resolved, that DSA will prioritize broad, coalitional mass organizing with other groups in the progressive and Palestine solidarity movement spaces against the fascist Republican agenda through means such as mass demonstrations, direct actions, and strikes similar to the Inauguration Day ‘We Fight Back’ actions and the April 5 ‘March on Washington’ Day of Action, and the NPC will create a toolkit for anti-fascist messaging in conjunction with chapters and national bodies; Be it further resolved, that the NPC, National Communications Committee, and National Political Education Committee will coordinate independent DSA analysis of the escalating fascist repression of the Trump Administration, as well as organizing tasks for socialists and the working class under Trump, encompassing spaces for internal (e.g., Discussion Board, facilitated discussion circles) and external (e.g., competing pieces in Democratic Left or Socialist Forum) member deliberation and public-facing communications in the form of pitched op-eds to media outlets; Be it further resolved, that the NPC shall provide a status update on the ‘Strengthening Organizational Security’ section of the Strengthening and Expanding DSA: Navigating the Post-2024 Election Landscape Resolution by October 30, 2025 and provide a timeline for the completion of the parts not yet enacted; Be it further resolved, that Red Rabbits will collaborate with the NPC to expand the number of chapters capable of self-sustaining post-protest jail support organizing and community defense through a coaching and chapter liaison program; Be it further resolved, that the National Abolition Working Group and Red Rabbits will, with the input of local chapters, submit a report to the NPC within three months of this resolution’s passage detailing immediately actionable steps that DSA can take on local, regional, and national levels to better prepare the organization for a national uprising against federal agents and police brutality. Full Text Whereas, * DSA employs dozens of staff to help carry out the democratically-decided priorities of members and elected leaders. * Staff are a valuable resource that enable the stability and day-to-day function of DSA to an extent that would not be feasible with unpaid member labor alone. * Staff have some special resources, privileges, and platforms that most members do not have. This can present a challenge to DSA’s internal democracy when staff are also tasked with carrying out decisions of the organization that they personally may not agree with. * The NPC is the highest authority between conventions and has the greatest responsibility in ensuring accountability to our priorities and values in the allocation of staff resources. * In the years to come, as in years prior, the NPC will be regularly charged with making decisions about hiring, staff work, and the budget.

Resolved, * DSA affirms that the role of staff is to make members more collectively self-sufficient to deliberate democratically and pursue our mission and priorities. * All DSA staff are encouraged to participate in political deliberation and exchange of ideas in DSA and state their views openly, provided they do not use the special resources available to them in their role as staff to organize members towards positions that are not already the policy of DSA. * Whenever feasible, DSA will ensure that the resources, knowledge, and skills available to staff are made available to members. * When hiring staff, DSA will prioritize considering applicants who share the understanding of the role of staff as laid out in this resolution and who have a history of participation and leadership in DSA nationally or their chapter. Qualified on May 5, 2025, with 327 signatures as of May 11, 2025. Status: Adopted, as amended Summary This resolution lays out a political vision and tasks for DSA to orient around in the leadup to May Day 2028. Full text Whereas, Shawn Fain and the UAW have called for working people across the US to make May 1, 2028 a day of major labor action that has galvanized working class people nationwide; and Whereas, while a nationwide general strike is unlikely to happen on that date, it is a rare opportunity to have a set future date for class struggle that many working class people and working class institutions are at least rhetorically committed to, and Whereas, organizing towards May Day 2028 provides us a concrete opportunity to build rank and file class consciousness, cross-union organization, popular support, and renewed ties between the socialist movement and the labor movement; and Whereas, building towards May Day 2028 is the kind of national project, like M4A, Bernie, and Strike Ready, that can unify members and chapters in very different circumstances and can be adapted to a wide variety of conditions; and Whereas, DSA has a crucial role to play in moving towards and shaping May Day 2028 in a way that gets the working class in motion and builds working class consciousness, organization, and power Therefore be it resolved, DSA will adopt the following political orientation toward organizing to May Day 2028 1. Political Vision and Strategy. Rather than simply being an amalgam of a variety of individual contract campaigns, unified by a similar expiration date, May Day 2028 must be a moment of mass class consciousness and class action. 1. Over the next three years, DSA will dramatically expand working class consciousness and organization so that, come May Day 2028, the working class can take action to demand a political transformation. This means that we must not only build the organization to get people in motion over the next three years, but also craft the political vision of what that day can be. Our vision of May Day 2028 is the collective action of workers across the country in pursuit of a democratically-determined set of central demands. We must go beyond calling for mass action to lay the foundations and build the structures to make it possible. DSA will help bring together working class leaders to discuss and plan in a structured way, develop an ideological framework and resources to popularize May Day 2028, recruit and develop shop floor militants ahead of May 2028 labor activity, and serve as the home for the millions of as-yet-unorganized workers who may nevertheless want to organize towards this goal. 2. While segments of organized labor have embraced the task of organizing for May Day 2028, much of the labor movement remain aloof from the possibility of coordinated action. DSA, with thousands of members embedded in their unions and their workplaces, is uniquely suited to organize the working class towards May Day 2028 and to bring their unions along with them. We will seek opportunities to work with union leadership where our goals and tasks align, but our focus and priority will be to organize the rank and file of the labor movement and the broader working class ahead of May Day 2028. Not only is that what we, as a mass organization, are best suited for, it is also a recognition that the power of organized labor lies with the rank and file. A union’s membership can move its leadership on a political question far more easily than vice versa. 3. The success of May Day 2028 will depend less on the best laid plans of labor movement top brass and more on the degree to which rank and file workers in and out of unions take initiative themselves. That in turn depends on our ability to publicize both the call for the general strike and effective instances of rank and file participation; provide resources and coaching for rank and file workers who want to find ways to participate with their co-workers; and creative efforts to link immediate shopfloor concerns to broader political demands. Be it further resolved that DSA will commit to pursuing to following actions between now and May 1st 2028: 2. Maintaining a Strategic Vision 1. DSA’s National Labor Commission will continue to collectively develop an analysis of which areas of the economy and labor movement are the most strategic places for DSA members to get involved. 2. This analysis will be done with an eye to where DSA and its members can have the biggest impact on orienting the labor movement and working class towards mass action for May Day 2028 3. Chapters and chapter labor formations will be encouraged to engage in the NLC’s collective analysis and to develop their own analysis of local labor conditions, considering their area’s major industries, employers, and unions, the relationship between the political terrain and the public sector, and any major contracts set to expire over the next three years. 3. Unified DSA Preparation 1. DSA will coordinate among chapters and national bodies to ensure that our efforts and resources are used in a unified way to prepare for May Day 2028. 2. A National May Day 2028 Committee (MD28) will be established to do this coordinating work. 3. DSA will aim to anchor a May Day Convention in late 2026 or early 2027, in concert with major unions that have taken up May Day 2028 as a priority, of unions and other organizations, with a priority on rank and file representation, with the purpose of collectively establishing a plan and set of demands for May Day 2028. 4. Embedding in the Labor Movement 1. DSA will continue to encourage members to get jobs in strategic workplaces, industries, and unions, either as a part of a short- to medium-term salting effort or as a long-term commitment to becoming a shop floor militant. 2. DSA will provide members interested in getting strategic jobs support, including through national programs like Workers Organizing Workers and through chapter-level jobs pipeline programs. 3. DSA will support its members in organizing on the shop floor. Shop floor organizing should start with the concrete issues workers are facing, and ideally should ultimately connect those issues to a broader set of demands and fights that can unite workers nationwide for May Day 2028. 4. DSA members are encouraged to organize around May Day 2028 in their unions. This will look different depending on particular circumstances, but this might include passing a resolution to create a May Day Committee in their union to organize the membership in advance of 2028, lining up contracts to expire on or around May Day 2028, and organizing political education and political discussion events around their union’s political action, cross-union solidarity, and May Day 2028. 5. DSA chapters and chapter labor formations shall be encouraged to conduct thorough mapping of where their members are concentrated, and promote trainings supported by the NLC and workshops that help rank and file members in less-engaged unions to get engagement in their workplaces. Where capacity allows, chapters and chapter labor formations will be encouraged to hold frequent May Day themed workers circles for rank and file workers to engage their co-workers around actions that advance their power on the job and build out the movement for a general strike. 5. Cross Union Organizing 1. DSA members are encouraged to organize cross-union rank and file networks and spaces to organize for May Day 2028. This can look like groups of rank and file workers and local unions coming together to develop an analysis of local conditions, local demands, and shared work, including but not limited to solidarity, new organizing, ballot measures, and local candidates, to build up our strength and power in the leadup to May Day 2028. It can also include industry-specific networks like the Federal Unionists Network organizing around sectoral issues. 2. DSA will nationally and locally build worker committees for particular strategic employers, industries and unions to coordinate around shared work and support each other in our organizing at work and in our unions. This will help our members organizing in their workplaces and their unions stay with it for the long haul to spend the next 3 years building towards May Day 2028. 6. Labor Solidarity 1. DSA will continue to do the kind of broad labor solidarity work we’ve done locally and nationally, including examples like our Strike Ready Campaign for the UAW’s Big 3 Auto Strike. Our work will prioritize supporting unions at the level of the rank and file to be able to stay on strike one day longer than the boss and will serve as a way to get our members who otherwise aren’t involved in the labor movement engaged in class struggle. By showing workers nearing or actually going on strike the power of class consciousness and class organization, and by giving working class people outside of organized labor an onramp into labor struggle, we will bring the working class together in class struggle as we build towards May Day 2028. 2. We will conduct this work both in our chapters, with local labor formations encouraged to use an analysis of local conditions to figure out what labor struggles they can be most useful in providing solidarity, and in our national organization, building on the work of our Strike Ready campaigns and the Solidarity Captains network. 7. Political Education and Agitation 1. DSA will develop materials for agitation and political education around the need to build class power ahead of May Day 2028. We will produce both materials that can be used in one-on-one organizing and in meetings as well as mass communications materials, including images, short videos, posters and flyers to assist members in having political discussions directly with their coworkers, community, and those they meet at actions. 2. Chapters will use these agitational materials and hold political education events directed at the broader working class, particularly in the aftermath of large actions (e.g. May Day rallies, anti-Trump protests) that can provide a political context for the present moment, a vision for the future, and a theory of change for how we get there. National DSA will, through the NPEC and the MD28, provide materials for chapters to do these events. 8. Tenant Union Involvement 1. Between 2025-2027, the Housing Justice Commission (HJC) in collaboration with the MD28 shall facilitate participation by DSA members in the tenant movement in national organizing trainings, conferences, and other programs aimed at supporting preparations for a May Day 2028. 2. The HJC shall coordinate with chapters to map out the presence of and their relationship with local tenant unions. 3. The HJC shall work with chapters and tenant unions to map out Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) properties with expired covenants, or covenants that will be expiring in the next several years in that are prime targets for organizing, and develop LIHTC-specific resources for the Emergency Tenant Organizing Committee. 4. The HJC shall develop draft resolutions for tenant unions to adapt and pass pledging support for May Day 2028 and develop their union's strategy for how they will be involved in labor actions and coalitions that year. 9. Chapter Capacity Development 1. Between 2025-2027, the Growth & Development Committee (GDC) in collaboration with the MD28, and any other relevant bodies as determined by the National Political Committee, shall coordinate chapters to engage in regular structure tests to increase internal strike preparedness, strengthen local coalitions, and develop capacity for supporting local strikes. 2. The GDC shall develop trainings and resources related to mobilizations for May Day as well as other significant dates such as International Women’s Day, Trans Day of Visibility, and other high-turnout annual mobilization dates which engage the multi-racial working class. 3. The GDC shall develop new strategies and tactics based on the Organizing Fairs conducted in Spring 2025 with a goal of engaging a broad range of left-wing and labor organizations in directly recruiting and onboarding new organizers into mass work projects related to building labor, tenant and community organizations. 4. The GDC shall encourage and provide space for chapters to report back via writings and group discussions on their experiences to learn from successes and failures in participating in these coalitions, mobilizations, etc. Capacity Commitment & Financial Impact Scores Capacity 4: High Finances 4: Greater than $50,000 The resolution is ranked a 4 for capacity commitment, as it entails sustained national coordination, deep chapter engagement, and long-term rank-and-file organizing infrastructure. It establishes a new national May Day 2028 Committee, tasks DSA with coordinating strategic labor organizing efforts across chapters, supports member salting and shop floor activity, and calls for a national convention with union partners to plan shared demands and action. It is also ranked a 4 for financial impact, primarily due to the costs associated with convening an additional national convention, producing education and organizing materials, and supporting new programs. Full text Whereas, Donald Trump has returned to the White House, launching unprecedented attacks on democratic institutions, the public sector, marginalized communities, and working people broadly on behalf of the billionaire class, which have fueled greater popular resentment of the current US political and economic order and contributed to a growth in class consciousness. Whereas, the failure of the Democratic Party leadership to seriously resist the Trump administration has galvanized the Democratic base against the party establishment. The Democratic Party's favorability has dropped to record lows, creating new openings for independent political organization. The current political moment demands that DSA work to cohere the working class around a new political opposition movement against both Trumpism and the Democratic Party establishment. Whereas, presidential campaigns present a crucial opportunity for socialists to spread our political vision. They can grow an organization’s membership and deepen its bench of down-ballot electeds. The 2016 and 2020 Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns were the most important factors in the growth of the modern socialist movement and modern DSA. Whereas, the lack of a viable left-wing challenger in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary was extremely detrimental for the left and the working class broadly. DSA was left in the difficult position of critiquing the two candidates of the status quo without organizing workers around our own alternative left candidate as a positive example of our political vision. Whereas, the Zohran Mamdani mayoral campaign shows the opportunity that executive office races present in reaching ordinary people and growing DSA’s profile. The Zohran campaign also shows that more work must be done in theorizing how exactly DSA should relate to a candidate’s campaign and vice versa, how to translate the momentum from a campaign into long-term growth for the organization, and how to coordinate our electeds into a single unified block behind a campaign. Whereas, Senator Bernie Sanders and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, two of the country's most well-known democratic socialists, have traveled the country to rally support for a new political opposition movement against the Democratic establishment. Sanders has stated he intends "to rally people to get engaged in the political process and run as independents outside of the Democratic Party," and the tour has drawn enthusiastic support from tens of thousands of workers. Whereas, with Congressional Democrats at record low popularity, the upcoming 2026 midterm elections present a unique opportunity for electoral success for DSA and the broader Left. Whereas, the 2028 presidential election presents an important opportunity for DSA and the left more broadly to field a serious challenger. A presidential campaign can grow DSA, raise the profile of our down-ballot candidates, popularize our socialist platform, and amplify class conflict between the Democratic Party’s capitalist donors and its increasingly unified working-class and left voter bases. Whereas, the 2028 election also presents an important opportunity to further the merger of the socialist and labor movements, and lay the foundations for a future left-labor party. With the election season coinciding with Shawn Fain’s 2028 May Day strike wave, socialists have an opportunity to connect the economic struggle of labor with political struggle, channeling the economic demands of labor into a political platform. Resolved, DSA should aspire to build a broad left-labor coalition, composed of labor unions and other mass organizations, which can draft a platform; recruit candidates for federal, state, and local office for the 2026 and 2028 elections; and draft a socialist candidate for the 2028 presidential election. In order to gain real traction and look more like Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns than past third-party campaigns, DSA should back a viable candidate in the Democratic presidential primary, such as a nationally known elected official, labor leader, or public figure, who will primarily publicly identify with and promote DSA, socialism, and/or a left-labor coalition rather than the Democratic Party. DSA will advocate for such a coalition to endorse independent and nonpartisan down-ballot candidates as well as candidates running in Democratic primaries. Resolved, DSA shall work to build this coalition as a formal electoral alliance of the working class and the political left in the United States. DSA shall reach out to labor unions, political parties, mass organizations, and notable public figures about forming such a coalition to run a slate of candidates in 2026 and 2028, including a possible presidential candidate. Outreach should prioritize: * Guest organizations represented at the 2025 DSA Convention * Labor unions such as UE, UAW, NNU, SEIU and CWA * Political parties such as the Vermont Progressive Party and the Working Families Party * Democratic Socialist elected officials and public figures, including Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and other Squad members Resolved, DSA shall work to align and cohere our allies into a unified federal political coalition through our work on immediate political tasks including coordinating grassroots activism, pressure campaigns and national days of action to oppose and defeat the Trump administration's fascist initiatives. DSA will advocate for expanding the Fighting Oligarchy tour and existing nationwide protests into a sustained campaign of rallies and mobilizations against fascism throughout the duration of the Trump administration, building towards the 2026 and 2028 elections. Resolved, the NPC shall form a multi-tendency exploratory committee tasked with reviewing the lessons of the 2016 and 2020 “DSA for Bernie” campaigns and explore the different possibilities for a 2028 DSA Presidential campaign (including the relative merits of an ‘independent expenditure’ campaign vs. a campaign in direct consultation with the candidate). The committee shall include at least 1 national co-chair, 3 at-large NPC members and 2 representatives from the NEC. The committee shall submit a report to the NPC prior to the 2027 convention. If DSA decides to endorse a candidate for the 2028 Democratic primary, the committee shall draft a consensus resolution outlining the campaign for the 2027 DSA convention. Resolved, DSA shall seek to form a broad left-labor coalition to run a presidential candidate and other federal candidates, but is not precluded from running federal candidates without one. If a labor-left coalition emerges, DSA should advocate for it to continue and grow through the course of the 2028 elections, toward a long-term goal of forming an independent working-class political party. Resolved, the NPC shall appoint DSA’s representatives to any national coalition body. If a coalition that DSA is a member of decides to endorse a presidential candidate, the NPC shall hold a national all-member referendum on whether to endorse that candidate. Resolved, the NPC shall develop a communications plan for DSA to publicly agitate for the creation of a broad alliance of the left and labor in the United States, including an NPC statement, social media communications, and a pamphlet modeled after the Rank and File Strategy and Workers Deserve More pamphlets. Resolved, if there isn't sufficient interest in forming a broad left-labor coalition, DSA should still attempt to endorse a viable and politically aligned presidential candidate. Likewise, if there is no sufficient presidential candidate, DSA should still attempt to cohere a larger left-labor coalition. Full text Whereas, a united front tactic has been instrumental throughout history in fighting fascism and imperialism, and in achieving unprecedented democratic victories for the Left on unfavorable terrain (e.g., the 1967 United Front in West Bengal; Full text A resolution for a program for the Democratic Socialists of America to be adopted at the 2025 DSA National Convention. Whereas in order to build a new society, our organization must have unity around our goals and beliefs and an ability to explain our politics to people in our lives and communities. Whereas historical socialist parties have developed unity by adopting a program which explains capitalist society, includes demands which connect to present consciousness, and clearly states that the working class will need to conquer political power. Whereas although DSA passed a platform in 2021 and a program for the 2024 elections, DSA has not adopted a clear and precise general program yet. Whereas while DSA remains a broad-tent embracing a diversity of socialist tendencies, a DSA program must clearly explain how we will end the capitalist state and place the working class in control of society; Therefore be it resolved, that DSA will adopt a political program to replace both the 2021 Platform and Workers Deserve More to be the basis of political unity with the organization and to provide an explanation of our political aims to the working class; and Resolved, that DSA's program will be posted prominently on our website and on other materials, included in new member materials, and will be distributed widely among both our membership and the wider working class; and Resolved, that the program so adopted may only be changed at a DSA National Convention; and Resolved, that a Program Coordinating Committee will be established and tasked with promoting chapter use of the program; and Resolved, that Program Coordinating Committee will be further tasked with assisting chapters in adapting an immediate program to local and tactical conditions, providing a practical bridge between the struggles chapters engage in and the long-term political struggle waged by DSA; and Resolved, that DSA adopts the following as its program: POLITICAL PROGRAM OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA We live in a country run by a class of bosses and billionaires called capitalists. They have bought and run the Democratic and Republican parties, most news outlets, colleges and universities, and every branch of government from city halls to the Senate. They use their power to exploit the vast majority who work to live—the hundreds of millions of us who make up the working class. This system can only be ended by the working class taking political power from the rich and building a new society. We in the Democratic Socialists of America fight for that society: a democratic socialist society. Our wages are stagnant, our hours are long, and prices are only growing higher. We increasingly live paycheck to paycheck, one bad day away from financial ruin. And yet it is our labor that powers this unjust system. The capitalists who own the businesses we work at take all the profits for themselves and use them to control our society. This is the exploitation that defines the capitalist system. The capitalist system exploits Black, immigrant, and Indigenous people by dividing them from the rest of the working class. Millions of people of color face discrimination, unemployment, and police violence, locking them out of political power and an equal quality of life. Oppressive laws restricting abortion, marriage, and self-expression force women and queer people to choose between being controlled by their family or living in poverty outside of it. Different people face different kinds of oppression, but as members of the working class we all want to control the direction of our lives. Every law, policy, or practice that oppresses us for who we are stems from the capitalists’ control over our society and reinforces it. We all have a common interest against the capitalist bosses: their rule threatens our freedom and safety. To be able to defeat the ruling class and end their exploitation of our labor, we need to fight the oppression every working person faces in this country. No matter their race, gender, or sexual orientation, we stand side by side. Capitalism is a global system that exploits workers around the world. The most powerful capitalists use their wealth to influence governments into waging wars, toppling other governments, and starving entire peoples with sanctions and embargoes. They use this power to coerce other countries into selling their natural resources, labor, and goods for cheap prices. This imperialist exploitation forces workers of wealthy and poor countries to compete in a race to the bottom. We are united by a program of putting workers in control. In our fight against oppression and exploitation, we sit with our neighbors on rent strikes, stand with unions in strikes to win better pay and benefits, protest oppression, and feed our communities. We elect our own members to legislatures around the country to speak out against injustices while fighting for healthcare and cheap groceries. What We Fight for Today DSA fights all over the country for policies that will improve the lives of working people today. Environmental regulations must be enforced to protect our communities. Grant all nations and colonies within the United States the right to determine their destiny, including separation or joining the republic. 3. Full text Whereas, as democratic socialists living in the heart of the U.S. empire, we have a responsibility to follow the leadership of oppressed people in their struggles against harm perpetrated by the United States government. Be it further resolved, DSA nationally will engage in the broadest coalitions possible to further Palestine solidarity organizing while limiting deeper partnerships to organizations that endorse the BDS movement and support the three demands outlined in its introductory call: ending Israeli occupation and colonization of all Arab lands and dismantling the Wall; recognizing the fundamental rights of the Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel to full equality; and respecting, protecting and promoting the rights of Palestinian refugees to return to their homes and properties as stipulated in UN Resolution 194. Status: Referred to NPC Summary Since 2016 the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism has been used as a tool to instrumentalize Antisemitism against the left and chill anti-Zionist free speech. Despite past blunders DSA has an opportunity to play a key role against IHRA adoption. This resolution adopts the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism as an alternative and corrective to the IHRA Definition, and establishes an ad-hoc working group to coordinate pro-active organizing against IHRA adoption. Full Text Whereas 1. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is an anti-Zionist organization opposed to racism in all its forms, including antisemitism. 2. In 2016, the 31 member countries of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) adopted a “working definition” of antisemitism as a “non-legally binding statement.” 3. One of the primary authors of the IHRA Working Definition, Kenneth Stern, has himself denounced the codification of the IHRA Working Definition into law and its use as a “hate speech code” stating that it was intended only for gathering data, and identifies the codification as a part of a broader scheme of lawfare intended to chill anti-Zionist free speech through intimidation. 4. Today, the IHRA plays a role in the Trump Administration’s fascist attacks on free speech and academia, particularly Palestinian Americans, as guided by the Heritage Foundation’s “Project Esther,” a document endorsed by no major Jewish organization in the United States. 5. It is necessary for opponents of the IHRA, including DSA, to offer an alternative and corrective tool to the IHRA. 6. A group of “International scholars in antisemitism studies and related fields” have crafted the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism (JDA) as a competing definition seeking to: “respond to the Working Definition of Antisemitism adopted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) in 2016. ‘The IHRA Definition’ (including its “examples”) is neither clear nor coherent. Whatever the intentions of its proponents, it blurs the difference between antisemitic speech and legitimate criticism of Israel and Zionism. This causes confusion, while delegitimizing the voices of Palestinians and others, including Jews, who hold views that are sharply critical of Israel and Zionism...A definition unique for clearly demarcating certain examples of what does not, on the face of it, constitute antisemitism, including the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions, and opposition to Zionism.” 7. Many Jewish anti-Zionist and anti-apartheid organizations have made statements celebrating the JDA as a counterweight against the IHRA and a tool to combat the instrumentalization of antisemitism. These organizations include Jewish Voice for Peace, If Not Now, International Jewish Anti-Zionist Network, and Diaspora Alliance, among others. 8. No other anti-Zionist organization in the US has DSA’s direct relationship with local and state level elected officials or cadre members elected to public offices. 9. In the past DSA chapters have been caught flat-footed by pushes for adoption of the IHRA Working Definition. In 2022, when DSA Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman voted for a resolution adopting the IHRA definition at the municipal level, it was large part because DSA LA was unprepared to educate or direct their Socialist in Office (SIO) on the topic. The incident eventually resulted in Raman’s censure by her chapter. 10. There have long been efforts by organizations aligned with DSA such as JVP’s “Fight antisemitism, reject the ADL” campaign that have sought to counter the efforts of Zionist lawfare groups and IHRA adoption. Therefore, be it resolved 1. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) hereby adopts the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism as an alternative and in opposition to the IHRA Working Definition, and as a framework to fight against both the instrumentalization of antisemitism as a cudgel against the left and antisemitism itself however it may manifest, including JDA’s FAQs, which include the guidance that: 1. The JDA may be used for a number of purposes, including “education and raising awareness about when speech or conduct is antisemitic (and when it is not), developing policy for fighting Antisemitism, and so on. It can be used to support implementation of anti-discrimination legislation within parameters set by laws and norms protecting free expression.” 2. But the JDA may not be used as a “hate speech code”...“nor should it be codified into law, nor used to restrict the legitimate exercise of academic freedom”…”nor to suppress free and open public debate”. 2. DSA shall establish the Fight the IHRA, Fight Antisemitism Working Group (FIFAWG) as an ad-hoc national working group with a 2 year mandate. 1. The NPC is charged with appointing, by a process of open application, a 5 member Organizing Committee of DSA members with relevant knowledge and experience which will govern the FIFAWG. 2. Following its appointment the FIFAWG Organizing Committee shall open applications for general membership. 3. The FIFAWG is charged with: 1. Creating resources for local chapters to educate their electoral committee leadership, Socialists in Office, and chapter leadership about the IHRA Working Definition and how to organize against it. Resources and information may be sourced from potential organizations with prior experience on this issue such as the Diaspora Alliance. 2. In collaboration with the NEC, holding at least 1 online training for local electoral committee leadership, Socialists in Office, and chapter leadership on why and how we must proactively oppose the IHRA Working Definition, and the instrumentalization of antisemitism. 3. Developing a framework to guide local DSA chapters and YDSA chapters in building local coalitions with interested groups such as Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP) and If Not Now (INN) chapters, local Palestine solidarity coalitions, independent Jewish Community Centers, and friendly synagogues against IHRA adoption at the local level (municipal, state, university, etc). 4. Identifying opportunities for DSA chapters to oppose the IHRA Definition and push organizations and municipalities at the local level that have adopted the IHRA Definition to either rescind their adoption or adopt the JDA as a corrective. And whereas, this deficit was resolved only through months-long, frequently vitriolic debate over budgetary priorities and extensive budget cuts which touched nearly every aspect of DSA’s work. And whereas, the National Convention has frequently attempted to create new staff positions without a complete understanding of the existing staff structure of DSA or a clear vision for their job duties, leading the NPC to ignore many hiring requests made by the Convention in favor of requests made by prior director-level staff. And whereas, in the course of the conflict over the 2024 budget, the right of DSA’s rank and file members to perform work within DSA has been called into question. And whereas, DSA has in the past spent frivolously on an external contractor charging rates well in excess of the cost of an additional staff member for a role initially intended to be filled by a member of DSA’s staff. And whereas, rank and file DSA members and even Convention delegates are not always aware of the full scope or functions of DSA’s staff, which limits the degree to which membership can exercise meaningful democratic oversight over the national organization. And whereas, DSA has in the past hired to a degree which we lacked the financial stability to confidently maintain over the long term. And whereas, DSA’s financial situation is significantly influenced by the external political situation in the United States, over which we have limited control. And whereas, for DSA to provide stable employment and stable access to organizing resources under these circumstances requires a degree of financial caution beyond what would normally be found in a 501c non-profit. And whereas, DSA is built by the contributions of its members through dues, which fund both national and local work, and strengthening the amount returned to chapters is essential to reinforcing the foundation of DSA as an organization – its members and chapters. And whereas, democratic, participatory budgeting is essential to ensuring that DSA’s expenditures reflect the priorities and values of its membership. And whereas, a full budget includes both income and expenses, and consists of dozens of technical line items that are difficult to meaningfully debate at Convention; moreover, financial projections—particularly dues income—are often uncertain until after Convention due to unpredictable political conditions, making it impractical to adopt a detailed line-item budget in August. Therefore be it resolved, that DSA adopts the following reserve policies: * DSA should seek to have 8 months of operating expenses in reserve. * If DSA’s reserves reach 6 months of operating expenses, an automatic budgeting process will be triggered with the goal of restoring positive net cash flow within 3 months. Be it further resolved, that DSA adopts the following policies regarding staffing: * Staff salaries and benefits, excluding full time paid leadership, should generally not exceed 40% of DSA’s recurring dues income. * Total staff salary and benefit expenditures, including full time paid leadership, should generally not exceed 60% of DSA’s recurring dues income. * The NPC may not create any new staff position which would cause staff salary and benefit expenditures, excluding full time paid leadership, to exceed 50% of DSA’s recurring dues income, and if staff expenditure exceeds 50% of DSA’s recurring dues income a hiring freeze will automatically go into effect. * All direct employees of DSA, including full time paid leadership, should have job descriptions published in a manner accessible to the general membership of DSA. * DSA should generally avoid contracting out or hiring additional staff for functions which could be performed by rank and file DSA members. * No external contractor may be hired for a continuous, long term, full time position which could be filled by an employee of DSA. External contractors should only be hired for functions with sporadic or unpredictable workloads, temporary functions, or functions with workloads that are sufficiently small that employing a contractor would be substantially cheaper than hiring a direct employee of DSA for the same task. Be it further resolved, that the above policies are intended primarily to limit hiring, and should not be used as sole justification for a reduction in existing staff expenditure. Be it further resolved, that DSA is not only member-led but member-run. The National Convention recognizes the essential role of rank and file members in organizing DSA at every level. Be it further resolved, the NPC is instructed to seek explicit acknowledgement of the right of rank and file DSA members to perform work in DSA in all future collective bargaining agreements with the DSA Union. Be it further resolved, that the National Political Committee is prohibited from adopting any contract with any party which would categorically bar rank and file DSA members from an area of work in the national organization, though it retains the authority to determine the division of labor between staff and rank and file members within national DSA and the specific conditions under which members may have access to DSA resources and member information. Be it further resolved, that any income that exceeds the staffing thresholds outlined above will prioritize increasing dues share payments and direct grants to chapters before allocating funds toward additional national staff, consultants, or administrative expansion. Be it further resolved, that the NPC and DSA staff union are encouraged to explore mechanisms for regular, transparent communication to strengthen mutual understanding and coordination, which may include joint meetings, designated liaisons, or other mutually agreed processes that respect the boundaries of the collective bargaining agreement, reciprocity and organizational governance. Be it further resolved, that DSA adopts the following policies and standing rules regarding budgeting: * The NPC will present to all future National Conventions a Spending Framework based on clearly defined Spending Categories, each expressed as a percentage of projected recurring dues income or total operating expenses for the following year for debate, amendment, and ratification. These categories shall reflect the strategic goals, resource needs, and political direction of DSA as determined through member engagement, chapter resolutions, and organizational experience. * Each Spending Category may include, but is not limited to: staffing (excluding or including leadership), organizing and regional work, administrative costs, political education, communications, and other relevant areas. The Convention may establish minimums, maximums, or target ranges for each category, allowing the NPC discretion to allocate funds within those parameters based on evolving conditions. * One full debate block will be allocated to the debate, amendment, and ratification of the spending framework at future National Conventions. * Any resolution calling for new spending in excess of $50,000 dollars which is not included in the proposed spending framework must be accompanied by an amendment to the accounting category for that spending, which may be approved, amended, or rejected independently of the underlying political content of the resolution. * Resolutions calling for new spending of less than 50,000 dollars may be considered as single resolutions, separate from the framework process, but passage of such a resolution will still cause the draft framework category to be amended to reflect any such spending, as necessary. * Spending frameworks passed by the Convention may be amended by the NPC to account for changes in DSA’s financial situation, organizing needs, or the external political situation. * Changes to the spending framework by the NPC should not disregard the basic political intent of the Convention’s budgetary decisions. Be it finally resolved, that the NPC and Budget & Finance Committee will investigate the feasibility of proposing and passing a full budget at future Conventions and moving to a biennial budgeting process, and will implement one if feasible. Appendix I: Capacity and Financial Scores Table of Capacity and Financial Scores Please refer to this spreadsheet: DSA 2025 Convention - Cost Out Report Scoring Explained The Budget & Finance Committee is happy to introduce the replacement for the “cost-out” process at the National Convention. At previous conventions, each resolution was individually “costed out” in isolation, often through detailed staffing hour estimates and financial spreadsheets. This system was time-consuming, confusing for delegates, and ultimately didn’t give a clear picture of how different resolutions interacted or added up in terms of total organizational impact. In conjunction with staff, Budget & Finance has decided to move away from the old cost-out system because it wasn’t helping delegates make informed, strategic decisions about what the organization could realistically afford to implement. Resolutions were often passed with staffing or spending mandates that exceeded our actual capacity. The replacement to the cost-out process is a clear, two-part scoring matrix that assesses: * Staffing and member capacity required (rated 1 to 4) * Non-current personnel financial costs (also rated 1 to 4) Each resolution will be scored in these two areas, and those scores will appear alongside each resolution during convention. This new system gives a holistic, accessible view of the practical impact of what we pass—without burying delegates in spreadsheets. Amendments are scored based on how it would affect the overall scoring of the underlying resolution if adopted. You can find the combined Cost Out Scores here! 2025 Convention Resolution Scoring Matrix Process Each resolution and accompanying amendments will receive scores in two categories as outlined below. These scores will be decided through consensus between staff, B&F and the Personnel Committee, and short explanations with backup information will be provided for each score so delegates understand how values were assigned. Capacity Commitment (Staff + Member Time) This category evaluates the total time required from both staff and members to execute the resolution. The scoring reflects the overall effort, combining staff coordination and member involvement. 1: Minimal * Staff: No significant involvement or minimal coordination required. * Member: Requires only a single action from members (e.g., a vote or one-time event participation). * Example: A resolution that requires a one-time vote or minimal member input 2: Low to Moderate * Staff: Some staff involvement needed but manageable by existing staff without significant strain. * Member: Requires minimal to moderate participation from the membership (e.g., attending a couple of meetings, completing a few tasks). * Example: A resolution that asks members to attend a few events or participate in a simple project, with minimal staff coordination. 3: Moderate to High * Staff: Involves moderate staff time and coordination (e.g., organizing multi-step initiatives or programs). * Member: Requires moderate to substantial participation from members (e.g., sustained volunteer efforts, multiple events, or ongoing actions). * Example: A resolution for a grant program and members to participate regularly in related actions. 4: High * Staff: Requires significant involvement from existing staff or the hiring of new staff. * Member: Requires heavy or ongoing time commitment from members, such as forming a new national body or long-term project participation. * Example: A resolution calling for major structural changes or national-scale mobilization, demanding substantial staff coordination and member engagement. Financial Impact This category assesses the financial costs and resource utilization beyond current personnel time. Each will be an estimate per year. 1: Less than $5000 * No additional financial cost or uses an existing resource (e.g., free software, in-kind donations/resources). * Example: A resolution that does not require financial expenditure or uses only existing resources that don’t require fee per use.

2: $5000 to $10,000 * Requires small spending or uses a limited amount of finite resources that can be easily managed. * Example: A resolution requiring small-scale purchases (e.g., printing, supplies for a single event). 3: $10,000 to $50,000 * Requires moderate financial outlay or substantial use of finite resources (e.g., marketing, external consulting). * Example: A resolution that needs funds for multiple in-person events, moderate campaigns, or external consultant fees. 4: Greater than $50,000 * Requires significant expenditure or major use of finite resources (e.g., large-scale campaigns, hires, major infrastructure investments). * Example: A resolution that requires large funds for national campaigns, extensive travel, consultant fees, hiring of new staff positions, or major infrastructure upgrades. scoped_text: R34: Workers Deserve More, Forever: For a Coherent and Continuous Program Befitting DSA’s Political Growth Submitted by Michaela B (NNJ), Alex P (NYC), Zev R (NYC), Oren S (NYC). Qualified on May 6, 2025, with 276 signatures as of May 11, 2025. Status: Adopted Summary This resolution would enshrine the Workers Deserve More Program as DSA’s platform. It also creates a committee to propose edits based on political commitments made by delegates at convention to the NPC, coordinate a public campaign to popularize Workers Deserve More using digital, press, print, video and social media interventions, and create political education training events to ensure WDM is incorporated into chapter campaigns and DSA elected officials’ platforms. Full text Whereas: Socialist and labor parties throughout the world have political programs that analyze history and political economy, put forward a coherent vision of the world they are fighting for, immediate demands to help get there, and a strategy to achieve both. These are written in a language accessible to broad layers of people outside the organizations and often include design elements that are transferable across mediums and easily recognizable. DSA’s organizational strategy has long included the promotion of some form of “Where We Stand” document or “platform” that explains what DSA is and what we are trying to do, versions of which are on our website and in many of our chapters’ bylaws. The resolution “Defending Democracy Through Political Independence” passed in 2023 resulted in the formation of a multi-tendency “For Our Rights Campaign Committee” (FORC) which successfully produced the short program “Workers Deserve More” (WDM) for 2024, outlining DSA’s current and evergreen political and social stances and demands in readable, attractive prose and artwork. Since the task of writing WDM was completed, FORC has been dissolved. Chapters and priority committees across DSA have found the printed booklet and the online version of WDM invaluable organizing tools to advertise DSA to newcomers, educate and orient new members, and as a guide for debate and deliberation among active members, and have innovated various short versions (eg palm cards) and digital media to further the WDM message and represent DSA as an independent political organization. The 2025 convention is the occasion for our organization to pass our 2025-27 agendas and elect our new leadership, and until the entire convention is over and any changes to our priorities are tallied and published, DSA does not know what a current program reflecting our political growth and what we have committed to setting forward ought to contain. Be it resolved: “Workers Deserve More” will remain the name of DSA’s program indefinitely, replacing all other organizational documents that represent our national platform and “Where We Stand” except within chapter bylaws, which may be amended according to the discretion of chapter members. The current WDM will stand as DSA’s political position statement until a new WDM is created to replace it. Future conventions retain the right to change the name of the political program. The NPC will hold an application period immediately after the new NPC is seated, starting in 2025 and ending 30 days thereafter, for an 13 member Program committee. The makeup of the Program committee will be: * one member of the GDC steering committee * one member of the IC steering committee * one member of the NEC steering committee * one member of the NLC steering committee * one member of the NPEC steering committee * four members of the NPC, including one YDSA co-chair and one DSA co-chair * four at-large members in good standing and will be approved and seated by the full NPC within two weeks of the conclusion of the application period. Committee members will be elected by the relevant bodies and submitted for NPC approval, and NPC and at-large members will be elected by the NPC via STV. The Program committee will then elect 2 co-chairs. The tasks of the Program committee will be to: * assess all the political commitments delegates made at convention, and propose WDM edits to the NPC to clearly and accurately reflect priorities, demands, continuities and new perspectives in a document that generally matches the length and prose style of WDM. * submit this document by December 1 of the same year for NPC approval * roll out a month long public national campaign to unveil the new WDM by February 1 of the year after convention, with digital, press, print, video and audio interventions, with support from the National Tech Committee, Democratic Left/Socialist Forum, the National Communications Committee and our national staff, as well as DSA-endorsed elected officials wherever possible * create and implement political education sessions and training to support rank and file members, DSA leaders, and DSA-endorsed electeds in the adaptation and use of WDM across our campaign and priority committees and chapters, in collaboration with the Democracy Commission and our national staff. The rollout of these sessions and training will begin by February 1 across the country, to take place relatively simultaneously over the course of a month. All curricular materials will be made available to DSA’s members in good standing. * oversee the distribution of WDM pamphlets to chapters, campaign committees, and the DSA store. After these tasks are completed, the Program committee will dissolve and the NPC members who had been on the committee will be primary liaisons and stewards to the organization’s various bodies and socialists in office to support and promote the effective use of WDM. In order to receive a national endorsement, electoral candidates will be expected to accept and promote DSA’s program, and align their own campaign platforms with its contents to the best of their ability. Capacity Commitment & Financial Impact Scores Capacity 2: Low to Moderate Finances 1: Less than $5000 This resolution received a 2 for Capacity Commitment due to the formation of a national Program Committee and the coordination required among multiple national bodies to produce and launch a revised political program. The most significant capacity demand comes from the creation and implementation of political education sessions and trainings for members and leaders across the country, in coordination with the Democracy Commission and national staff, all on a six-month timeline. It was scored a 1 for Financial Impact because the expected costs—such as printed materials and digital rollout—are relatively limited and can be absorbed within existing infrastructure, keeping expenditures under $5,000. [PDF page 2] DSA’s 2011 convention: Building socialism, forming comradeship, resisting corporate domination By Michael Hirsch Americana, a blue glass multi-story pile. As The hotel housing the convention was contemporary architecture and location, the area was capitalism regnant, situated in a right-to-starve state where unions are under the gun and socialism is a word used to scare the horses. No one was scared this time, as Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) held its 2011 biennial convention and marked its tasks and perspectives at a time when resistance, emboldened by the Arab spring, the Wisconsin mass demonstrations and the Occupy Wall Street movement’s confidence that “we are the 99 %” is on the rise. Inside the capacious convention hall, under a scarlet banner proclaiming “Obama is No Socialist, But We Are,” over 100 delegates and observers, including a far-right blogger from the misnamed Accuracy in Media, planned their fightback for the New Year. Delegates savored the impact of the Wisconsin protests that built massive resistance to the state governor’s union busting, the huge outpouring of opposition to Big Oil’s environmentally calamitous effort to import Canadian tar sands crude, and the full-bore effort of Ohio unions in defeating a draconian anti-labor law by an almost two-to-one margin in a high- turnout contest just days before the convention. And then there was Occupy Wall Street’s exemplary populist effort to speak for a disenfranchised majority, fan the proverbial flames of discontent and turn class war from a slur by the right into a description of a compelling left politics. If one thing crystallized the convention consensus, it was naming and targeting criminal mismanagement by the nation’s financial institutions, the laggard government response to the economic crisis, and resistance in the streets, on the job and ideologically to free-market fundamentalism and the plutocrats who benefit from it. Had the convention thought to adopt a theme song, a fitting one would have been Chumbawamba’s refrain “I get knocked down, but I get up again, you’re never gonna keep me down.” But this was no tub-thumping exercise. Washington, DC. page 2 • Democratic Left • Winter 2011

[PDF page 3] Delegates from some 22 states came not just to celebrate victories, but to work on planning the next ones. And work they did, in plenary sessions, workshops and widely advertised and well-attended public sessions. First things first. Delegates entertained a resolution blasting the state of Virginia for its 1993 legislation making it just one of five states denying public employees collective bargaining rights. The organization chose a northern Virginia site only after assurances from the hotel workers’ union that holding the convention there breached no boycott or compromised any organizing efforts, and comrades warmly talked union with hotel staff. The convention held several educational workshops, including training in the DSA economic literacy project. Now known as the ‘GET UP’ Project – Grassroots Economics Training for Understanding and Power,” it is an “each one teach one” out-of-the-box radical economics weekend training program aimed at enabling every DSA member to speak knowledgably about the origins of and solutions to the economic crisis. The convention also formulated plans to implement its priorities resolution (see sidebar, page 4). Delegates also passed two other resolutions. The first offered direction on how DSA should support the Occupy Wall Street movement. Delegates approved continuing to embrace the movement, as DSA members have done without hesitation nationwide, while suggesting in the spirit of solidarity a series of political demands that could give the movement a coherent political orientation. These included a public jobs program; bank nationalization; Medicare for all; the forgiveness of student debt; an end to foreclosures; substantial investment in clean energy; a progressive income and corporate tax structure; a tax on all speculative financial transactions; and the immediate enactment of worker-friendly labor law reform legislation. The second resolution made explicit DSA’s longstanding support for the gay liberation movement and its battle for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer (LGBTQ) rights. The resolution called for federal legalization of same- sex marriages; enactment of antidiscrimination laws in housing, jobs, education, and health care, including measures prohibiting religious beliefs from being a basis for justifying bias; repealing state sodomy laws and anti-lesbian and gay restrictions, including rights to parenting and recognition; and welcoming the formation of a DSA gay rights commission. Public events with high-profile speakers included a Friday evening forum at the magnificent St. Stephen and the Incarnation Episcopal Church, operated by a multiracial social activist congregation in Washington’s Columbia Heights section. The evening featured greetings from Metropolitan D.C. Central Labor Council President and longtime DSA supporter Joslyn Williams, who said he welcomed the audience to “America’s last colony,” adding that “the principles of Occupy America are the principles this organization espouses…America is just now catching up to the Democratic Socialists of America.” Democratic Left (ISSN 1643207) is published quarterly at 75 Maiden Lane, Suite 505, New York, NY 10038. Saturday’s dinner featured remarks by Washington Post columnist and DSA Vice-Chair Harold Meyerson, who gave a synthetic and well-received talk on the inherent tension between democracy and capitalism – this while competing with roaring bhangra music from a Sweet 16 party in the adjoining ballroom. The conference dinner also honored outgoing National Director Frank Llewellyn, longtime DSA labor activist Skip Roberts, former National Director Jack Clark, and incoming National Director Maria Svart. Workshops, which consumed the bulk of meeting time, centered on the DSA GET UP Project to fight the austerity agenda when it rears its ugly head again in the spring. Others dealt with resistance to attacks on public sector workers; countering voter suppression and the right wing’s manipulation of racism; tips on tabling and public recruiting; building strong locals; engaging in coalitions while maintaining one’s socialist identity; planning campaigns; working with traditional and new media, and implementing the YDS Affordable and Accessible Higher Education Campaign. Elected to serve on the National Political Committee – the leadership body described as “the engine room of the organization” – were Theresa Alt (Ithaca, NY), Stuart Elliott (Wichita, KS), Paul Garver (Boston, MA), Virginia Franco (San Diego, CA), David Green (Detroit, MI), Barbara Joye (Atlanta, GA), Frank Llewellyn (New York, NY), Dan Michniewicz (Pinckney, MI), Simone Morgen (Columbus, OH), Joseph Schwartz (Philadelphia, PA), and Peg Strobel (Chicago, IL), plus the two YDS co-chairs, Sean Monahan (Philadelphia, PA) and Jackie Sewell (Lawrence, KS).
