[PDF page 1] DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA 2019 National Convention Rules I. Preconvention Rules I.A. Delegate Credentials 1. The NPC has established a target goal of 1,000 delegates to the 2019 DSA National Convention. Of the total number of delegates, 100 delegates will be reserved for at-large delegates who are not members of a chartered chapter. The remaining delegates will be distributed among chapters using a delegate-to-member ratio of 1-to-51, or one delegate per every 51 members, based on chapter membership numbers determined by the National Director 4 months prior to the Convention (Tuesday, April 2nd, 2019). Locals with fewer than 51 members will be apportioned one delegate. Locals with at least 51 members will get one delegate for every 51 members or greater fraction thereof. That is, the number of delegates allocated to each local is the number of members of the local, divided by 51, rounded to the nearest whole number. As an example, a local with 149 members will get 3 delegates, and a local with 199 members will get 4 delegates. The National Director shall include these calculations in a delegate apportionment announcement to all members. 2. Locals may elect alternates so as to ensure that their delegation is represented in full strength, even if initially-elected delegates are unable to attend. Alternate delegates only gain voting rights if an elected delegate needs to surrender their responsibilities for any reason, either before the Convention or during. Some alternate delegates shall be allowed to attend the Convention, regardless of whether their duties as alternate delegates are needed. Observers cannot under any circumstances get voting rights, although some, such as National Political Committee (NPC) members, have speaking rights. 3. The National Office shall inform locals of the delegates apportioned to them as of four months prior to the start of the convention, Tuesday, April 2nd. 4. Locals shall conduct and supervise their own elections of Convention delegates and alternate delegates in accordance with the applicable provisions of the DSA Constitution and Bylaws not before the apportionment of delegates and no later than June 18th, 45 days prior to the start of convention. Locals will be advised that delegate elections should use a proportional representation method of election, and of DSA Bylaws Article VI, Section 3, which requires that they use the Hare method upon petition. Any member in good standing of a local may run for delegate and vote in their local’s delegate election. The National Office will offer to locals help with the use of OpaVote.com or a similar online election system to help them

[PDF page 2] conduct their delegate election, and will publish this offer in a communication to the full national membership. 5. Each local must report the result of its elections in writing to the National Office no later than June 23rd. The report must include full contact information, including an email address, for all delegates and should indicate if any delegate is requesting full or partial relief from the Travel Share requirements (outlined in future rules documents). 6. The National Office shall conduct and supervise the election of at-large delegates. A call for candidates for at-large delegates shall be sent to all at-large members no later than Friday, March 1st. At-large delegate nominations will be open 60 days, through Tuesday, April 30th. Candidates for delegate may submit a brief statement to be made available to voters. If at the close of nominations the number of candidates is less than or equal to the number of positions (taking into account the diversity requirements), the candidates will be considered elected by acclamation. Otherwise, no later than Thursday, May 2nd, the National Office shall administer an online Single Transferable Vote election using OpaVote.com or similar online voting system. Every at-large member will be eligible to vote in the election. Voting will be open through Thursday, May 23rd. As required by DSA bylaws, no more than one- half of the available positions for at-large delegates may be filled by men and one-fifth of the available positions must be reserved for national and racial minorities. Those candidates who have been elected shall be immediately informed of their election by the National Office. 7. No person not in good standing as a DSA member through the end of the convention may be seated as a delegate or alternate delegate. 8. Based on the reports of local delegate elections and the outcome of the at-large elections conducted by the National Office, the National Office shall prepare a temporary roster of delegates and alternate delegates, which shall be sent to delegates, alternate delegates, locals, commissions and officers of DSA no later than Friday, July 12th. 9. Challenges to the credentials of any delegate or alternate must be submitted in writing to the National Office no later than Friday, July 19th and shall be forwarded to the Credentials Committee appointed by the NPC for consideration. Challenges must either name individual delegates or alternates from one delegation, or may name any one entire delegation, and must include a reason for the challenge that applies to all the credentials challenged. Challenges may include replacement(s) for the delegate or alternate challenged, or challenges may seek to seat additional delegate(s) or alternate(s) as part of a delegation. However, challenges that would result in a delegation exceeding its apportioned number of delegates will not be valid. 10. At the opening plenary, the Credentials Committee shall report to the Convention any challenge(s) filed according to rule 9 and may report its recommendation concerning them.

[PDF page 3] There shall be no more than one speaker for and one speaker against each credentials challenge. 11. The delegates listed on the Temporary Roster of Delegates shall vote on the Credentials Committee's recommendations, except that no delegate may vote on a challenge to his or her own credentials. Upon acceptance of the Credentials Committee those persons listed on the Temporary Roster of Delegates who are not subject to successful credentials challenge shall become the Permanent Roster of Delegates. 12. Each Local delegation and the At-Large delegation shall elect a chair who shall be responsible for official communications with the Administrative Committee. I.B. Resolutions, Constitutional Changes, and Bylaws Changes 1. Any member or group of DSA members in good standing may propose changes to the DSA National Constitution or Bylaws electronically via Google Form between Saturday, March 2nd and Thursday, May 2nd. To be considered for debate at the Convention, proposed amendments to the Constitution or Bylaws must have a minimum of 50 signatures of support from DSA members in good standing. There is no limit on the number of Constitutional or Bylaws changes any member in good standing may sign as a supporter; however no individual may propose more than 4 Constitutional or Bylaws changes for debate at the Convention. Constitutional changes require a ⅔ vote of the Convention to pass; Bylaws changes require a 3/5 vote, but, in accordance with DSA Bylaws, the Bylaws may also be amended by majority at a National Convention if the amendments in question have been discussed at an NPC meeting at least three months prior to the Convention. 2. A Constitutional or Bylaws change should pertain to one topic. Constitutional or Bylaws Changes may propose to: (1) delete specified language from the Constitution and/or Bylaws, (2) add certain language in specified places to the Constitution and/or Bylaws, or (3) replace existing language with new language, indicating all the places in the Constitution and/or Bylaws where the specified language occurs. All supporting materials submitted along with Constitutional or Bylaws Changes (i.e. Whereas clauses) will be included in a compendium of Convention items released to the membership of DSA for background reading in advance of the Convention but not open to amendment. 3. Any member or group of DSA members in good standing may propose political or organizational resolutions electronically via Google Form between Tuesday, April 2nd and Sunday, June 2nd. To be considered for debate at the Convention, resolutions must have a minimum of 50 signatures of support from DSA members in good standing. There is no limit on the number of resolutions or amendments to resolutions a member in good standing

[PDF page 4] may sign as a supporter, however no individual may propose more than 4 resolutions for debate at the Convention. 4. The Resolutions and Amendments Committee will issue a resolutions template to guide resolution drafting. In keeping with Roberts Rules of Order Newly Revised, only the operative sections of resolutions (i.e. Be it therefore resolved clauses) will be recorded and subsequently published following the Convention. The Resolutions and Amendments Committee will work with authors of proposed Convention items to encourage authors writing on the same topic to combine items or adopt “friendly” amendments in advance of the Convention wherever possible. The Resolutions & Amendments Committee will release a compendium of proposed resolutions and bylaws and/or constitutional amendments to the membership of DSA no later than Sunday, June 23rd via email and on the Convention website. 6. Any member or group of members in good standing may submit amendments to Resolutions, as well as amendments to Constitutional and Bylaws Changes, electronically via Google Form until the submissions period for amendments closes Tuesday, July 2nd. To be considered for debate at the Convention, amendments must have a minimum of 50 signatures of support from DSA members in good standing. There is no limit on the number of amendments a member in good standing may sign as a supporter or submit for debate at the Convention. 7. If there are more than 10 proposed resolutions, changes and amendments, the Resolutions & Amendments Committee will poll the delegates as to which require more time for discussion and should be scheduled earlier, which could be included in a consent agenda. 8. The Resolutions & Amendments Committee will release a final compilation of all proposed Constitutional and Bylaws Changes, Resolutions, and Amendments electronically via email to the entire organization and on the Convention website by Friday, July 26th. 9. If major events occur too late for a resolution to be submitted through the above-described process, resolutions about them may only be considered under suspension of Rules.

[PDF page 5] I.C. NPC Nominations 1. The National Political Committee will release a description of the NPC and its members’ duties after the January NPC meeting. 2. Any DSA member in good standing may be nominated as a candidate for the NPC elections through a nominations resolution passed by a majority vote of either: (1) any chapter or OC; or (2) by a national committee, commission, working group, or the Afro-Socialist Caucus. Chapters and OCs are strongly encouraged to make decisions on nomination in a way that includes the broadest number of members as the chapter shall determine is practicable, such as at membership meetings or through membership-wide online votes. Nomination should not be seen as an endorsement of a candidate or their politics, but as an affirmation that the member is active in the work of DSA and is constructive and comradely towards their fellow members. To formalize their candidacy, each nominee must complete the candidate questionnaire furnished by the national organization between Tuesday, April 2nd, and Sunday, June 16th, including a copy of their nominating resolution signed and dated by the co-chairs or equivalent of either the local or national body issuing the nomination resolution. 3. Caucuses, Slates, & Interest Groups 1. The organizers of this Convention cannot and will not forbid the formation of caucuses, factions, or slates, but will not recognize them by offering any quasi-official platform space. 2. The National Convention program will set aside time and space for self-organized meetings. A caucus, regional group, committee, or any other ad hoc group may register for space to hold a self-organized meeting during this time.

[PDF page 6] II. Convention Rules II.A. Convention Committees 1. The Rules Committee has drafted these Rules and will remain available to interpret them. 2. The Resolutions & Amendments Committee receives resolutions submitted to the Convention and makes recommendations to the Convention on the disposition of resolutions and changes to the Constitution, Bylaws and resolutions submitted after the resolution deadline. Its work is detailed above under Resolutions, Constitutional Changes, and Bylaws Changes. 3. The Elections Committee oversees election of the at-large delegates and election of members to the National Political Committee. Its work is detailed above under Delegate Credentials 6. and NPC Nominations. At the Convention it will oversee voting for the National Political Committee. 4. The Credentials Committee is responsible for reporting to the Convention the roster of delegates and making recommendations on any properly filed challenges to the credentials of any delegate. The Credentials Committee may also make recommendations to the National Director concerning any need for subsidies for housing, registration fees or travel. 5. The Administrative Committee is responsible for making recommendations to the National Director regarding any issue that arises on the administration of the Convention, particularly recording credentials changes, such as in the event a delegate needs to transfer their voting credentials to an alternate. The committee will also make recommendations around issues of climate or accessibility at the Convention. Members of this committee shall include the Preconvention Program & Logistics Committee, DSA’s National Director, DSA national staff, and the Convention marshals team. Members of the committee will be stationed throughout the duration of the Convention at: (1) a credentials table outside of the main Convention hall; and (2) at a recording table at the front of the main Convention hall. 6. These committees propose their chairs at the beginning of the Convention. II.B. Program 1. The preconvention Program and Logistics Committee has broad discretion in designing the program. Certain parts, however, are required.

[PDF page 7] 2. An officer of the organization shall call to order the opening session of the Convention at which time the Convention shall elect one Chair for the convention, who may delegate the task of chairing for a period to someone from a pool of members trained for the task. 3. At the opening plenary, membership on all committees and chairs for each shall be confirmed by the Convention. 4. The Convention shall vote to adopt the II.D. Procedural Authority section of the Convention Rules. 5. The National Director shall submit to the Convention on its opening day a report on the activities of the staff since the 2017 National Convention. 6. The Secretary-Treasurer shall submit to the Convention on its opening day a report on the finances of the organization. 7. Reports by the NPC, by YDSA, and about the political situation in general are strongly recommended. A brief introduction to Robert’s Rules is also recommended. 8. The program will to the extent possible follow the recommendations of the Resolutions and Amendments Committee as to the order in which items are considered and the time allocated to each. II.C. Recording 1. The National Director of DSA shall work with the Administrative Committee to keep the official record of the Convention and may appoint assistants as they deem necessary following the Convention to form a Styles Committee responsible for editing small typos, punctuation, and grammatical errors, etc. and incorporating adopted amendments into the body of Resolutions and Constitutional or Bylaws changes. II.D. Procedural Authority 1. A quorum of the Convention shall consist of fifty percent plus one of the registered delegates and seated alternate delegates. 2. An accredited alternate delegate may be seated for a delegate temporarily or permanently. The permanent seating of an alternate must be reported immediately to the Administrative Committee.

[PDF page 8] 3. Each delegate and seated alternate shall be entitled to one vote on all questions coming before the Convention, except that each local chapter delegation may vote its full strength, provided that no individual casts more than three votes unless authorized to do so by the Convention. 4. Resolutions before the Convention shall be decided by majority vote of the delegates and seated alternate delegates present and voting. Proposed changes to the DSA Constitution shall require a ⅔ majority of present and voting delegates and seated alternates, and to the Bylaws shall require a 3/5 majority. All procedural motions shall be passed by the majorities required by Robert’s Rules of Order. 5. No secret ballot shall be conducted. No Convention committee meeting or Convention session may be closed to DSA members pending space capacity, except that any meeting or session may be deemed closed to press. 6. All votes other than election of officers shall be by hand with Voting Cards issued by the Administrative Committee. The Chair of the Convention session (see Rule II.B.2) shall determine the results of hand votes and report the results to the Administrative Committee as well as announcing it to the convention session. A vote will be recorded at the request of any delegate or seated alternate, or if in the judgment of the Chair it is warranted due to closeness of the initial count. The Chair shall appoint such tellers as needed to assist in the counting of the vote. 7. Roll call votes shall be conducted at the request of thirty percent of the delegates and seated alternates present and voting, and shall consist of a recorded vote by delegation and individual at-large delegates. 8. Only delegates, seated alternate delegates, NPC members, national DSA officers, and DSA staff members may speak on questions coming before the Convention in plenary session. Speakers on all motions shall be limited to two minutes, unless the convention accepts a different limit. 9. No amendments to Resolutions or amendments to Changes to the Constitution and Bylaws may be made from the floor (except in the event of the suspension of these rules pursuant to Robert’s Rules of Order). A Styles Committee shall be appointed by the NPC, subsequent to the convention, whose responsibilities will include, for instance, spelling and grammatical corrections and incorporating enacted amendments into the Constitution and Bylaws. All changes made by the Styles Committee shall be subject to approval by the NPC.

[PDF page 9] 10. Except as provided in these Rules, the Constitution or the Bylaws, the latest edition of Robert's Rules of Order, Newly Revised shall govern the proceedings of the Convention. 11. The Chair of each Convention plenary session shall be the sole interpreter of the Convention Rules. The administrative committee may provide for the appointment of a parliamentarian and such other assistants as needed to provide assistance as requested to convention chairs. 12. Any delegate or seated alternate may appeal any ruling of the Chair or of the Resolutions Committee to the Convention. In such instance, the person making the appeal may speak for up to two minutes to advocate the appeal and the Chair may speak for up to two minutes to defend the ruling. No other debate shall be permitted. The ruling of the Chair may be overturned by a vote in favor of the appeal by a majority of delegates and seated alternates present and voting. Challenges to a ruling by the chair shall be decided by majority vote of delegates present and voting. 13. The election for the NPC shall be conducted by preferential ballot. The Elections Committee shall count the ballots using an online voting system with a Single Transferable Voting method. All ballots from which the voter's preference can be clearly determined shall be counted. Ballots are not secret, so if ballots are not correctly filled out, the Elections Committee will help delegates to correct them. 14. In the event that the Convention is at risk of not completing all necessary tasks, the Resolutions and Amendments Committee shall be responsible for proposing schedule changes to ensure that Convention completes its needed work. 15. Constitutional and Bylaws changes and resolutions will take effect only after the Convention Minutes have been approved by the NPC. 16. There shall be no division of the house on procedural motions. II.E. Registration, Housing and Travel 1. Convention registration will open Thursday, May 30 and close Monday, July 1st. All delegates, alternates, NPC members, observers and DSA officers attending are responsible for paying the Convention Fee, which includes breakfasts and lunches. a. The regular registration fee is $263. Those who register by Thursday, June 20 can pay an early-bird regular Convention rate of $215. b. Low-income members whose chapters cannot subsidize their registration may pay $100, or if they register by Thursday, June 20 they may pay $65.

[PDF page 10] 2. Upon registration, each member will be given a link to book a hotel room directly through the hotel. Hotel booking too closes Monday, July 1st. The special rate for those attending the convention is $159.31 per night or $478 for three nights. a. The room rate is the same for one, two, three or four persons in the room. Therefore, with roommates the room rate can be as low as $39.83 per person per night or $119.48 for three nights. In exceptional cases, DSA will be able to book a room and thus put in payment and possible subsidy up front. 3. The Administrative Committee will administer the travel share system. The travel share is designed so that delegates who travel long distances or live in communities with less affordable flight access have their costs subsidized by delegates who have lower costs, thus equalizing access. Actual fares (or mileage at $0.58/mile for those who do not fly) will be averaged among all delegates, based on proof of payment or mileage calculation from point of origin. Those delegates and alternates whose intercity costs are lower than the average will pay the difference into the pool. Those delegates whose costs are higher than the average will be reimbursed for the difference, providing that they exercised reasonable diligence in their ticket purchase. Those who commute locally are also in the pool and will pay the average cost. All delegates and alternates must meet their obligation to the travel share before receiving and maintain their credentials for voting. 4. Any delegate whose chapter cannot afford to subsidize them may request a subsidy toward registration, housing or travel based on hardship, which will be considered by the Credentials Committee. Such requests must be submitted by June 23, 2019.

[PDF page 1] National Electoral Committee Report to the DSA National Convention Table of Contents Introduction - Page 1 National Electoral Strategy - Page 2 Subcommittee Reports - Page 4 ● Endorsements Subcommittee Report - Page 4 ● Chapter Outreach Subcommittee Report - Page 8 ● Training Subcommittee Report - Page 9 ● Compliance Subcommittee Report - Page 10 DSA In Office Network - Page 10 Looking Forward to 2019-2021 - Page 11 Introduction In April 2017, the National Political Committee (NPC) voted to end making ad hoc electoral endorsements and established the National Electoral Committee (NEC). The NEC’s role would be to research and make endorsement recommendations to the NPC Steering Committee (SC). Forty people initially applied to serve on the NEC, and the SC chose 10 to serve after considering experience and regional, age, and demographic representation. Following the passage of the National Electoral Priorities Resolution at the 2017 DSA National Convention in Chicago, the NPC was committed to expand the work of the NEC, including to support chapters’ efforts to develop and run viable openly socialist candidates for office. Committees were formed to focus on researching endorsements, designing and delivering electoral trainings, reaching out to chapters, and researching electoral and campaign finance laws. By the end of the fall 2017 cycle, DSA chapters around the country endorsed 32 candidates, 21 of whom won, and 6 of whom were endorsed nationally. Seeking to improve the work of the NEC and build on recent wins, electoral organizers from chapters across the country, including members of the NEC and NPC, came together to develop a new electoral strategy. The National Electoral Strategy (NES) put forth a model of electoral organizing for DSA centered around building a sustainable socialist political organization. Rather than loaning out volunteers to endorsed campaigns, DSA is to develop its independent electoral 1

[PDF page 2] capacity, accountable to the organization and democratically controlled by the membership. The NES unanimously passed at the January 2018 NPC meeting. In April 2018, the NEC held elections, expanding from a 14-member volunteer body to an elected 25-member committee. Since then, the NEC has hosted numerous trainings, endorsed dozens more candidates running at all levels of government across the country, and has worked one-on-one with chapters to kickstart their electoral programs. Recently, the committee along with national staff has helped form the DSA In Office Network to connect DSA electeds so that they can share lessons and experiences and build off of each other’s work. National Electoral Strategy Read full National Electoral Strategy here A survey of locals conducted in late 2017 revealed only a small number of chapters heavily engaged in electoral work and only a slightly larger number of chapters somewhat involved, but seeking assistance for how to best engage in electoral organizing. Hoping to build off of DSA’s 2017 electoral victories and expand chapter engagement in electoral work, the NEC brought together electoral organizers from across the country to develop a plan for growing our electoral victories in the coming cycles. From this organizing, the National Electoral Strategy was formed. Summary The NES is organized around the following principles: 1. National Locals will have the authority to choose their own electoral strategies. 2. The National Electoral Committee will be elected, transparent, and accountable, and its primary role will be to support locals in their electoral work through skills building. 3. The NEC will focus on helping to build each chapter’s capacity to create independent electoral structures and facilitating cross-local collaboration and communication. 4. Electoral work, as only one aspect of building power, will to the greatest extent possible be the natural extension of other local campaigns around issues like housing, racial justice, mutual aid, etc. The Strategy The NES outlines an “old model” of electoral organizing that DSA should move away from. In the old model, the goal of progressive and left organization is to elect as many candidates as possible who are sympathetic to left ideas by serving as a base of volunteers and donors. The result of such a strategy is a serious lack of candidate accountability: while candidates are 2

[PDF page 3] elected to office and have built the resources and networks to win reelection, the organizations have developed no mechanisms to meaningfully hold candidates accountable and are not larger, stronger bodies as a result of their electoral engagement. Instead, the NES recommends DSA follow a “new model” of electoral organizing focused around developing independent electoral capacity and building a sustainable socialist organization. The new model entails chapters building an independent field and canvassing operation around endorsed candidates. DSA locals should strive to build the tools and skills necessary to run a campaign: from running canvasses, to maintaining data, developing Democratic Socialist messaging, and conducting policy and opposition research. The goal of the strategy is twofold. First, it will allow chapters to break out of the electoral cycle. The skills necessary to run an electoral campaign are transferable to running issue-based canvassing, and the data collected during an electoral campaign is especially useful when developing targeted canvasses to push for issues. Second, the strategy will allow DSA to operate as an independent electoral force and build working-class power outside of the Democratic party. To quote the NES directly, “Discussion of independence from the Democrats tends to revolve around the question of the ballot line, but it shouldn’t: most party power rests not in ballot access as such but in the network of consultants, politicos, lawyers, and party functionaries who control the means of electioneering in each state. Like most in DSA, we see the ballot line question as a tactical one to be addressed by local chapters in accordance with local circumstances—but we consider it essential that DSA escape the welter of Democratic patronage networks that have controlled and limited politics in the US for too long. To operate independently of this network we need to build our own electoral capacity, democratically controlled by DSA. Ultimately, it is not the name of the party under which a candidate runs that governs their decisions while in office, but the material conditions that inform the composition and capacity of the groups that form their coalition.” While the NES outlines a philosophy for approaching electoral organizing, it is imperative that chapters develop their own strategies for running an independent field operation, answering the ballot line question, and identifying candidates to recruit or support that are based on local material conditions. Rather than mandating a one-size fits all approach, the NES encourages locals to experiment and adapt the strategy to their local contexts. The NEC will serve as a democratic, accountable, and transparent body focused on carrying out the NES. Through its work, it will amplify local electoral organizing and assist chapters in developing their electoral programs. To the end, the NEC will organize trainings, skill sharing, 3

[PDF page 4] and workshops, provide advice on compliance, facilitate cross-chapter communication, and work to boost and aid nationally endorsed campaigns. Subcommittee Reports Endorsements Subcommittee Members: Austin Binns (co-chair), Spencer Chan (co-chair), Christian Bowe, Jason Clayton, Allie Cohn, Jessica Culbertson, Marianela D'Aprile, David Greve, Devin McManus, Mark Masaoka, Alex Nagle, Adam Parsons Summary Since the creation of the National Electoral Committee in 2017, DSA has nationally endorsed 48 candidates and 1 Ballot Measure. Of these endorsements: ● 19 eventually went on to be elected (39%) ● 26 were defeated in a primary or general election or dropped out (53%) ● 4 (including the Tiffany Cabán campaign) are on-going (8%) Endorsement Process Chapters seeking the national endorsement of a locally endorsed campaign must complete the following national endorsement process. The process generally takes 5-6 weeks to complete in full, with the goal of publicizing endorsements no later than 4 weeks before the date of the election. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Chapters nominate a campaign for endorsement using this AirTable form: https://airtable.com/shrj2ko4sD5ErMdSY . Campaigns must have the support of a local in order to receive a national endorsement. The NEC Endorsements Subcommittee (NEC-ES) reviews the application and sets up a phone call with representatives of the local to discuss the campaign, including how the campaign builds upon the local’s organizing efforts, the local’s field plan, and any support the local is seeking from national. The Local is to complete the National Candidate Questionnaire, found at the end of the NES webpage. The local is also to complete a detailed campaign dossier detailing the state of the race and the local’s relationship and planned engagement with the campaign. Once the above documents are completed, the NEC-ES reviews them and votes on whether or not to recommend the endorsement to the full NEC. Next, the full NEC deliberates and votes on whether or not to recommend the endorsement to the NPC. Finally, the NPC deliberates and votes on whether or not to nationally endorse the campaign. If approved, national staff publishes the endorsement within a couple days. 4

[PDF page 5] Support for Endorsed Campaigns To assist nationally endorsed campaigns and their chapters, the NEC organized support such as fundraising emails, remote phone banking from other chapters and at-large members, and even a few weekend trips to knock doors. The worked with national staff to have graphics designed and to amplify the campaigns’ messages through social media. In many elections, these actions had small impacts, but in at least one election they likely made the difference: voters contacted due to remote phone banking efforts far exceeded the margin of victory. And in at least one other race, the margin was within a few phone banks short of a win. This is why we knock every door and make every phone call. Chanan Suarez - Bellingham City Council, Ward 5 (Whatcom DSA) Marguerite Green - Louisiana Agriculture and Forestry Commissioner (New Orleans DSA) Sean Parker - Nashville Metro Council, District 5 (Middle Tennessee DSA) Damon Krane - Athens City Mayor (Southeast Ohio DSA) Jivan Sobrinho-Wheeler - Cambridge City Council, At-Large (Boston DSA) Chapter Outreach Subcommittee Members: Lucas Pérez-Leahy (co-chair), Tascha Van Auken (co-chair), Peter Simon, Jay Clayton, Devin McManus, Janet Tucker The chapter outreach committee was created to open up regular dialogue with chapters so that the expertise of the NEC was accessible and so that chapters beyond those who knew to reach out could be trained by and consult the NEC. Starting in 2018, they worked on building up a list of electoral chapters and reached out by email and phone to every single chapter. It was a slow process, and many chapters did not respond despite repeated outreach, possibly due to outdated points of contact, especially since working groups are not in the practice of notifying National Staff when their leadership turns over like steering committees are. But far more chapters are in touch and know to ask the NEC for advice now. These regular calls from chapters, asking about everything from building an electoral working group for the first time to running a member for office, are still an almost weekly, if not more frequent, part of the NEC schedule. Much of this is thanks to the work of the chapter outreach committee. Recently the chapter outreach committee has been bottomlining Zoom calls with members to both share positive practices and further connect with members interested in forming electoral work. The calls, all recorded and put on with the help of training team members, included: -Cross chapter electoral check-in: In December of 2018 we held a call for chapters who did electoral work to report about their work on the call. 8

[PDF page 9] -How to build power through electoral work beyond the election cycle: We had Natasha Fernandez-Silber from Detroit DSA and Cea Weaver from NYC DSA speak about how electoral work contributed to other work in the chapter. -Chapter Bernie work: Renée Paradis joined the call to answer compliance questions first and then we discussed specific organizing questions and strategies that chapters were working through. -Local Endorsements: Several chapters gave report backs on their endorsement processes and then there was q&a for chapters looking to develop their own. One goal may be consolidating all of these resources into a single accessible place, perhaps better organizing the NEC resources folder and creating guides. Like most subcommittees in the NEC, the chapter outreach subcommittee suffered from loose ends when an electoral campaign would require a member’s full participation. Such is the danger of having folks experienced in electoral work, they often are still doing electoral work and have to step back as campaigns reach their peak months. Training Subcommittee Members: Abdullah Younas (co-chair), Chris Riddiough, Sarah Ganong, Katrina Bergstrom, Abdullah Younus, MaryCate Brower, Max Cotterill, Amelia Dornbush, Luke Hayes, Beth Huang, Jasmin Oppenheimer, Asher Ross, Tootie Welker The training subcommittee started the work of building resources for new chapters, though many members became busy with campaign work and it occasionally slowed. They put together videos on subjects such as DSA Campaign Strategy, Voter Registration, Recruitment Through Public Events and Movies, Research, and Expanding Active Chapter Membership Through Electoral Work. The subcommittee also held calls with members, such as one with DSA elected officials around the country, where they shared their experiences governing as socialists. They put together a folder with examples of literature, research dossiers, endorsement processes, and chapter tracking tools to show as examples to new chapters. 9

[PDF page 10] Compliance Subcommittee Members: Katrina Bergstrom, Renée Paradis The compliance subcommittee started out by sending compliance questionnaires to chapters and received 119 responses. After sorting through them all, they began regularly handling requests for guidance on election law, researching electoral law and providing support for local elections, chapter spending, and use of resources such as emails in support of National endorsed candidates. This was an essential service that helped develop chapter expertise and kept our work within the bounds of election law, provided in large part by volunteers. Our electoral work simply could not do without it and they stepped up to the plate. They continued to support chapters experienced and new through present day, but suffered attrition due to the massive workload and the difficulty of replacing folks when they got busy with lawyers who could properly fulfill the duties of the subcommittee. While the compliance subcommittee, combined with consultation of a lawyer, was able to handle requests so far, the workload will simply require a staff member in order to properly get done as DSA continues to grow, which is one reason why a compliance director is in the process of getting hired. Already the Bernie campaign has grown that work. The DSA In Office Network Built on the desire to build deeper relationships between DSA-endorsed and DSA member elected officials and their chapters, and work together towards common goals, the NEC came up with a plan for and began organizing meetings for the DSA In Office Network. They reached out to chapters and elected officials around the country and built up towards monthly calls in which elected officials would come together to discuss the challenges of governing while socialist, train each other, and plan the first major event of the network: The DSA In Office Gathering. At the DSA In Office Gathering, held at the same time as the convention, members from around the country will come to the convention to meet delegates, present a unified message to press, and go through workshops and discussions on subjects such as working with DSA chapters on pressure campaigns, organizing with your constituents against ICE, and strategic campaign strategy. 10

[PDF page 11] The NEC has already started to talk about a policy library of bills introduced by DSA members and endorsed by DSA chapters to combat the ALECs of the world, calls with members, and videos of the trainings at the Gathering. It is a new project, and will likely change a ton throughout the next two years. Looking Forward to 2019-2021 The National Electoral Committee built an entirely new endorsement system from the ground up and provided support for 48 campaigns from Hawaii to Maine. It regularly talked with chapters looking to build electoral working groups from the ground up. It brought elected officials from around the country together and began building that National Electoral Strategy together. There were bumps along the way in getting in contact with chapters, loss of capacity due to the way an electoral campaign can take away every hour of an organizer’s free time and leave loose ends, and unclear procedural structures sometimes gummed up the works even when everyone knew what they wanted to do. There are a ton of challenges for a new NEC, or whatever takes its place, to overcome, but we’ve seen it’s potential. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez lead to our largest membership spike by numbers in history. Chapters like Heart of the Valley doubled their size during electoral work one year, then elected the first openly non-binary elected official in history the next. One Chicago DSA Alderman became a caucus of 6 with an army of organizers alongside them. Sex workers canvassed alongside members for decriminalization and a Senator who would fight for it in Brooklyn, gaining national attention. Three new branches of Central CT DSA were built from conversations over a State Senate campaign. Black Lives Matter organizer khalid kamau was voted in to city council in South Fulton, GA and the architect of anti-Native American voter suppression laws was voted out of the North Dakota State House, replaced with Native American Ruth Buffalo. Rashida Tlaib and Detroit DSA stood side by side with GM Poletown factory workers. These races can jumpstart movement work and transform chapters. Ending cash bail, Just Cause Eviction, Paid Sick Leave, Elected Civilian Police Review Boards, local Green New Deals, all of these wins are power restored to the working class, lives saved, and a statement stronger than any focus group tested ad about where we stand. Their money can’t beat the recruiting power of our work. Electoral work can be transformative on a massive scale if we give it the support it deserves to flower in every chapter across the country. We’re not there yet, so let’s recommit ourselves to getting there. 11

[PDF page 1] DSLC SC Report The following is a summary of written assessments from DSLC SC members regarding the first iteration of the Democratic Socialist Labor Commission. Regional Representation The original Organizing Committee tasked with establishing the Commission determined that there should be geographic diversity on the DSLC SC and thus mandated that no single DSA chapter could be represented more than once on the SC. Members of the DSLC SC reported that the geographical mandate was easily met, and that it provided a variety of labor perspectives as well as touchpoints for labor struggles around the country. However, members also reported that the geographical mandate was limiting. Large, vibrant labor branches were not allowed to be represented more than once on the SC, thus excluding potential candidates with extensive leadership experience. Alternatives to the geographic quotas were proposed including a cap on chapter representation on the SC, or changing from a chapter-based quota to a region-based quota. Organizing, Engagement, and Leadership Development The DSLC SC established subcommittees to engage members and distribute work beyond the Steering Committee in specific areas of expertise. At one point, the SC aimed to hold regional membership conferences with the goal of drafting a comprehensive DSLC strategy document, but this project was abandoned due to lack of capacity. Ultimately, the SC agreed to do regular direct chapter outreach to facilitate member engagement and provide support to chapter labor leaders. SC members reported that the subcommittees were a good way to initiate member collaboration, and to engage non-SC members in DSLC work. The Mapping Subcommittee and the Education Subcommittee were referenced as examples of success. However, it is speculated that the path to joining the subcommittees was unclear, subcommittee purposes were undefined, SC members had insufficient capacity to organize or direct these subcommittees, and subcommittees were generally not able to meet consistently. Thus their function as engagement vehicles and leadership development programs was limited. The direct chapter outreach was praised as the SC’s best strategy for organizing, engagement, and leadership development, and SC members wished it had been adopted from the beginning. SC members

[PDF page 2] also wished that other candidates who ran in the original SC election were reached out to directly in the beginning to serve as key DSLC leaders. SC members pointed to the lack of a central campaign as being a reason for poor engagement, and suggested that the strategy document project should have been pursued for its potential to identify such a campaign. SC members suggest that direct chapter outreach should be continued, and that this practice could be used to continue the existing mapping project. National Structure and Support The DSLC SC held conference calls on a monthly basis, and was joined by one staff member on most calls. Midway through the tenure, the SC began including alternate members on the conference calls as well. These alternates were the runners-up in the original SC election. Midway through we also requested that YDSA designate a permanent member to attend SC meetings. The SC met in person twice, once at the 2017 Labor Notes Conference, and once in New York City in conjunction with a meeting of the NPC. While in New York, the SC presented to the NPC. The SC worked directly with other support committees and priorities committees including YDSA, the NEC, the Tech Committee, and M4A. The SC communicated directly with members primarily via the DSA Labor Activists Google Group, or by direct member contact. The SC also established a website where basic info and written materials are housed. The SC recently introduced a new communication platform for the DSLC based on Groups.io. SC members report a positive workflow between each other, high turnout to conference calls and meetings, and a high level of engagement among the SC. SC members found the in-person meeting especially productive. SC members report that the work demanded of them was higher than anticipated, and that monthly calls were not enough to achieve the level of coordination necessary for the tasks at hand. It was noted that most labor activists within DSA are not only active in their local chapters and labor branches, but are also active in their workplace organizing efforts and are thus spread thin. SC members suggest implementing a regular schedule of monthly SC conference calls staggered with regular subcommittee calls. SC members also suggest maintaining the structure of alternates, or else expanding the SC. SC members report that the communication tools and structures in place were insufficient for creating the kind of member engagement deemed necessary. It’s also reported that there was a lack of communication regarding what structures and tools were already in place and at the ready. SC members report a long learning curve in discovering how basic organizing and administrative needs could be met.

[PDF page 3] SC members also report that much of their political efforts were subsumed by the larger political and administrative needs of the organization. SC members report that a significant amount of their time was spent performing administrative functions, with assigned staff being too overwhelmed to support the auxiliary or organizing needs of the DSLC. SC members also note a lack of significant attention paid to the DSLC by the NPC. SC members suggest establishing a regular schedule for in-person meetings, and to send representatives to meetings of the NPC to report on the DSLC and gather pertinent updates. SC members also advocate for comprehensive travel budgets to accommodate regular in-person meetings, possibly at the quarterly NPC meetings. Lastly, SC members suggest staff reorganization in order to better serve the needs of the DSLC, which could consist of redirecting current staff or increasing staffing.
title: Democratic Socialists Labor Commission Report

[PDF page 1] Resolution #34 Title & Author “Ecosocialist Green New Deal Priority” by Matthew H. of Huron Valley DSA: Sydney G, of LA DSA; Ashik S. of Metro DC DSA; Ted F. of East Bay DSA; Shauna M. of San Diego DSA; Jeff G. of Austin DSA; Becca M. of Boston DSA. (friendly amendments added 7/26) Budget Analysis Staff Costs $74,610 National priority - full time staffer. 12% Overhead $8,953 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $83,563 Resolve Be it resolved, National DSA resources shall be committed to building the movement for a radical Green New Deal (GND) to address the climate emergency and ecological crisis. To accomplish this task, the NPC & national DSA staff, in collaboration with the national DSA Ecosocialist Working Group (DSAEWG), other relevant national committees & working groups as well as local chapters, shall: A. Establish a national DSA priority campaign to fight at the national, regional, & local levels for a radical GND that is aligned with the DSAEWG’s Guiding Principles to decarbonize all sectors of the U.S. economy by 2030; democratize control of major energy systems and resources through public ownership; center the working class in a just transition to a caring economy with a job guarantee that expands the public sector; decommodify survival by ensuring basic necessities and services are guaranteed public goods; reinvent communities to serve people & planet, not profit, and plan equitable resilience & adaptation strategies to prepare for inevitable climate impacts; demilitarize, decolonize, and strive for international solidarity toward global climate justice; and redistribute resources from the worst polluters. This priority campaign will incorporate & embrace all of DSA's national campaigns & priorities, organizing for a society that is democratically run by working people; ecologically sustainable; free of oppression based on race, religion, national origin, gender, age, disability, or sexual identity; & rooted in internationalism & solidarity rather than imperialism & war. To this end, the DSAEWG will incorporate a campaign subcommittee (hereinafter the GNDCC) that will develop an organizing strategy & coordinate within DSA the work of organizing for a GND. The DSAEWG will be tasked with organizing the subcommittee & its leadership selection, as well as strategic outreach to other national working groups whose charges intersect with GND goals to ensure their leadership & perspectives are reflected in the campaign.

[PDF page 2] B. Popularize the demand for an ecosocialist GND through outward-facing education, media, outreach, & other efforts aligned with the DSAEWG’s Guiding Principles. Direct the DSAEWG, the GNDCC, & the Political Education Committee to develop educational programs & materials that connect the latest environmental science, climate-related disasters, & related movements to broader struggles against capitalism to our fight for a GND. Utilize DSA listservs, social media platforms, publications, & other communication resources to amplify local & national work as part of an overall struggle for democratic ecosocialism & a GND. C. Support the demand for a GND process that is transparent, inclusive, & democratic & includes the voices of frontline, disproportionately impacted, & threatened communities at all stages. Work to develop partnerships with anti-capitalist networks of organizers from communities that have always been at the forefront of struggles for environmental justice, and amplify the perspectives & insights of impacted communities through national media platforms. Recognize the sovereignty of Indigenous peoples, with rights to free, prior, and informed consent before activities that will affect Indigenous peoples’ territory or environment. D. Devote staff capacity (& expand staff as necessary) to coordinate with the GNDCC & local chapters engaged in GND & ecosocialist work & to maintain relationships with national & local organizations aligned toward a radical GND. Staff will partner with the DSAEWG & GNDCC in parlaying local efforts into a focused & effective national campaign, with at least one staff member entirely dedicated to this purpose. E. Work to build a powerful alliance of the labor, social justice, progressive, leftist, youth, racial justice, Indigenous liberation, and climate & environmental justice movements to win a radical GND & just transition policies at local, regional, national, & international levels based on our common demands around ecology, labor rights, jobs, justice, equality, & peace. F. Task DSA’s Democratic Socialist Labor Commission (DSLC), in partnership & close collaboration with the DSAEWG & GNDCC, to work with & support union organizing & worker struggles for a GND alongside the development of Just Transition implementation plans. These efforts should coalesce with broader alliance-building initiatives. G. Support political candidates & organizations that aid in the fight for a radical GND and, in electoral campaigns in which DSA participates, agitate for elements of a radical GND described in the DSAEWG’s Guiding Principles. H. Direct the GNDCC, in partnership with the DSAEWG, DSA staff, & each region’s field organizer, to provide support to chapters with analyzing their local contexts, developing individual climate/environmental justice plans, & counseling on implementation tactics. Provide education & mentorship to help chapters develop

[PDF page 3] organizing strategies, knowledge, & skills most relevant to implementing radical GND efforts in their localities, recognizing the varying political terrains they face. Help develop materials & resources for local ecosocialist campaigns that can cohere as part of the broader struggle for a GND. Facilitate collaboration & political interaction between chapters working on similar campaigns, & between chapters & allied groups outside DSA. I. Direct the GNDCC & designated staff to work with national working groups & appropriate DSA bodies to develop alliances of solidarity & cooperation that build an anti-imperialist, anti-racist, feminist, working class, internationalist movement here & abroad for an ecologically thriving & just world. Insert into Section C. Amendment #1 on Resolution #34 Title & Authors “ Amendment on the Red Deal and Rejecting a Green Military” by Sofia A. (NYC), Sydney G. (Los Angeles), Brian W. (Madison), Rory F. (Chicago), Spenser. R (NYC), Joe A. (Chicago), Nazir K (Twin Cities). [from Resolution #34] “ …Amplify the perspectives & insights of impacted communities through national media platforms… ” As part of this effort, this Convention will endorse the Red Deal, launched by comrades in The Red Nation, a radical anti-capitalist Indigenous liberation group, and its principles on the fight for non-reformist reforms. As described by The Red Nation, “The Red Deal is not a counter program of the GND. It’s a call for action beyond the scope of the US colonial state. It’s a program for Indigenous liberation, life, and land—an affirmation that colonialism and capitalism must be overturned for this planet to be habitable for human and other-than-human relatives to live dignified lives.” At the end of this Convention, the GNDCC will be tasked with initiating a more direct working relationship between DSA and The Red Nation. The GNDCC will make direct connection with The Red Nation, dedicate one person to serve as the main point of contact, and collaborate with the comrades on joint actions, statements and local, national and international campaigns around indigenous liberation and climate justice. Insert into Section I. [from Resolution #34] “...abroad for an ecologically thriving & just world… ” This Convention will also reject any effort at promoting a “Green Military” GND plan, as proposed by Senator Elizabeth Warren, including the bill she recently introduced in Congress, known as S. 1498, Department of Defense Climate Resiliency and Readiness Act. Any literature, statements, memes,

[PDF page 4] and other communications produced to support the Green New Deal should also clearly state DSA’s opposition to this plan, which is not simply a policy proposal from Warren, but represents a wider consensus within the Pentagon, and therefore risks undermining and rolling back the democratic socialist vision for an end to the military industrial complex. These are similar to arguments about the precision of “surgical strikes” and expanded drone warfare made during the Obama administration. Recent arguments for “climate resilience” and the fear of climate change producing a “threat multiplier” represent an effort by the US military to maintain its operations, occupations and bases around the world and to win back legitimacy for its endless wars today. The DSAEWG will work over the next year alongside the DSA for Bernie campaign to produce materials for GND organizing that challenge the greenwashing of the military and US imperialism, whether from Elizabeth Warren, Joe Biden or other members of the Democratic or Republican Party in office or running for president. Add Section J. Amendment #3 on Resolution #34 Title & Authors “ Amendment on the September 20th global #ClimateStrike” by Robert L. (Seattle) Endorse the September 20th global #ClimateStrike led by the Swedish teenager Greta Thunberg and the Fridays for Future movement. The student strikers have called for all students and workers to go on strike just before a crucial UN summit about the climate emergency. They already organized an unprecedented wave of student strikes and protests in approximately 1,594 cities in 125 countries this spring. DSA will engage and coordinate with groups leading this effort, such as environmental groups like 350.org, Extinction Rebellion, and Fridays for Future, and labor groups like the Massachusetts Teachers Association who have joined the call to strike. We urge all DSA local chapters to actively and urgently build toward this potentially historic strike, making it a priority for the next two months, with a high DSA profile. We also encourage DSA union members to put forward proposals in their unions to join the strike. While some workers who cannot convince their co-workers or their union to join can call in sick to work, we don’t call on individual workers to get fired by going on strike as a minority of the workplace or as individuals. However, DSA can contribute to the pressure in labor to at least organize at workplaces informational pickets or educational activities, lunch-time actions, symbolic strikes or actions in the workplace. DSA urges the AFL-CIO and all unions to be part of this fight.

[PDF page 5] Amendment #14 on Resolution #34 Title & Authors “ Amendment on Diversity of Approaches” by Nishikant S. (SF), Emily A. (East Bay) Advocate for a GND that embraces a comprehensive approach to addressing climate change, including both mitigation strategies, through a just transition to a zero-emission economy, as well as resilience and adaptation strategies, such as disaster preparedness/relief and adaptive infrastructural projects to cope with climate change’s inevitable impacts; utilizing a full spectrum of tactics both nationally and locally. [PDF page 1] Resolution #42 Title & Author “Endorse the Great Lakes Authority (GLA) Campaign” by Natasha F.S., Jessica N., Peter L., Jane S (Metro-Detroit DSA) Author’s Cost Estimate Resolve Background Information $1,500 annually to reimburse organizers for such expenses as printing literature, paying for a zoom account, and producing multimedia (video, graphic work, etc.). Staff time for following announcements, disseminating throughout the organization, and processing reimbursements is estimated to be roughly 20 hours annually. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) endorse the cross-chapter campaign around the creation of the Great Lakes Authority, a regional-planning agency enacted through federal legislation under the umbrella of the “Green New Deal” with the mandate to bring green union jobs, environmental justice, and sustainable economic development to the Great Lakes region of the United States, consistent with DSA’s Guiding Principles of an Ecosocialist Green New Deal. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that DSA shall assist those chapters involved in this campaign with reasonable material resources, including funding and staff time, to further the campaign. WHEREAS the Great Lakes basin is home to precious natural resources, including the Great Lakes (which contain one-fifth of the world’s freshwater and provide potable water to over 40 million people), 55 million acres of productive land, and myriad low-carbon recreation options. WHEREAS the Great Lakes Region (Michigan and portions of Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin) overlaps substantially with the “Rust Belt, ” which has been ravaged for decades by free trade deals, deindustrialization, and corporate pollution, and has yet to recover from the Great Recession of 2008. WHEREAS the Rust Belt’s long economic decline -- combined with the increasing regional impact of the climate crisis -- has produced a host of calamities, including the degradation of our air, water, and ecosystems; the privatization of both essential public services and natural resources; decrepit roads and bridges; inadequate mass transit; a housing crisis; the abandonment of entire communities. WHEREAS “market solutions” and “benevolent billionaires” have not and cannot address these problems, and have in fact exacerbated them, and only massive public investment and government planning can restore the region’s economy, environment, and infrastructure.

[PDF page 2] WHEREAS when General Motors announced plant closings and mass layoffs in 2018, Detroit DSA organized a demonstration demanding that the government seize the Detroit plant by eminent domain and use it to address the climate emergency and build green infrastructure, and a coalition of environmental, labor, and community organizations in Detroit formed around these demands and this radical vision for a Green New Deal. WHEREAS Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-13), a member of DSA who was part of that coalition, asked Detroit DSA to develop legislative ideas in furtherance of a Green New Deal and to present them to her and her staff. WHEREAS Detroit DSA determined that the Rust Belt should be the “Engine of the Green New Deal,” meaning that much of the green infrastructure (solar panels, wind turbines, electric transit, etc.) needed to avert a climate catastrophe should be manufactured in the Rust Belt, where millions of people already have manufacturing expertise and experience, and hundreds of underused or idled manufacturing facilities already exist. WHEREAS Detroit DSA determined that this goal should be achieved through what it calls the “Great Lakes Authority” (GLA), a new, federal, regional planning agency (enacted through federal legislation under the umbrella of the “Green New Deal”) with the mandate to bring green union jobs, environmental justice, and sustainable economic development to the Great Lakes region. WHEREAS the GLA would prioritize (1) creating green, prevailing-wage, union-backed jobs, including in green manufacturing, (2) creating millions of zero-carbon public housing units and weatherizing existing homes, and (3) restoring the region’s infrastructure, including its energy and water systems; its roads, bridges, and waterways; and its public transit, and be guided by the principles of (1) local control, (2) worker dignity, and (3) a just transition. WHEREAS Detroit DSA has shared the idea of the GLA with great success in print and social media, as well as in person at labor events, in community forums and town halls, at the Midwest DSA Regional Convention, etc. WHEREAS, in light of these efforts, DSA members from across the Rust Belt (including Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee, Toledo, Flint, Cleveland, Columbus, Huron Valley, Cincinnati, and Pittsburgh) are now actively thinking through the idea of the GLA, what such a unifying demand could mean for our ecosocialist work, and organizing to make the GLA a reality.

[PDF page 1] Resolution #56 Title & Author “Ecosocialism as a Guiding Principle” by Michelle B. of Orlando DSA. Updated 7/22/2019 with friendly amendments. Resolve Be it resolved, The Democratic Socialists of America will include ecosocialism as a guiding principle in recognition that ecology and climate change are intertwined with all of our organizing and effect the working class on many levels, and will not compartmentalize it or relegate all ecosocialist work to a single working group. This includes the platform, About Us section on the website, and all other descriptive documents for the organization. Democratic Socialists of America will also develop and conduct virtual trainings and reading materials to educate membership about ecosocialism and facilitate building ecosocialist organizing at the state and local level. Be it further resolved, DSA will prioritize and support campaigns: ● That uphold and defend the land use rights of indigenous people and stand in solidarity with them in their conflicts with corporate raiders ● To support opening U.S. borders to Central Americans and other climate change refugees ● ● ● To collectivize and bring under community control the energy infrastructure To address unsustainable, unjust, and inefficient food systems To recognize and combat instances of environmental racism Which use realistic and science based models of climate change to inform discussion Background Information Whereas, climate change is impacting and will continue to impact the working class significantly more than the ruling class and will continue to apply greater stress to people of color, people in the Global South, and our poorest comrades. Whereas, capitalism is the cause of climate change and environmental destruction and the movement to protect our planet is essential to the struggle to end capitalism. Whereas, in our current environment, no leftist organizing is relevant without the consideration of climate change and environmental destruction. Immigration, labor protections, houselessness, food insecurity, environmental racism, and feminism all intersect with and cannot be separated from climate change and environmental destruction caused by capitalism.

[PDF page 2] Whereas, current climate change discourse often distorts science-based models either to imply that climate change is minor and distant, or to imply that it is too late. These sentiments make effective environmental organizing feel pointless or hopeless. Whereas, many modern environmental movements focus on blaming the working class, pushing for corporate responsibility and consumerist solutions to climate change; all of which limits both the effectiveness of their tactics and their inclusion of marginalized groups. Whereas, the United States has also been the leading country in exploiting the Global South, distorting their economies and social structures and depriving them of the resources they need to adapt to climate change. Whereas we can create more effective organizing tactics in multiple areas of struggle by establishing ecosocialism as not just a separate form of organizing but instead as a core value integrated into all areas of our work;

[PDF page 1] Resolution #74 Title & Author “Bernie Policy Recommendations” by Jennifer L. (NYC), Andrew H,. (NYC), Sarah R. (Chicago), Karen N. (NYC), Cea W. (NYC), Beth H. (Boston), Richard M. (East Bay), Alicia H. (St. Louis) Staff Costs 12% Overhead Budget Analysis Direct Costs Total Cost No additional upfront costs. Resolve Be it therefore resolved, we call on Bernie Sanders to support Reinvesting in the Nation’s Existing Public Housing Stock by directly appropriating the many billions needed in funding for the Public Housing Operating and Capital Funds; working with housing authorities to ensure needed renovations and repairs are undertaken with the utmost urgency; ending the Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) program; securing additional funding to weatherize and decarbonize public housing stock; removing restrictions to public housing based on income, immigration status, and criminal record; and building mechanisms to transition to the democratical control of public housing, by residents themselves as opposed to state managers. Be it therefore resolved, we call on Bernie Sanders to support Dramatically Expanding the Nation’s Social Housing by repealing the Faircloth Amendment; building new ecologically sustainable, permanently affordable, municipally/publicly owned, resident-controlled homes; creating new flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., loans and capital grants) to municipalities to fund forms of social housing, including public housing, alternative community ownership models, and low-income co-ops; creating, maintaining, and protecting mechanisms by which existing for-profit housing can come under public (municipal and/or national) control, or by residents themselves, like Washington D.C.’s Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (TOPA) and District Opportunity to Purchase Act (DOPA); and immediately providing stable, permanent, unconditional (and/or supportive) housing that affords and fosters people's agency and autonomy regardless of their ability to comply with any prescribed program, goal, regulation or bureaucratic requirements.

[PDF page 2] Background Information Be it therefore resolved, we call on Bernie Sanders to support Guaranteeing Renters’ Rights by guaranteeing all renters the right to renew their lease and prohibit unjust evictions and exorbitant rent increases, based on local conditions, with federal rent control legislation; ensuring and protect the right of all tenants to collectively organize for better conditions; creating federal regulations on the quality of housing conditions and ensuring that enforcement mechanisms are fully funded and that the burden of enforcement does not lie on the renter; and Prohibiting discrimination based on tenants’ criminal records and income levels Be it therefore resolved, we call on Bernie Sanders to support Enacting Progressive Tax Policy by instituting a progressive tax structure—including luxury taxes, vacancy taxes, and corporation taxes—to fund the restoration and expansion of public housing, and ending public subsidies to for-profit real estate developers, including the phasing out of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), as we move away from dependence on the private market to provide housing and toward the expansion of social housing. Be it therefore resolved, we call on Bernie Sanders to support Ending Housing Discrimination and Implementing Reparations by, in conjunction with, or as part of, HR 40, enacting a reparations program that explicitly addresses wealth that has been extracted from communities of color through housing discrimination and unequal access to land and housing; forcefully implementing the Fair Housing Act to dismantle discriminatory practices and tools that exclude people of color, LGBTQ+ and disabled people from access to housing; providing public investment, in part through direct, significant, and community-controlled federal grants, to spatially concentrated low-income communities of color; and encouraging regional planning that targets city-suburb and inter-city inequalities. Whereas, more than two million people experience homelessness over the course of a year, and those with homes, whether rented, owned, or on loan from banks, are increasingly seeing them targeted as vehicles for speculation by managers of a global mass of investment capital seeking profit, leaving an epidemic of foreclosures, evictions and displacement in their wake. Whereas, the United States has a long history of deploying racist land and housing policies to grant wealth and resources to white communities while segregating and disinheriting communities of color, and in the midst of an historic nationwide shortage of affordable housing, this burden is falling disproportionately on communities of color who are more likely to be rent burdened, housing insecure and homeless. Whereas, the Sanders presidential campaign provides an important opportunity to articulate a vision for housing priorities that advances key socialist demands, forcefully changes the narrative at the national level, connects disparate housing-related struggles across the country, and unlocks some of the keys, held at

[PDF page 3] the federal level, to transforming the social role of housing from a market commodity to a guaranteed human right. Whereas, a truly transformative housing platform should put forth a renewed vision of public housing as a haven for the multi-racial working class; it should provide a roadmap for the large-scale decarbonization of the nation’s housing stock; it should incentivize states to enact broad and meaningful rent control measures; it should aggressively dismantle racist housing policies and practices while proactively remedying racial inequities that have resulted from centuries of white supremacy; and it should radically expand people’s capacities to self-organize and democratically control their homes and their communities.
