[PDF page 1] Resolution #82 Title & Author Budget Analysis “DSA National Electoral Priority Resolution” by Michael K. & Abdullah Y. of NYC DSA; Tim Z. of Honolulu DSA; Hannah A. of Lawrence KS. DSA Staff Costs $37,305 Appears to require priority campaign level support as exists now - 1/2 staffer. 12% Overhead $4,477 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $41,781 Resolve Background Information Therefore, be it resolved that: 1) The NPC should expand the work of the National Electoral Committee in supporting chapters’ efforts to develop and run viable openly socialist candidates for office, on Democratic, independent, or other ballot lines. The priority of the NEC should be to support locals in building electoral infrastructure that is democratically accountable to the membership and engages as many people as possible. 2) DSA cannot engage in mass politics without building solidarity with aligned political forces and the broader working class. Wherever possible, DSA chapters should work to build diverse, multiracial electoral coalitions grounded in working-class institutions, unions and community groups. In selecting candidates to support, DSA chapters should be encouraged to prioritize races that have the potential to form a broader multiracial coalition 3) DSA chapters must be given wide discretion to support candidates whose campaigns offer strategic opportunities within their concrete local contexts, but chapters are encouraged to prioritize candidates who stand for class-struggle politics and strive to support open socialists wherever possible. 4) DSA should recognize that electoral work is not a strategy or an end in itself, but a tactic to advance broader movement struggles, and should link electoral work to our core strategic goals, like abolishing ICE, implementing the Green New Deal and passing Medicare for All. 5) DSA should continue to pursue electoral organizing as one of its national priorities for the next two years, in order to advance a political revolution up and down the ballot and in every region of the country. Two years ago at its previous national convention, DSA chose electoral work as one of its three national priorities. Since that time, DSA chapters across the country have achieved extraordinary successes in municipal, state and federal elections. DSA has not

[PDF page 2] only helped elect committed leftists all over the US, but has built movement power, sharpened organizing skills and expanded its membership in doing so. DSA must continue to reject the false opposition between movement work and elections. State power and movement power condition each other; grassroots movements can alter the context in which elected officials operate, and legislative power affects the possibilities for democratic social change. Furthermore, electoral work can build the po wer and visibility of the socialist movement. Many people who are open to radical politics first enter organized politics through election work, and DSA’s size and strength today is a testament to how left-wing campaigns like those of Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez can inspire people to get involved in organized left politics for the first time. In a nation where politics is increasingly dominated by the billionaire class, DSA’s electoral effectiveness is tied to the volunteer power of our chapters. Ensuring that left-wing elected officials will remain accountable to the working class requires building a strong organizational infrastructure and robust coalitions determined not only to elect working-class candidates but also to advance an ambitious political program between elections. Add the following resolved clauses at the end of the current resolve Amendment #9 on Resolution #82 Title & Authors “ Adding Bernie to the DSA National Electoral Priority Resolution” Ramy K. (Seattle), Stuart S. (Seattle) 6) In particular, DSA will make campaigning for Bernie our top priority—a historic opportunity that we must seize while this rare window of opportunity exists. The DSA national convention urges all chapters to use the Bernie campaign to recruit thousands of new DSA members across the country and develop deeper roots in the multi-racial working class. DSA commits to integrating Bernie’s campaign into our other related campaigns wherever possible. 7) DSA will not restrict our messaging to Bernie’s messaging. DSA’s campaign for Bernie will boldly speak out against sexism, racism, heterosexism, and all forms of oppression. DSA’s campaign for Bernie will advocate an anti-imperialist foreign policy of bringing home all US troops from abroad, ending US military aid to right-wing regimes (such as Guaido in Venezuela, the right-wing Israeli government, Bolsonaro in Brazil, and the Saudi monarchy), on top of slashing the military budget. DSA’s campaign for Bernie will also call for working-class democratic control and public ownership of key sectors of the economy such as the banks, energy companies, and internet companies even though Bernie himself has so far not advocated this.

[PDF page 3] 8) As Trump and the Republicans attack socialism, the DSA for Bernie campaign will fight back. Bernie presents socialism as a major expansion of social welfare programs like FDR’s New Deal, but Bernie fails to link these positive reforms to the need to end capitalism itself. In contrast, our Democratic Socialists for Bernie campaign will proudly explain the need to replace the failed, crisis-ridden capitalist system with a new socialist society. 9) DSA’s campaign for Bernie will use a strategy of maintaining our own independent political position within the Bernie campaign. While collaborating with coalition partners where we are legally allowed, the DSA national convention calls on all local chapters to organize our own independent “Democratic Socialists for Bernie” activities. DSA will seek to recruit Bernie supporters and volunteers to DSA in order to strengthen the left wing of the Bernie movement. The DSA national convention suggests that all chapters organize meetings and study groups to politically prepare our members to push back against the Democratic Party sabotage of the Bernie campaign and pave the way for the construction of an independent socialist party. Add the following paragraph at the end of the background information In particular, Bernie’s 2020 campaign may become a historic event of immense proportions. We may elect for the first time ever a self-described socialist as president of the US. This raises the prospect of major social upheaval and intense clashes between the ruling elite and the rising aspirations of the 99%. Bernie’s campaign will raise the expectations of millions of working people and the confidence of social movements. The capitalist media and the Democratic Party establishment are attempting to sabotage Bernie’s campaign, like they did in 2016. DSA is the organization in the best position to push back against the attacks. If DSA focuses on Bernie’s campaign, we have a rare opportunity to potentially triple the size of DSA and sink roots in the working class and communities of color.

[PDF page 1] Resolution #57 Title & Author “Strengthening the Working Class Through Tenant Organizing” by Arielle S. of Los Angeles DSA. Budget Analysis Staff Costs $74,610 National priority - full time staffer. 12% Overhead $8,953 Direct Costs $4,185 Costs of in person meeting for coordinating committee. Total Cost $87,748 Author’s Cost Estimate Resolve ● Cost of hiring one staff member at comparable pay to other paid organizers for DSA, including benefits. ● Toolkit would be digital only, incurring no material cost. ● Pay for one in-person convening of the Steering Committee; thereafter, all meetings will be digital or self-funded. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED: ● DSA will form a Housing Justice Commission to help coordinate national and regional campaigns for tenants’ rights and support locals in the creation and expansion of Tenant Associations and housing justice working groups/campaigns, with intentional outreach to other national working groups and external tenants’ rights organizations. ● The Housing Justice Commission shall be comprised of representatives from each local with a housing justice working group or ongoing campaign, and will elect a Steering Committee of nine (9) members. Locals will be responsible for developing and overseeing the selection process for representatives to the Housing Justice Commission. ● The National Political Committee (NPC) shall hire at least one (1) staff housing justice organizer dedicated solely to supporting the Housing Justice Commission

[PDF page 2] Background Information and local/regional tenants' rights work, including facilitating regional tenant organizing trainings. ● The Housing Justice Commission shall develop a toolkit for chapters to start tenant organizing work. This toolkit should support locals in the dual mission of raising class consciousness as it intersects with the housing struggle, embedding the organization in our communities, and growing DSA’s membership. ● DSA will formally acknowledge that the current crisis is one driven by capitalism, not supply and demand, reframing the “housing” crisis as a “tenants” crisis. ● DSA will utilize outward facing communications channels to spread a socialist analysis of the housing affordability crisis and build momentum for the tenants’ rights movement, with an eye toward building popular support for alternatives to the capitalist housing market, such as community land trusts and social housing. DSA will commit to never endorsing any candidate that takes money from real estate interests. WHEREAS: ● The dispossession of people from their homes is key to the accumulation of capital. Across the globe, landlords, developers, and investors are making exorbitant profits off skyrocketing rents and manufactured land values, while wages stagnate for working-class tenants. ● The definition of a tenant includes anyone who does not have control over their housing, including the unhoused and the incarcerated. ● We should aim to develop DSA into a mass working class organization able to wield power in our workplaces, at the ballot box, and in our neighborhoods. ● With only 11% of the U.S. workforce in existing labor unions, it's increasingly hard to organize the working class at the point of production, but we can also organize at the point of social reproduction and dispossession. Tenants must organize to fight rent increases, evictions, landlord and police harassment, housing discrimination, and more. ● DSA chapters of varying sizes and geographies — from Los Angeles to Central Iowa — are already organizing tenants and forming Tenant Associations, with little resources for sharing experiences and best-practices beyond individual members’ social networks.

[PDF page 3] ● ● DSA chapters across the country are engaging in tenants’ rights work at the ballot box, building popular support for demands like universal rent control and the right to counsel for tenants facing eviction. Given the necessity of organizing on an accessible, neighborhood basis to build local membership more representative of the working class, this strategy would support the development of intentional, base building work that is structured by geography.

[PDF page 1] Resolution #64 Title & Author “Housing For All: Analysis and Recommendations for DSA Chapters” by Sarah R. of Chicago DSA; Karen N., Cea W., & Jennifer L. of NYC DSA; Richard M. of East Bay DSA; Alicia H. of St. Louis DSA; Beth H. of Boston DSA. Budget Analysis Staff Costs $0 No additional up front costs. 12% Overhead $0 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $0 Resolve BE IT RESOLVED THAT: We must fight to dismantle the private property market and fight for housing as a human right. This means that everyone has an affordable place to live; it means resident self-determination and control — through strong tenant unions, rent controls, democratically controlled social housing, and alternative community ownership models. We believe that the struggle for fully decommodified housing requires a struggle for renters’ rights in the short and medium term. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT: DSA chapters should fight for rent control laws that limit rent increases, include enforcement mechanisms and protect against eviction. Rent control allows tenants the opportunity to remain in their communities even as they become susceptible to gentrification. We demand rent control because it is uniquely able to unite a mass working-class movement, and to ease the path to social housing. By challenging the profits of landlords and their direct power over our rents, we can also challenge the political power of the real estate industry. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT: We believe that only universal social housing can provide affordable homes to the entire working class. Federal, state and local governments should spend public funds directly on creating millions of publicly- and socially-owned housing developments that are permanently affordable, democratically controlled, and available to residents of all incomes. Since the 1970s, the US government has privatized public housing and subsidized private landlords. However, we can draw on models from around the world to create an alternative system of social housing in the US, both by bringing existing market housing under social control and by building new social housing.

[PDF page 2] Background Information BE IT FINALLY RESOLVED THAT: When possible chapters should pursue these strategies for housing organizing, taking into account that each chapter faces a unique political landscape and housing market. ● Incorporate the housing crisis into their political analysis and candidate selection process, and encourage DSA-endorsed candidates to include rent control and social housing in their platform. ● Join or help launch campaigns for tenant protections through universal rent control, just cause eviction, and enforcement of health and safety regulations. ● Target bad landlords and lead campaigns that call attention to their abusive practices. ● Highlight the influence of real estate money in politics, either by calling on candidates and elected officials to pledge to reject real estate donations, or by targeting politicians who refuse to do so. ● Organize for a Green New Deal that will repair public housing and create new social housing. ● Promote equitable and democratic development, including maximum affordability, abolishing tax incentives for for-profit developers, and community control of land. ● Support tenant organizing efforts; strengthen DSA’s connection to the existing tenant movement while helping it to expand and radicalize. ● Work to address long-lasting racial discrimination in housing and support full funding and enforcement of fair housing and civil rights laws. WHEREAS: The ongoing commodification of land and housing is driving a housing crisis that harms millions of working people across the country and reproduces racial inequities. The neoliberal response—rolling back local regulations and starving public housing authorities while letting Wall Street buy up private housing—only boosts the profits of the real estate investor class. As a result, homelessness is widespread, rents are skyrocketing, and entire communities are being displaced. In the wake of the foreclosure crisis, private equity firms and other corporate investors have played an increasingly large role in the housing market, making rental housing an asset for global capital. AND WHEREAS: Rental housing is a key site of struggle for many working-class people. Housing issues affect DSA members and the working class directly, and organizing around them gives us the opportunity to confront real estate capital and build coalitions with other tenants. Running electoral campaigns that highlight housing for all as a demand and reject real estate donations helps DSA connect with a broader base of tenants and link housing to other issues as part of a socialist platform. We hope to help make tenants as a political force that can challenge the power of the real estate industry in politics.
title: Resolution #64: Housing For All - Analysis and Recommendations for DSA Chapters

Resolve BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED: 1. To have all federal, state, and local candidates endorsed by DSA vocally, enthusiastically, and unequivocally support abortion rights, access to abortion, the repeal of the Hyde amendment, and full federal funding of abortion. 2. To dedicate DSA resources to organizing the fight for abortion access, not only to oppose current efforts to criminalize abortion but also to eliminate all obstacles and expand access. These efforts should be undertaken in collaboration with DSA members who work in abortion care as well as with existing reproductive justice organizations such as the National Network of Abortion Funds and local abortion funds. 3. To declare that Medicare for All must include free reproductive healthcare for all people, including unrestricted access to abortion. 4. To frame our demand for free and unrestricted abortion within an overall vision grounded in reproductive justice. Consistent with the framework developed by Women of African Descent for Reproductive Justice and SisterSong, we envision reproductive justice to encompass our right to not have children, to have children, to be treated with dignity and respect in accessing all forms of reproductive healthcare freely and without restriction, and to be able to parent the children that we do have in safe and sustainable communities. We also advocate for centering and uplifting the marginalized voices of working class people of color that are most affected by abortion restrictions. 5. To challenge the dominant narrative that abortion should be “safe, legal, and rare” and replace it with the call for abortion to be fully funded and freely available without stigma. WHEREAS: Background Information

[PDF page 2] 1. Our socialism is feminist, anti-racist, anti-heterosexist, anti-cissexist, anti-ableist, pro-worker, and unabashedly supportive of everyone’s bodily autonomy without stigma or shame. 2. Abortion rights are under attack in the United States, both on the federal level and in the states. Within the first five months of 2019, draconian abortion bans have passed in Ohio, Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, Georgia, and Alabama. Once the newly passed laws are enacted, legal abortion will be dramatically limited or completely prohibited, either altogether (in AL), after six weeks from the first date of the last menstrual period (in OH, KY, MS, & GA), or after eight weeks (in MO). These attacks on reproductive freedom are increasing in frequency and intensity, and there is every indication that they will continue. 3. In many places where abortion is technically legal, financial and logistic barriers to accessing it creates an intolerable hardship for many members of the working class needing abortions. As long as abortion is treated as a separate category of healthcare, the difficulties inherent in navigating the legal restrictions, waiting periods, shortages of providers, and expense of abortions blatantly discriminates against people who are already oppressed by capitalism. This is felt even more keenly by incarcerated individuals who are or can become pregnant, who are routinely denied appropriate reproductive healthcare. 4. As abortion rights become further restricted and abortions become criminalized in several states, the impact of these injustices will be visited most severely on individuals who are already marginalized in our society. This means that our focus must address not only cis women who are centered within much advocacy for abortion rights, but also consider the additional risks of the carceral state for people of color, trans men and non-binary individuals, undocumented persons, sex workers, and disabled individuals, who may be at increased risk of incarceration and state violence where abortion is criminalized. 5. These attacks are grounded in misogyny, transphobia, and the desire to uphold a cis-heterosexual normative model of reproduction within “traditional marriage,” and we cannot rely on the courts to protect our reproductive freedom;
title: Resolution #38: Fight for Abortion Access

Author’s Estimated Cost Could vary greatly depending on how the NPC chooses to implement the resolution. Minimally, $10 for a domain name and +/- 50 hours of staff time for coordination a year, assuming that we use the same hosting as the national web site and have volunteers doing the editorial work. Resolve Background Information Be it resolved, the National Political Committee will establish a Spanish-language DSA web site with a goal of launching within 90 days after the 2019 DSA convention, if possible. The web site should have both translations and material directly generated for it. Be it further resolved, the National Political Committee will initiate the selection of an editorial board for the web site to include a diverse group of Latinx and other comrades, especially those fluent in Spanish, but without precluding the inclusion of others. Be it further resolved, in collaboration with the National Political Committee, this editorial board shall have the additional responsibilities of developing our work with Latinx communities, establishing relations with organizations, and promoting collaboration and the exchange of information between Locals involved in this work. Be it finally resolved, these additional responsibilities are not meant to be permanent but a transitional step towards the creation by the NPC of a working group or other body focused on the Latinx communities and their issues. Whereas: The Latinx communities are now the largest oppressed minority in the country, with 18% of the country’s population, some 60 million people, and concentrated among young people. One in five millennials is classified as “Hispanic” by the census bureau; among post-millennials, one in four. Whereas: The United States has the second largest number of Spanish-speaking people in the world after Mexico, some 55 million people over the age of five. Some 41 million over that age are considered native speakers as that is the main language used in their homes, a number comparable to native speakers in Colombia, Argentina and Spain itself. Whereas: Due to common oppression, language and cultural elements, as well as modern communications and mass media, these communities have developed a common political identity as shown, for example, by the millions who marched for immigrant rights in the spring of 2006.

[PDF page 2] Whereas: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a millennial Puerto Rican woman and democratic socialist, has become by far the single most prominent Latinx political figure in the community and media, presenting extraordinary opportunities for the DSA. Whereas: Addressing the Latinx community in the Spanish language is both a needed practical measure and an important political statement given the size of the DSA and its national presence. Whereas: A socialist transformation of the United States is unthinkable without the massive, militant participation of Latinx working people.
title: Resolution #6: Orienting to Latinx Communities

(Lawrence, KS) Resolve BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, the NPC create a Nationwide Red Rabbits Team responsible for training DSA members in protest marshalling, meeting security, infosecurity and other skills which will allow chapters to reduce the damage caused by threats to the organization and protect its members from right-wing violence and state disruption. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the Nationwide Red Rabbits Team open membership to elected leadership of security working groups, steering committees or equivalents created by DSA chapters. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the membership of the Nationwide Red Rabbits Team conduct monthly calls to coordinate trainings, refine the training curriculum, develop best practices, and coordinate to meet emergent security threats to DSA. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the Nationwide Red Rabbits Team coordinate with trainers from other organizations and coalition partners to improve DSA’s practices around infosec, marshalling, direct action and security. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the Nationwide Red Rabbits Team: ● Develop guides for deescalation, meeting security, protest, rally, picket and general action marshaling, rally security, jail support, action planning, working with local or statewide bail funds and/or starting bail funds, and on building new Red Rabbits Marshal Teams within their chapter. ● Develop guides for doxxing-prevention and data security (handling member data, chapter data, and financial data) ● Update those guides twice a year. ● Conduct video conference and in-person trainings at regional conferences to train chapter leaders and members on the aforementioned skills. ● Provide support for researching and maintaining information on local laws and adverse local conditions to advise chapters about their rights, risks and responsibilities.

[PDF page 2] Background Information ● Work with chapter leaders to help chapters perform security audits, and assist chapters, members, and member groups in determining next steps after encountering an information security issue (exposure of member data, a doxxing event, etc.) ● Partner with field organizing staff to train newly-approved DSA chapters and national working groups in security best practices. BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that National DSA staff: ● Provide logistical support to the Nationwide Red Rabbits Team in resource development and assist with communications with the NPC, chapters, and working groups ● In the event of a security crisis, liaise with chapters and the Red Rabbits Team to respond rapidly and help chapters deal with the breach. ● Integrate the Red Rabbits Team Guides and Trainings into the chapter pipeline process and a regular training program for DSA organizing committees and chapters ● Make the guides easily accessible to all DSA chapter leaders and working groups ● Incorporate Red Rabbits recommendations into all national operations, including the national convention Whereas, DSA’s successes in building power have come at a cost - we have become a target for right-wing, white supremacist and misogynist violence. Members of DSA have been doxxed, harassed, attacked and disrupted by hostile actors. Every time DSA has a big win, they have a big loss, and are likely to become increasingly hostile and determined to attack DSA as we continue our work. Whereas, conducting demonstrations comes with risks as well. Law enforcement and non-state right-wing groups consistently attempt to disrupt our efforts to mobilize. At actions when our coalitions are not united, strategic and disciplined, our actions suffer. Whereas, in response to these threats, chapters have begun to create marshalling, infosec and security programs, with the support of national staff. Many of these teams go by the name of “Red Rabbits” teams. These efforts, housed under the National Tech Committee, have resulted in dozens of chapters being trained in security, infosec and marshalling. Chapters with security programs have connected to one another through informal networks as well, sharing best practices and developing their teams. Whereas, National DSA Staff and chapters have been able to reach out to existing security teams for support and training during times of crisis. However, there is

[PDF page 3] currently no formal, consistent, large-scale or structured security program for all of DSA. Most chapters do not have security programs, and are often unprepared to resist right-wing blowback to their work. Whereas bail funds are important tools to support the work of our chapters and members as acknowledged during the 2017 DSA Convention when Resolution #14: Bail Fund for DSA Members was passed, and creating a member-led subcommittee to take point on best practices we can empower chapters to establish the best solution for their members.

Whereas we have seen over the last two years that organizing skills training, grounded in this materialist analysis, has helped socialist organizers in DSA develop and share the skills necessary to wage strategic campaigns and build our political organization. [PDF page 1] Constitution/Bylaws Change #2 Title & Author “National Stipends to Chapters” by Erika P . (Lincoln), Jennifer B. (San Francisco), Tawny T . (NYC), and Zac E. (Red River Valley) Budget Analysis Staff Costs $4,000 Working with chapters to get bank accounts, testing deposits, remedying errs, processing payments, etc. 12% Overhead $480 Direct Costs $210,000 Cost of stipend for all chapters. Total Cost $214,479 Rationale Amended Language Socialists should redistribute wealth from each according to their ability, to each according to their need. This proposal would require National to pay a flat stipend totaling $1,200/year to each chapter that possesses a valid bank or credit union account in its own name, whether or not separately incorporated. Because National’s resources come from member dues and donations, this proposal effectively represents a redistribution of resources from the wealthiest sections of DSA to the poorest. The stipend would be independent of any current or future dues-sharing measures that National implements. This proposal is long overdue. Many chapters, particularly those in the poorest parts of the country, lack the bare financial resources necessary to hold meetings, print literature, or fund basic organizing efforts. At the same time, current dues-sharing measures only return a small portion (~$75,000/year in total) of monthly dues to the home chapters of members voluntarily paying monthly dues, effectively perpetuating geographic wealth disparities. DSA needs to invest in its small and poor chapters, which present our greatest opportunity for growth. This proposal will comprise only a small fraction of our annual budget (approximately $180,000/year if all of our nearly 150 chapters qualify) but will provide a critical investment to nurture chapters seeking to grow a militant socialist movement in the country’s poorest regions. Moreover, it will help restore chapters’ faith in the National Organization, which is viewed with skepticism by many chapters, thereby bringing them closer to it and incentivizing ongoing coordination. DSA Bylaws Article II. Dues Section 7.

[PDF page 2] In addition to any procedures determined for the sharing of dues, the National Organization shall pay a standard monthly or quarterly stipend to each Local, whether or not incorporated as a separate entity, that (1) has a valid bank or credit union account into which the stipend can be deposited; and (2) regularly provides the National Organization with updated contact information for the Local and its leadership. Locals may use their stipends for any lawful purpose in their sole discretion, with the exception of electoral contributions or expenditures implicating campaign finance requirements. The standard stipend shall be no less than $100 per month if paid monthly or $300 per quarter if paid quarterly. The standard stipend may be adjusted upward by the NPC, but shall always be the same for all Locals receiving it.

Total Cost $44,396 Background Information Ask a DSA member about “DSA National,” and, as with anything in DSA, you’ll get a variety of responses. Many in DSA simply don’t think about National—it has little to do with their local work. Some are frustrated with decisions being made. Some assume things will naturally improve once our “growing pains” subside. But DSA was never structured to be an organization of this size, with hundreds of locals in such disparate terrain. Currently, the 16-person NPC has a wide range of duties, from issuing political statements to overseeing finances to planning conventions. But the weakness of the NPC structure isn’t simply that there’s too much work for 16 people, but that decision-making power does not belong to the people most affected by those decisions. As socialists we should be ambitious. We must develop radical democracy by practicing it. This amendment restructures National to redistribute power to the locals. A new body, the Assembly of Locals, becomes the center for political decision-making, with representatives elected by each chapter, leaving the NPC (now simply called the Board) to focus on key fiduciary and administrative duties. Our vision is of a national organization that’s not just “responsive” to membership but *is* membership. An announcement… Article X XI. National Political Committee Board Section 1. The at-large members of the NPC Board shall work with the appropriate staff persons to ensure the completion of administrative duties and responsibilities. be liaisons to the Commissions, Regions, State and Local Organizations. The agendas for the NPC Board meetings will be proposed by the SC. [PDF page 1] Credentials Committee Report for the 2019 National Convention of the Democratic Socialists of America July 30, 2019 Committee Members: Bryan LaVergne, Zac Echola, Andrej Markovčič, and Laura Gabby

[PDF page 2] Contents I. Summary 2 II. How The Committee Acted 5 III. Nick J. Challenge 7 A. Facts 7 B. Findings 9 IV. East Bay Challenge 10 A. Facts 10 B. Findings 16 V. Recommendations 17 VI. Appendix 18 1

[PDF page 3] I. Summary A. Introduction The Credentials Committee (hereafter referred to as the Committee) is a four member body established and defined by the 2019 National Convention Rules and appointed by the NPC. The Committee interprets our responsibility as to review, report, and opine upon both the challenges that delegates make regarding the credentials of other delegates and the credentials of delegates overall. We do not believe it is the responsibility of the Committee to approve challenges on merit, but rather to report any orderly challenges and offer a recommendation. The Committee undertakes this responsibility with utmost sincerity and respect for both the members of DSA and the delegates to the 2019 DSA National Convention, and for the democratically determined processes and rules that govern our organization. When reviewing challenges, we used the Constitution and Bylaws of DSA, the 2019 National Convention Rules, and also the latest edition of Robert’s Rules Rules of Order and the values of DSA as we believe them to be. We strongly suggest that delegates consider these same things when they make a decision on credentials challenges. We created and submitted a report for all delegates to review that is intended to be the sole and exhaustive opinion of the Committee on these challenges. This statement is a non-exhaustive summary of that report, and we ask that delegates refer to the rest of the report if they wish to review all of the details of our Committee’s investigation and the subsequent facts and findings we produced. In the complete report we strived to achieve maximum transparency and clarity. This summary was created for the sake of brevity. The Committee received two orderly credentials challenges. One challenge is against the credentials of Nick J., an at-large delegate. The other challenge is against six delegates from the East Bay chapter. There were no further orderly challenges that were made. B. Nick J. Challenge The Committee received a challenge against the credentials of Nick J. as an at-large delegate. The challenge was made by Sarah L. from the Columbus chapter. Sarah challenged Nick’s credentials on the basis that Nick is allegedly a member of the Columbus chapter and thus violated the Rules requiring at-large delegates to not be members of any chapter. The Committee found that Nick J. communicated to the Columbus chapter leadership of their resignation in November, 2018 and that Nick J. also communicated their resignation to a member of DSA staff, Lisa F., in January, 2019. Lisa told Nick J. in an email that Nick should no longer appear on the Columbus chapter membership list. 2

[PDF page 4] Because Nick J. resigned from the Columbus chapter well in advance of both the election of at-large delegates and the election of the delegates for Columbus, the Committee recommends that Nick J. ’s credentials be upheld and that the respective challenge be overruled. C. East Bay Challenge The Committee received a challenge against the credentials of six delegates from East Bay, who are named as follows: Shane R., Emma G., Andrew R., Max L., Richard M., and Charlie H. The challenge was made by twelve members of the East Bay chapter, who are named as follows: Karina S., Lawrence L., Sergio G., Ted F., Bonnie L., Steve W., Susan S., Mike H., Eric G., Michael K., Stan W., and Gerald S. The Committee interpreted that the challenge was made on several bases: 1. that DSA requires that chapters use a proportional voting method when electing delegates; 2. that the voting method used by East Bay to elect their delegates, referred to as Modified Borda, was a non-proportional method; 3. that there was impropriety in how the election was handled, including the communication to voters of how Modified Borda works and how Modified Borda was selected as a voting method, and lastly; 4. that absentee votes were submitted without clear enough instruction on how Modified Borda works. Firstly, DSA does not require that delegate elections use a proportional voting method. The challengers misinterpret the Rules, which only advise that chapters use a proportional voting method. The challengers also misinterpret the Constitution’s requirement that apportioning of delegates be done according to the principle of one-member, one-vote, as this also does not require that chapters use a proportional voting method. There is a process in the Bylaws for members to force the delegate election to use the Hare system, and the challengers alleged that members pursued this process but then voluntarily abandoned it twice. Because of these findings, we believe that the challengers’ argument around Modified Borda being a non-proportional voting method is irrelevant to the credentials challenge. We took the claim of impropriety in the election very seriously. After reviewing the emails sent out to East Bay members communicating the delegates election, including mentioning and describing Modified Borda, we believe that the description of the voting method was clear enough and was made in a timely enough manner for members before they voted. Additionally, this information was communicated before any member could receive an absentee ballot. Furthermore, how the voting method was chosen did not violate the Bylaws of East Bay and the procedure seemed to be in-line with how elections have been handled in the chapter’s past. Members of East Bay could change their Bylaws at a general meeting to enforce a voting method in future elections if they choose to go through that process. Regarding voting data, the election ballots were counted by volunteers who were not attending the Convention and who represented various political groupings within East Bay. Leaders of the East Bay chapter published most voting data, only excluding individual ballots. The Committee wants to emphasize that the Constitution requires that “[a]ll Local elections of delegates shall be 3

[PDF page 5] by secret ballot. ” With the data published, members of East Bay are able to review and confirm that the scores were correctly computed according to Modified Borda. The Committee believes that one of the strongest held values in DSA is that of local rule, where chapters are allowed many freedoms in determining their democratic processes and activities. So while ultimately East Bay’s delegate election may have contained serious flaws of which may require further deliberation and decision making within their chapter, their delegates election followed all rules required and did not demonstrate any malfeasance serious enough to warrant a national intervention. Thus, the Committee recommends that the credentials of the six named delegates from East Bay be upheld and that the respective challenge be overruled. D. Recommendations To summarize, the Committee recommends that the credentials of both Nick J. and the six named delegates from East Bay be upheld, that all challenges be overruled, and that the Temporary Roster of Delegates, as duly elected representatives of the largest socialist organization in the country, be accepted as the official delegates to the 2019 National Convention of the Democratic Socialists of America. This concludes the summary section of this report. 4

[PDF page 6] II. How the Committee Acted The Credentials Committee ( the Committee ) is a body established and defined by the 2019 National Convention Rules for the 2019 DSA National Convention and appointed by the DSA National Political Committee. The Committee interprets our responsibility as to review, report, and opine on both the challenges that delegates make regarding the credentials of other delegates and the credentials of delegates overall. As the Committee, we want to emphasize that according to the 2019 National Convention Rules, it's not our responsibility to approve challenges but rather to investigate challenges orderly presented according to the Rules and offer a recommendation on these challenges as we report them on the convention floor, as defined in 2019 National Convention Rules, Sections 1.A.9-11. The basis on which we review and opine on each challenge is foremost upon the governing language found in the Constitution and Bylaws of the Democratic Socialists of America and the latest version of the Rules as published by the Rules Committee, and additionally upon RONR (11th ed.) and the values of the Democratic Socialists of America as the members of the Committee believe them to be. We believe that convention delegates should utilize this same basis just mentioned when considering credentials challenges. We recognize that while it is not the responsibility of the Committee to interpret the 2019 National Convention Rules, in writing this report we exercise discretion in interpreting the Constitution and Bylaws of the Democratic Socialists of America. This report serves only as an independent communication of facts, findings, and recommendations based ultimately on our interpretations as a Committee. As such, this report is not a legal nor binding opinion and serves only to inform the 2019 DSA National Convention plenary of the information contained within as an official report of the Committee. This report is intended to be the sole and exhaustive opinion of the Committee on these challenges. The Committee undertakes this responsibility with utmost sincerity and respect for both the members of DSA and the delegates to the 2019 DSA National Convention, and for the democratically determined processes and rules that govern our organization. We aim to treat each challenge of which the Committee is responsible for with due diligence and fairness, striving to disregard any political opinions we may individually have as members of DSA or as delegates to the 2019 DSA National Convention. This report was drafted according to the guidelines prescribed in RONR (11th ed.), pp. 503 - 529 . Section I of this report presents a non-exhaustive summary to be read aloud by a member of the Committee on the convention floor on August 2, 2019 and is intended for the ease of delegates who do not wish to review the full report. The Committee received two credentials challenges that were in order according to the Rules. The Committee investigated each claim by contacting the relevant parties as we decided necessary. The facts based on sources derived from investigation 5

[PDF page 7] and our subsequent findings are listed per challenge within Sections III and IV . First names and initials are used to protect the identity of individuals named in this report. The Committee’s recommendations are listed in Section V . Appendices containing relevant source information referenced throughout this report can be found in Section VI . We have included all relevant source material as possible, including statements from relevant parties as we saw necessary, in the Appendices for delegates to consider. 6

[PDF page 8] III. Nick J. Challenge A. Facts 1. Relevant Language from the Constitution, Bylaws, and Rules (Appendix F) a) The Constitution, Article III, Section 3 states that “Applicants who have been accepted by the Local organization shall, upon receipt of dues and approval of same, automatically become members of the National Organization. Applicants who have been accepted by the National Organization shall, unless otherwise requested by the applicant, become members of the Local organization in the area in which they reside. Members of the National Organization who are not members of a Local organization shall be members-at-large. ” b) The Constitution, Article V, Section 5 states that “No election for delegates to the National Convention shall be held more than four months, or less than forty-five days, prior to the opening of the National Convention. No election for delegates shall be conducted before the apportionment of delegates according to Section 3 of this Article. All Local elections of delegates shall be by secret ballot. Election of delegates may be by proportional representation within the conditions prescribed in the Bylaws. ” c) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.1 states that “Of the total number of delegates, 100 delegates will be reserved for at-large delegates who are not members of a chartered chapter. ” d) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.3 “The National Office shall inform locals of the delegates apportioned to them as of four months prior to the start of the convention, Tuesday, April 2nd. ” e) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.4 “Locals shall conduct and supervise their own elections of Convention delegates and alternate delegates . . . not before the apportionment of delegates. ” f) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.6 states that “A call for candidates for at-large delegates shall be sent to all at-large members no later than Friday, March 1st. At-large delegate nominations will be open 60 days, through Tuesday, April 30th. ” g) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.9 states that “Challenges to the credentials of any delegate or alternate must be submitted in writing to the National Office no later than Friday, July 19th and shall be forwarded to the Credentials Committee appointed by the NPC for consideration. Challenges must either name individual delegates or alternates from one delegation, or may name any one entire delegation, and must include a reason for the challenge that applies to all the credentials challenged. Challenges may include replacement(s) for the delegate or alternate challenged, or challenges may seek to seat additional delegate(s) or alternate(s) as part of a delegation. However, challenges that would result in a delegation exceeding its apportioned number of delegates will not be valid. ” 2. The Challenge a) On July 18, 2019, an email was sent from Sarah L. to the email addresses “convention@dsausa.org” and “abonomo@dsausa.org” communicating a credentials challenge, which was subsequently shared with the Committee on July 20, 2019. (Appendix A.1) (1) The challenge lists Sarah L. as the challenger. 7

[PDF page 9] (2) The challenge is against the credentials of Nick J., as an at-large delegate. (3) Challenger alleges that “[Nick J.] is still on the membership rolls of Columbus DSA and, based on the most recent information we have, still lives within the geographic area of our chapter. ” (4) Challenger alleges that “[Nick J. ’s] presence as a voting member of the convention serves not only to give our chapter an outsize influence (and therefore reduce the influence of truly at-large members), but was also not run through our chapter's democratic processes for delegate determination. ” 3. Subsequent Communications a) On July 22, 2019, the Committee contacted Nick J. asking if Nick J. was a member of the Columbus local as of May 23, 2019, if Nick J. ever resigned from the Columbus local, and if so is there any evidence of such a resignation. (Appendix A.2) (1) Nick J. responded the same day and alleges that Nick J. did “resign from Columbus DSA in November, 2018 due to conflict between [Nick J.] and another chapter leader. ” (2) Nick J. alleges that Nick J. has “not participated in or been a member of Columbus DSA since” a mentioned conflict. (3) Nick J. alleges that “[a]t the encouragement of other DSA comrades both in Columbus DSA and around the country [Nick J. has] remained an at-large member of Democratic Socialists of America, and [Nick J. has] continued to stay as informed and involved in DSA as possible, ” and that “[Nick J. has] been a member in good standing since 2016, was an observer at the 2017 convention, and chose to run for at-large delegate to the 2019 National Convention. ” (4) Nick J. attached a set of screenshots detailing communications around Nick J. ’s resignation. b) On July 29, 2019, the Committee contacted Nick J. asking for a source that can confirm the date on which Nick J. officially resigned from the Columbus local and become solely an at-large member of the Democratic Socialists of America. (1) Nick J. responded the same day with a forwarded email thread detailing communication between Nick J., Lisa F. from DSA staff, and Chris M. from the DSA National Political Committee. (Appendix A.4) 4. Documents a) Nick J. shared a set of screenshots with the Committee on July 22, 2019, two of which were clarified with a forwarded email as mentioned in § III.A.4.b. (1) One screenshot presents an email sent on November 9, 2018, addressed to the Coordinating Committee of the Columbus Local from Carolyn C. (Appendix A.3) (a) Carolyn C. states in the email that Carolyn C. “received a statement of resignation on Thurs evening from [Nick J.]” and that Carolyn C. “will be reading and submitting that statement for the official record during the Nov 29th Coordinating Meeting. ” b) Nick J. shared an email thread with the Committee on July 29, 2019, regarding communication of Nick J. ’s resignation from the Columbus local to the DSA national office. (Appendix A.4) (1) The email thread contains a response from Lisa F. of DSA staff to an email sent by Nick J. on January 20, 2019 requesting to resign from the Columbus local but remain an at-large member. (2) The thread shows that Lisa F. “removed [Nick J. ’s] zip code from [the DSA] database which will prevent [Nick J. ’s] name from appearing on [Nick J. ’s] local chapter's membership list. ” 8

[PDF page 10] B. Findings 1. Candidates for at-large delegate to National Conventions must not be a member of any local of the Democratic Socialists of America. a) 2. The Rules require that at-large delegates are “not members of a chartered chapter. ” (§ III.A.1.c) Members of any local of the Democratic Socialists of America may resign from their local while remaining as at-large members of DSA. a) The Constitution states that individuals who join the Democratic Socialists of America “become members of the Local organization in the area in which they reside” , but allows them to not be members of the respective local if “requested by the applicant. ” (§ III.A.1.a) 3. a) The challenge was submitted in compliance with the 2019 National Convention Rules. The challenge was “submitted in writing to the National Office no later than Friday, July 19th” (§ III.A.1.g) as required by the Rules with the email sent by the challenger. (§ III.A.2.a) 4. Nick J. resigned from the Columbus local in advance of both the nominations period and election of at-large delegates and the earliest election date possible for delegates apportioned to the Columbus local for the 2019 DSA National Convention. a) Nick J. clearly indicated to both the leadership of the Columbus local on November 9, 2018 (§ III.B.4.a.1.a) and to the DSA national office on January 20, 2019 (§ III.B.4.b.1) that Nick J. is resigning from the Columbus local. b) Nominations for at-large delegate occurred starting March 1, 2019 and ending April 30, 2019, well after both dates that Nick J. indicated Nick J. ’s resignation. (§ III.A.1.f) c) The earliest date that the Columbus local could have legally elected their delegates was April 2, 2019, the day the National Office apportioned delegate numbers to locals (§ III.A.1.d), because of the requirements of the rules. (§ III.A.1.e) 5. Nick J. was legally elected to be an at-large delegate to the 2019 DSA National Convention. 9

[PDF page 11] IV. East Bay Challenge A. Facts 1. Relevant Language from the Constitution, Bylaws, and Rules (Appendix F) a) The Constitution, Article V, Section 4 states that “Locals shall conduct their own elections for delegates and the NPC shall conduct elections for at- large delegates according to the guidelines set forth in the By-laws. ” b) The Constitution, Article V, Section 5 states that “All Local elections of delegates shall be by secret ballot. Election of delegates may be by proportional representation within the conditions prescribed in the Bylaws. ” c) The Bylaws, Article VI, Section 3 states that “Locals may determine their own method of election of delegates to the Convention except that a petition from 10% of a Local’s membership or a motion supported by 15% of those present and voting at the Local meeting which determines the method of election will require the use of the Hare system in that Local’s election of delegates to the National Convention” d) The Bylaws, Article VI, Section 3 states that ““Representation shall be based upon dues-paying membership of the organization as of four months prior to the Convention. Apportionment of delegates shall reflect the one-member, one-vote principle, as shall be ordered by the NPC within the guidelines set forth in the Bylaws. However, all Locals shall be entitled to at least one delegate. ” e) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.4 states that “Locals shall conduct and supervise their own elections of Convention delegates and alternate delegates in accordance with the applicable provisions of the DSA Constitution and Bylaws . . . Locals will be advised that delegate elections should use a proportional representation method of election, and of Bylaws Article VI, Section 3, which requires that they use the Hare method upon petition. ” f) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.6 states that “The National Office shall conduct and supervise the election of at-large delegates . . . the National Office shall administer an online election using OpaVote.com or similar online voting system using a Borda counting method” , although it should be noted that there was a technical failure to update this part of the Rules on the DSA website but the change was approved by the NPC (Appendix email from Theresa) g) The 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.9 states that “Challenges to the credentials of any delegate or alternate must be submitted in writing to the National Office no later than Friday, July 19th and shall be forwarded to the Credentials Committee appointed by the NPC for consideration. Challenges must either name individual delegates or alternates from one delegation, or may name any one entire delegation, and must include a reason for the challenge that applies to all the credentials challenged. Challenges may include replacement(s) for the delegate or alternate challenged, or challenges may seek to seat additional delegate(s) or alternate(s) as part of a delegation. However, challenges that would result in a delegation exceeding its apportioned number of delegates will not be valid. ” 2. The Challenge 10

[PDF page 12] a) On July 19, 2019, an email was sent from Ted F. to the email addresses “npc@dsausa.org” and “convention@dsausa.org” communicating a credentials challenge, which was subsequently shared with the Committee on July 22, 2019. (Appendix B.1) (1) The challenge lists Karina S., Lawrence L., Sergio G., Ted F., Bonnie L., Steve W., Susan S., Mike H., Eric G., Michael K., Stan W., and Gerald S. as the challengers. (2) The challenge is against the credentials of Shane R., Emma G., Andrew R., Max L., Richard M., and Charlie H., as six delegates from the East Bay local. (3) Challengers allege that “East Bay DSA's Bread and Roses Caucus (B&R) violated basic democratic principles by unilaterally imposing a non-proportional method of election. ” (4) Challengers allege that “Convention Rules call for proportional representation in delegate elections, ” also citing the “the one-member, one-vote principle” in the Constitution, Article V, Section 5. (5) Challengers allege that “B&R abused power by choosing a non-proportional voting method. ” (6) Challengers request that the Temporary Roster of Delegates, excluding the delegates who are challenged according to the 2019 National Convention Rules, Section I.A.11, vote to “replace the 6 B&R delegates ranked lowest in the delegate election [Shane R., Emma G., Andrew R., Max L., Richard M., and Charlie H.] with the six registered nonB&R alternates who are able to attend the Convention [Bonnie L., Colin PBM., Dan E., Ted F., Colin M., and Jackie A.]. ” b) In the challenge received by the Committee was referenced a longer statement in PDF form entitled “Impropriety in the East Bay DSA Delegate Election” and authored by “Proportional Election Group” , which was used by the Committee for consideration. (Appendix C) (1) The longer statement is authored by all challengers except for Stan W. and Gerald S. (2) The authors allege that the manner in which the East Bay local selected and implemented the voting method used for the delegate elections was “not transparent [nor] open to candidate or member debate. ” (3) The authors allege that “this series of events calls into question . . . the legitimacy of our delegation at the DSA national convention. ” (4) The authors allege that “[i]nformation given to membership about the Borda count and how it works was misleading, particularly regarding . . . the consequences for short-balloting. ” (5) The authors allege that “[i]nsistence that these instructions be amended to inform voters of the consequences of not ranking all 63 candidates led to instructions being officially emailed to membership on June 15, the day before the election meeting, after many absentee ballots had already been completed” (§ IV.A.4.d) (6) The authors allege that the East Bay local “uses secret ballots and voting data contains no identifying information. ” (7) The authors allege that the delegate elections set for June 16, one month after the East Bay local’s annual convention on May 18, “allowed limited time for members to process new, unfamiliar voting procedures and organize responses to decisions made by leadership. ” (8) The authors allege that on May 29, 2019 members first learned that the leadership of the East Bay local “decided to use a ‘first-past-the-post’ system to elect [the] chapter’s 38 delegates. ” (9) The authors allege that “a group of members . . . met and discussed the possibility of petitioning . . . for the use of an STV system” per the Bylaws, Article VI, Section 3. (10)The authors allege that on June 5, 2019, “it was announced via email that the election would be held using a modified Borda count. ” (true, according to § IV.A.4.a) 11

[PDF page 13] (11)The authors allege that in light of the decision to change the voting method from “a ‘first-past-the-post’ system” , the “plan to circulate the petition more widely” , in attempting to follow the process described by the Bylaws, Article VI, Section 3, “was shelved. ” (12)The authors allege that the “possibility of resurrecting the petition” , in attempting to follow the process described by the Bylaws, Article VI, Section 3, “was debated and though some people wanted to continue to push for the clearly proportional and familiar STV system, in the end, the view won out that the little time left before the election was better spent on campaigning. ” (13)The authors allege that the choice to use the modified Borda count was made by a co-chair of the East Bay local who was also the chair of the respective election committee for the delegate election. (14)The authors allege that this “election chair” made the decision to use the modified Borda count with “[n]o oversight or input from the general membership. ” (15)The authors allege that “[c]ommunications about the Borda system from leadership in official chapter emails also did a poor, and even misleading, job of explaining some aspects of the Borda count . . . [p]articularly, the consequences for short-balloting were only superficially addressed. ” (16)The authors allege that “DSA guidelines recommend the use of a proportional system. ” (17)The authors allege that “in reaction to a potential petition for STV, leadership undercut the member-driven initiative for a proportional voting system by switching from first-past-the-post to a modified Borda count. ” (18)The authors allege that the “character, modifications, and consequences of” the modified Borda method ”were poorly explained to voters, if not outright misrepresented. ” (19)The authors allege that at the East Bay Steering Committee meeting on June 22, the “debrief from the election chair made it clear that, due to various circumstances, [the election chair] was left to deal with the selection [of the East Bay local’s] delegate system. ” 3. Subsequent Communications a) On July 24, 2019, the Committee received an email from the co-chairs of the East Bay local, Abigail, Keith, and Hannah, per request of the Committee. (Appendix D.1) (1) The co-chairs submitted their statement that was published on the East Bay local’s website on July 19, 2019. (§ IV.A.4.f) (2) The co-chairs submitted a resolution passed by the East Bay Steering Committee on July 26, 2019, which they allege “addresses lessons learned from the delegate election with the hope of improving processes moving forward. ” (§ IV.A.4.g) (3) The co-chairs state that “[they] urge the Credential Committee to respect the democratic process of our chapter and to please seat the entire elected East Bay DSA delegation. ” b) On July 27, 2019, the Committee received an email mentioning a resolution passed by the East Bay Steering Committee on July 26, 2019. (§ IV.A.4.i) c) On July 27, 2019, a member of the Committee contacted Zach M., and East Bay co-chairs Abigail and Keith, with questions for clarification regarding the timeline around absentee ballots and mentions of the Modified Borda Count. (Appendix D.3) (1) Zach M. responded on the same day with statements and a screenshot of the first email sent to absentee voters in the East Bay delegates election on June 11, 2019, and stated that all absentee voters received a duplicate email. 12

[PDF page 14] (2) Zach M. alleges that on June 5, 2019, “the EBDSA newsletter went out to all members and prominently featured comprehensive information about the June 16th delegate elections (including an explanation of Modified Borda Count). ” (3) Zach M. alleges that on June 11, 2019, regarding requests for absentee ballots, “a PDF ballot was sent out to all requesters whose memberships could be verified against our member list to that point” and that before this “PDF ballot” was sent on June 11, 2019, “only 2-3 dozen requests had been received” and that the “vast majority of requests were made within a few days of the request deadline. ” (4) Zach M. alleges that regarding absentee ballots “[o]nly 3 ballots were received by mail before the day of the election” and that “one came in the week after the election. ” (5) Zach M. alleges that “[o]ut of the 174 absentee ballots counted in the election, 171 were turned in on the day of the election by surrogates turning in ballots on someone else’s behalf. ” (6) Zach M. alleges it was not possible for a member to obtain an absentee ballot before June 5, 2019, the day that it was announced that Modified Borda Count was being used, because “[t]he first absentee ballots were emailed out on June 11. ” (7) Zach M. alleges that “[t]he explanation of modified Borda appeared in the newsletter email sent to the entire membership [of the East Bay local] on June 5, which also announced the email address to contact in order to receive an absentee ballot. ” (8) Zach M. alleges that “[t]he ballots themselves did not explicitly reference modified Borda, only Borda count” and that “[t]he email containing the ballot and instructions explained that unranked candidates would be ‘tied, ’ but did not explain how that tie would be scored. ” d) On July 27, 2019, a member of the Committee contacted Zach M., and East Bay co-chairs Abigail and Keith, with a question for clarification regarding the Bylaws of the East Bay local. Confusing Voter information and Unranked Candidates (Short-balloting) Communications about the Borda system from leadership in official chapter emails also did a poor, and even misleading, job of explaining some important aspects of the Borda count. Particularly, the consequences for short-balloting (ranking only the candidates you are particularly interested in, and leaving others unranked) were only superficially addressed. This is especially relevant, since one of the stated reasons for NOT using STV was that it would be too much to ask members to rank people for all 38 delegate positions. In contradiction to this reason, for a ballot to have full impact with Borda count, a voter needs to rank all 63 candidates. This is clearly not an improvement. Let's take a moment to explain the basics of the Borda count, and the short-balloting modification: Under Borda, in EBDSA's field of 63 candidates, a top ranking gives that candidate 63 points, second place gets 62, third 61 and so on. The initial email sent to membership stated that: "Although you can, you do not have to rank all of the candidates. For example, if you only like 10 of the candidates, you can choose to only include those people 1-10 and leave out the rest. If you choose this method, all other candidates will be tied for eleventh place on your ballot. " It did not explain clearly what "being tied for eleventh place" means. The Borda Wikipedia page, linked to in the very same email, states that the most common method for dealing with short balloting is to assign 1 or 0 points to unranked candidates. In response to individual questions from confused members, leadership clarified in individual emails that they had chosen to do something quite different and that all unranked candidates would receive the same number of points as the rank at which the voter stopped ranking. So - if a voter only ranked 10 candidates, all 53 unranked candidates would receive 52 points each - severely diluting the voter's rankings since their 1st place and 11th through 63rd place would represent only a slight difference in preference. Proportional Representation Proportional Representation : A group of voting systems used in many democracies whose major goal is to ensure that parties and political groups are allocated seats in legislative bodies in proportion to their share of the vote (from fairvote.org/glossary ). At the first Steering Committee meeting after the delegate elections (June 22), the question was raised, "What is proportional? Proportional to what?" This is a valid question which we would like to address in a fairly simple manner. Proportional representation means that if a group/slate has 60% of the support of the chapter, that they should receive 60% of the delegates to the national convention. If another has 5% support, they should get 5% of the delegates. Many of us rightfully bemoan electoral systems where the minority has no chance of having a voice because they have to gain 50%+1 of votes, as happens with a plurality, “winner take all” , “first past the post” voting system - this is a particularly familiar issue to US voters who often look with envy at parliamentary systems where minority parties, with 10-15% of the vote, can still get seats in governing bodies. It should be no surprise then, that DSA guidelines recommend the use of a proportional system for electing delegates to the national convention, because we should be doing better than the systems we aim to dismantle. The DSA Constitution Article V. Section 3 states that “Apportionment of delegates shall reflect the one-member, one-vote principle. ” The 2019 National Convention Rules also explain that, "Locals will be advised that delegate elections should use a proportional representation method of election ” , and of DSA Bylaws Article VI, Section 3, which requires that they use the Hare (STV) method upon petition. Appendix I: Inherent Biases in Borda To begin with, there are a couple of different inherent disproportionalities at play within Borda Inherent Bias #1: Bigger slates with equal support get proportionally more delegates, just for running more candidates. This is a form of strategic nomination called teaming or cloning . For example: In an election where group A and B compete for 30 seats, group A runs 40 candidates while group B runs 20 candidates. Both groups have the same support - 50% of the votes. Using modified Borda count will benefit the larger slate, which could secure around 20 spots (not the proportional 15). This is because the 50% of voters who support group B with its fewer candidates still have to rank, and give points to, all 40 candidates on group A. The result is even worse if members of group B chooses to short-ballot. In effect, group B assigns points to twice as many members of their opposition as from their own slate. While, Slate A only has to rank 20 candidates of their opposition. This is how modified Borda sucks votes away from small slates even if voter support for those slates is dead even. This dynamic was noticed by some voters before the election, as can be seen in this leaflet explaining this very concern among some members of a minority caucus. This graph also illustrates the effect of teaming. To analyze the effect of teaming, we analyze Borda’s sensitivity to difference in slates size. In a proportional system, A gets roughly 20 and B roughly 15 delegates (Slightly more and slightly less than half). With Borda, group A will get 30 delegates since their majority support and tactical voting can lock in all or almost all of their 30 candidates for those 35 seats. That's 10 more than A's proportional 20, and group B is left with 5 (10 less than proportional). Hence, with 55% of voter support, group A can get around 85% of the delegates. Borda is susceptible to manipulation through tactical voting As we will demonstrate, Borda is vulnerable to, and has dynamics that encourage, tactical voting, as opposed to sincere or honest voting. As FairVote.org defines it, tactical voting is "when a voter votes for a candidate other than her sincere choice to prevent an unwanted outcome. " Two types of tactical voting relevant to this discussion are compromising and burying. ● Compromising : voters can benefit by insincerely raising the position of their second choice candidate over their first choice candidate, in order to help the second choice candidate to beat a candidate they like even less ( for example, if they suspect their sincere first choice doesn't have a good chance at winning and don't want to "waste" their vote). ● Burying : voters can give a more-preferred candidate an added advantage in the relative rankings by insincerely lowering another candidate. * This both numbers for unseating and seating were initially at 9. [PDF page 39] While tactical voting is not an inherent bias, Borda has inherent bias that magnifies the effect of tactical voting as described above. This is because the extra voting power afforded to large slates and majorities in Borda allow them to exert disproportionate influence over opposition candidates' rankings. The illustration of both dynamics used by Wikipedia is a hypothetical election for the capital of Tennessee, where polls indicate the two front-runners are Nashville and Chattanooga. Citizens of Knoxville might change their ranking to: 1. Chattanooga (compromising their sincere first choice, Knoxville) 2. Knoxville 3. Memphis (burying their sincere third choice, Nashville) 4. Nashville This tactical voting thereby exaggerates the preference between the perceived frontrunner candidates. In a context like the recent EBDSA delegate elections, with a much larger field of candidates than this simple illustration, examples of tactical voting could include the following: ● Within the ranking of a voter's own slate's 30 preferred candidates, a voter might compromise their sincere first choice if they think that candidate is a shoe-in (on whom the extra points would be "wasted") and boost a less preferred candidate they still wish to support. ● After ranking all their preferred candidates, a voter may insincerely rank a candidate they have no wish to support (but who they think is a shoe-in) higher than a candidate they dislike less but that they think is more vulnerable in the rankings. This would confer "extra" points to a candidate they strongly dislike but figure they can't defeat and deny points to a candidate they dislike a bit less but who they think they can keep from placing. Repeat these tactical voting decisions over and over throughout the voting process and the final points tallies may be very far from a sincere expression of the voters' preferences. In STV, on the contrary, there is really no tactical advantage to doing anything other than putting your favorite candidates first. If, for example, EBDSA had used STV and asked people to rank their preferences for 38 delegate seats (not all 63 candidates), people could really only focus on who they sincerely support, and would have had no disproportionate power to additionally destroy opponents who enjoy some significant (but minority) support among voters.
