[PDF page 52] Appendix E.5 Statement on East Bay Delegate Elections July 19, 2019 02:33 The upcoming DSA National Convention comes at a moment of historic opportunities for our organization and the multi-racial working class movement as a whole. While there is a great deal to be excited about, and we fully expect the convention to be a huge success, we were disappointed to hear that several members of DSA are challenging East Bay’s election of delegates to the DSA National Convention. As the co-chairs of East Bay DSA, we want to address that challenge directly. The challenge rests primarily on the claim that Borda count — the system of ranked-choice voting we used for our elections — is an illegitimate method for electing delegates to the national convention, and that the Single Transferable Vote system would be preferable. In this response we address the question of why we chose Borda count first and then address several of the other concerns raised. We hope that DSA members will uphold our election and reject the credentials challenge — though as we note below we agree with the challengers that DSA should have a standardized election system for national delegates across the country. We would support working with the challengers to write an amendment to the DSA constitution along those lines. And as we outline at the end of this statement, there are certainly important changes we can make to how East Bay runs elections to make them more efficient and more clear. We plan on carrying these changes out this year, and hope other chapters will also do the same. Why did we choose Borda count? For at least the last three years that we have been members, East Bay DSA election methods have been decided by chairs. In 2017, and in prior years as far as we know, East Bay used a simple first past the post system for electing national delegates. After our chapter convention in May, our outgoing co-chair Zach M. and reelected co-chair Abi had to quickly pick a voting system for the national delegate elections. Like most DSA members, none of us claim to be experts on the use of different systems for electing delegates, so we initially planned on using the same system as was used in 2017. Three weeks before the start of the delegate election, some of the writers of the credentials challenge contacted Zach and Abi to request that we switch to ranked-choice voting. We were convinced by their arguments that a simple first past the post system would not ensure that all tendencies would be represented at the national convention. We respect and support DSA’s big tent character and believe all points of view should be represented. Zach was not running to be a delegate so he took the lead to research options for ranked-choice voting. As anyone who has looked into the options knows, Zach found that every ranked-choice system for multi-winner elections has serious flaws in the context of a 63-candidate, 38-winner election. 52

[PDF page 53] At the time we were particularly concerned that STV seemed to be biased towards the most well known figures in a tendency because the person who receives a certain number of first place votes is almost guaranteed to win, despite the fact that they might not have a broader base of support. We were concerned that explaining and understanding the results from STV elections can be very complicated. And we were concerned that STV breaks ties randomly — meaning that you can run an STV election multiple times with the same ballots and get significantly different results, essentially meaning candidates can win or lose an election due to a coin flip. As an alternative, Zach proposed the Modified Borda system. Both Zach and Abi felt this was the best choice given the options and the fact that we were running up against the deadline to elect delegates and had to act fast. Our understanding is that Borda is also a system of proportional representation, but one that gives candidates who are less high profile but have broader bases of support in a chapter a better chance of winning. We also learned that other chapters had used Borda count for national delegate elections and that Borda count had been used by some branches in New York City for their city convention election. Most importantly for helping us make our decision, we learned that national DSA had used Borda count for the election of the 100 at-large delegates (at-large delegates are delegates who do not live in the area of an officially-recognized DSA chapter). Were there other flaws in the election? We absolutely reject the insinuation in the challengers’ letter that there were other improprieties in the election. The challengers argue that the modified Borda system we used was particularly flawed. We do not believe this is the case. There is a version of Borda that allows voters to game the system by “bullet voting” — that is, just voting for a few candidates so they get the most points. We wanted to avoid this so we used the Modified Borda system that disincentivizes bullet voting. We also ensured that the votes were counted by members from many different tendencies, none of whom were running to be delegates. Unfortunately it took us several days to count the votes. In the past our chapter has not used online voting, so we did not use online voting for this election. In hindsight we recognize that that was a foolish decision, as it took several days to count so many votes. In the future we will support switching to online voting for big elections. Why not rerun the election using STV? Some have suggested that we should rerun the election using STV — using the same ballots cast last month. The flaw with this is that voters were given instructions on how to vote using Borda count, not STV. It would therefore be impossible to fairly rerun the elections using STV, since had we used STV voters would have ranked candidates differently. Why were the results different between our chapter convention and the national delegate election? The challengers note that a higher proportion of members of one tendency were elected in the national delegate election in June than were elected to our chapter Steering Committee in May. 53

So far, we know that Fresno and Louisville DSA used Borda count, national DSA used it for at-large delegates, and we suspect other chapters did as well. Seattle and Los Angeles (and likely many other chapters) did not even use a system of proportional representation — instead they used a simple first past the post election in which candidates voted for as many candidates as there were spots for delegates without any ranking system. [PDF page 59] Appendix E.8 EBDSA’s Bloom Reflections on the Credentials Challenge Over the last few weeks, East Bay DSA Steering Committee members of the Bloom slate, including Rex LC (Communications Secretary), Maura M, Marissa S and Allie L (all three At-Large), have spent dozens of hours researching bylaws and election methods, talking to our comrades, and consulting with each other in the wake of the recent credentials challenge of our delegate election for the 2019 DSA Convention. We are deeply troubled by the surge of factionalism and harm that the internal democracy of our chapter has caused on a local and national level. What Happened? The beginning of the delegate election process began shortly after the massive Oakland Teachers Strike and our local chapter convention. Our chapter bylaws dictate that delegate election methods will be determined by an elections subcommittee appointed by the Steering Committee . As detailed in a Steering Committee meeting in July, in our latest National Convention Delegate Elections, all but one member of the elections subcommittee recused themselves to avoid potential conflicts of interest, since they were running to be delegates amongst a candidate pool of our 63 most committed organizers. This meant that at the last minute, a single person from the dominant caucus within our Chapter was left with all decisions about how the election would run. This decision was based on the recommendations of a small number of members who were not elections experts. The decisions included what voting method was used, how that voting method was presented to membership, how ballots would be tallied, and what ballot data would be released. While we cannot know the intentions behind the decisions that were ultimately made, we condemn the failure of leadership to fully address the concerns expressed by voices across tendencies about those decisions. We know that several proactive comrades repeatedly reached out asking for voting methods with better proportionality and more transparency throughout the planning process, and that those concerns were acknowledged but not fully addressed. Our national convention happens only once every two years and is an incredibly important opportunity for chapter members to build their leadership, strengthen connections with comrades from across the country, and debate key priorities for our organization. East Bay leadership was entrusted with the extremely critical task of making sure our Chapter’s diverse perspectives would be heard in our elections, and we believe that the current process described in our bylaws and convention rules, although legal, failed to create the trust needed to engage in a healthy election process. As socialists seeking to build a mass movement against overwhelming odds, we believe that every single member that joins our movement is precious and valuable. Members of the Bloom slate ran for office because we wanted to represent those folks within our Chapter who are feeling silenced and discouraged. Working across tendencies and healing factionalism is a core part of our platform. We are in a historical moment for the labor movement and for socialism, and it will take all of us for this movement to succeed. 59

[PDF page 60] Credentials Challenge With that said, we also disagree with several aspects of the credentials challenge brought forward to the convention floor by members of our chapter. According to the national bylaws, Article V. National Conventions, Section 5 the text reads: No election for delegates to the National Convention shall be held more than four months, or less than forty-five days, prior to the opening of the National Convention. No election for delegates shall be conducted before the apportionment of delegates according to Section 3 of this Article. All Local elections of delegates shall be by secret ballot. Election of delegates may be by proportional representation within the conditions prescribed in the Bylaws. The last line - as interpreted by Bloom and many others - does not indicate that proportional methods must be used, just that they may be. Several other Chapters did not in fact use a proportional method whatsoever for their election. Therefore, we do not believe that our Chapter’s election violated the national bylaws, despite being totally flawed procedurally. We also struggled to define proportionality and understand how different systems compare to each other in this respect. Until quite recently, it was impossible to know or to prove what the actual proportional will of our Chapter was in the election because none of the raw ballot data was made available, despite Bloom’s attempts to push for a full data release. We appreciate that there has now been a partial release of that data which gives us a somewhat clearer picture of the voter breakdown, but we still felt unclear on how to define proportionality in our analysis of the election, lacking clear guidance from National on what that means. None of us are experts in this highly technical area and we have done a lot of research to come to a better understanding of voting systems. Ultimately, we believe that a chapter-wide discussion would have been crucial to define what kind of proportionality we want as a local body. We are also worried about how this challenge could impact how our Chapter and our delegation are viewed by other Chapters, by National, and by other groups outside of DSA who we hope to work with on our major priorities. Our Chapter has done critical, inspiring work in the last year in our electoral campaigns, supporting the Oakland teacher’s strike, fighting for rent control, and calling for public ownership of PG&E. We do not want the tireless work of a huge amount of our members to be overshadowed by the missteps of the few leaders who made this error. Furthermore and probably most important to our ultimate decision, we strongly disagreed with the method of redress proposed by the challenge . While we definitely recognize the deep harm felt by many in our Chapter from the failures of our democracy, we feel that the responsibility and accountability for that failure should rest upon the leadership of our Chapter. We have great respect and close working relationships with several of the comrades who would be unseated by the election challenge. As far as we know, they were not involved in planning or running our election . We feel that unseating them simply because they are part of the dominant tendency that may have benefited from those decisions without consulting our whole membership would increase the harm to more people within our Chapter and build greater discord. We also worry 60

[PDF page 61] about the precedent set by removing members of a delegation selectively on the basis of their caucus affiliation when we cannot prove intent, given that we see great value in our own caucus affiliations and appreciate the ways in which caucuses can strengthen our movement. The Recent Steering Committee Resolution All of these factors weighed very heavily on us as newly elected Steering Committee members who truly love our Chapter and dedicate the vast majority of our free time to socialist organizing, often at great personal and emotional cost. Every one of us is grappling with how to honor the trust members have placed in us and make principled leadership decisions in extremely complicated and difficult circumstances. Based on the aforementioned, and as newly elected members of our Steering Committee, we decided the best course of action would be to propose significant amendments to a resolution addressing the credentials challenge introduced by chapter co-chairs Keith and Abigail, recognizing the limitations of our current process and calling the national convention to seat the entire delegation as elected. Our amendments were all accepted and Bloom has resolved to: 1) Require that our full general membership have input into our election method moving forward and work toward establishing that method within our bylaws so this never happens again 2) Require the full release of secret ballot data following every delegate election and work toward a permanent bylaws amendment to this effect 3) Ensuring that there is an open meeting with all delegates following the election in the future where members can give their input on national resolutions and bylaws to build a more truly representative delegation 4) Urge National to standardize voting procedures, which would provide much clearer guidance and leadership to locals on the election methods that are recommended to ensure the most fairness and the best proportionality moving forward. None of the solutions proposed by our chapter or the challengers so far seem sufficient to address the harm that has been done. We believe that the nature of the challenge does not only rely on the legality of the process, but the nuances required to legitimize democratic participation . [PDF page 1] Report of the Medicare for All Campaign Committee to the 2019 Convention of the Democratic Socialists of America Submitted to the National Political Committee of DSA by the Medicare for All Campaign Steering Committee on July 14, 2019. The purpose of this report is (1) to provide the membership of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) with an overview of campaign objectives, organization, and activities; (2) to provide the Convention with a report of how campaign committees and volunteers carried out the tasks committed to them; and (3) to inform the assembled membership of the successes and shortcomings of our campaign in a way that allows them to plan more effectively in the future. To that end we have included key recommendations throughout the report and in the report’ s conclusion. Table of Contents Campaign Committee 2 Overview 3 Objectives 3 Communications 4 Tactics 7 Regional Organizers 9 Organizational Challenges 11 Goals for 2019-2021 1 2 Collected Recommendations 13 Appendix I. 14 1

[PDF page 2] Campaign Committee DSA’ s Medicare for All campaign is composed of the following committees: Steering Committee: Dustin Guastella (Chair), Megan Svoboda (Secretary), Ash Clark, Benjamin Fong, Jeremy Gong, Chris Riddiough, Luke Thibault Communications Subcommittee: Luke Thibault (Co-chair), Ash Clark (Co-chair), Chris Middleman, Chuck McKeever, Kirsten O’Brien, Stephen Gose, Andrew Hudson, Brian Cipriano, Cale Brooks, Connary Fagen, Tim Higginbotham Organizing Subcommittee: Megan Svoboda (Chair), Benjamin Fong, Frances Gill, Matt Stone Regional Organizers: 1 James Dunn, Emily Betoma, Chris Diehn, Cris Carlson, Sean Mason, Kate Schneider, Christie Offenbacher, Jamie Munro, Tim Johnson, Paul Alexander, Brent O’Reilly, Allison Tebbe, Sheridan Aspinwall, Matthew Monteverde Policy Subcommittee: Andrej Markovcic, Chris Middleman, Tim Higginbotham Political Subcommittee: Coalition Partners: Michael Lighty (Sanders Institute), Mark Dudzic (Labor Campaign for Single Payer) DSA Working Groups: Justine Medina (Queer Socialists), Andee Sunderland (Socialist Feminists), Andrew Porter (Democratic Socialist Labor Commission), Max Cotterill (National Electoral Committee) At-Large Members: Nick Condor (Louisville), James Cole (Austin), Valerie Davis (N. Texas) , Ashlyn Velasquez (Denver) , Sam Forman (Los Angeles), Jen James (NYC BUM), Jorge Roman-Romero (Green Country, OK), Mariana Pineda (Suffolk County), Ben Himmelfarb (Hudson Valley), Ben Beckett (NYC Queens), Devin Howard (Phoenix) 1 A volunteer organizer corps under the umbrella of the Organizing Subcommittee 2

[PDF page 3] Overview DSA’ s Medicare for All Campaign Committee was established by the August 2017 Convention. The Steering Committee of the campaign was appointed by the National Political Committee and first convened in October of the same year. The Steering Committee met weekly via teleconference since its first meeting through April 2019 and has recently moved to meeting every other week. The Organizing Subcommittee, including the Regional Organizers, have convened every other week since the beginning of the campaign. The Communications Subcommittee met regularly with the Steering Committee from December 2017, and began meeting independently of the Steering Committee on a bi-weekly basis in March of 2019. The campaign structure was effective: the Communications Subcommittee has been remarkably successful at building a vast media presence for the campaign, and the Organizing Subcommittee has similarly been successful in developing a Medicare for All field presence. The Organizing Subcommittee established a particularly effective Regional Organizer program, which represents a mid-level structure within DSA that can help facilitate a cohesive and coordinated approach to campaigns while aiding locals in a host of organizing skills. Finally, the committee has developed a working relationship with National Nurses United and Our Revolution in their campaign for Medicare for All. Overall, the campaign has developed a broad all-volunteer organizing structure, making great strides in member-mobilization capacity, and has made significant interventions in policy debates and public perception. Objectives No one could have predicted the success of Bernie Sanders ’ s 2016 run, which thrust single-payer healthcare into the limelight and revealed it to be a remarkably popular working-class demand. This presented a unique opportunity for DSA, not because there existed an already vibrant single-payer movement for us to plug into, but because the organization had the chance to shape the discourse around Medicare for All with a democratic socialist framing and to build our organizational capacities in the process. In these twin goals, the Committee believes the campaign has been largely successful: DSA has held nationally coordinated “ weekends of action ” around Medicare for All at a time when there was nothing similar happening in the field, and to this day DSA bears the largest field presence of any organization in the fight for single-payer, despite having a fraction of the resources. In addition, chapters and chapter leaders around the country have developed their organizing skills through the organization of canvasses, tables, town halls, speaking tour stops, and more. The Committee does not have precise metrics to gauge the success of these two goals, however, and will speak more about this in the “Tactics ” section. The Medicare for All campaign was organized around five principles: 3

[PDF page 4] 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. A Single Health Program : Everyone will be covered by one health insurance program, administered by the federal government, and have equal access to all medical services and treatments. Comprehensive Coverage : All services requiring a medical professional will be fully covered. You go to the doctor of your choice. Dental, vision, mental health, and pharmaceuticals are all included. Free at the point of service : All healthcare costs will be financed through tax contributions based on ability to pay: no copays, no fees, no deductibles and no premiums. Ever. Universal Coverage : Coverage for all United States residents — non-citizens included. Jobs : A jobs initiative and severance for those affected by the transition to government-run healthcare. The aim of the Medicare for All campaign from its inception was to use DSA’ s five principles not to plug into an already existing movement or coalition, but rather to foment excitement and organization around a tremendously popular proposal. This was made clear in the campaign ’ s founding document : “Our immediate tasks are twofold: 1) to raise the political profile of Medicare for All such that it becomes an issue of national political importance and 2) to build DSA as a nationwide force with a coherent organizing infrastructure and salient political orientation to mold and direct mass political activity. ” In both cases, the stated aim was to create something where it did not before exist. These five principles allow us to judge the merits of proposed legislation, as the Committee has done with our Nothing Less! policy comparison pamphlet . The Committee also believes that the five principles were sufficiently broad to encompass the range of demands the Committee wanted to see included in Medicare for All legislation. Among other things, these included coverage for undocumented immigrants (included in principle #4) and repeal of the Hyde Amendment (included in principle #2). As the Committee states in our original organizing guide , “ repealing the Hyde Amendment (which bars use of federal funds for abortion) would liberate working-class women from dependency on their or their partners ’ jobs while taking the greatest leap forward in reproductive healthcare in 45 years. ” Communications The scope of communications work for our Medicare for All campaign primarily includes: original campaign branding and design assets including merchandise, web design, print graphics, a blog, email blasts, a monthly newsletter, press releases, traditional media outreach, articles, videos, and a website, as well as maintaining our own social media, email and various messaging platforms for internal and external campaign communications. In addition to populating our own channels with high-quality Medicare for All content, we also assist with talking points and communications support for DSA staff, members and coalition partners when interacting with the press. 4

[PDF page 5] The Communications Subcommittee was formed during the inception of the Medicare for All priority campaign in 2017. It went without dedicated leadership, answering to the Steering Committee as a whole until January 2019 when the Steering Committee adopted a motion to expand to include members of Communications. Shortly thereafter, Ash Clark and Luke Thibault were elected Communications Subcommittee Co-chairs to oversee and direct our growing communications work. The subcommittee began holding bi-weekly communications meetings in February 2019. Today, there are ten members of the subcommittee from chapters all across the country. The first priority for our communications work is to define and broadcast our demands with five principles. Listed above, these principles provided a simple democratic socialist framework within which to propagate, agitate, and educate around single-payer healthcare. Our high level goals are to explain to the general public what Medicare for All is (and is not), connect Medicare for All to democratic socialism, and support the healthcare activism of chapters. In the process of achieving these goals, the subcommittee facilitated communication between DSA members and the national campaign; coordinated the national campaign with coalition partners and DSA staff; produced a variety of articles, videos, flyers, materials, apparel, and resources; and amplified the bottom-up work of chapters through social media, blogs, newsletters, and press releases. In the effort to create materials and propaganda we are guided by best practices determined at the onset of the campaign. First, we have made our campaign cohesive with a strong identity so that chapters across the country know they are participating in a national effort. Second, we set an expectation for accessibility, making sure that every video we produced was closed-captioned and that our core materials were made widely available with Spanish print and audio versions. Lastly, we strive to provide template formats, volunteer time, best practice guides, and design resources so that chapters can easily adapt materials as needed (e.g. by providing chapters with everything from fonts to full videos). To that end, we piloted a “ campaign in a box ” program that guaranteed that chapters of all sizes had everything they needed to start their own grassroots campaigns, no matter where they were located or what resources they started with. Combined with support from Regional Organizers, these boxes helped develop members ’ canvassing skills and start thousands of organizing conversations. The Communications Subcommittee created a website (medicareforall.dsausa.org) to house all of the above materials—organizing guides, canvassing resources, videos, etc. In addition, the website includes a blog, maintained by our Blog Editor, to provide further education, propaganda, and campaign news. It contains 95 articles, most of which are original content. The website is built against the same design and style guide as the rest of our campaign materials in order to provide a consistent look and feel. The site was built using a general-purpose web framework which can be repurposed for future campaigns. The DSA for Bernie campaign is already using this framework, which has greatly reduced time to launch. The website is driven 5

[PDF page 6] by a Content Management System backend in order to, over time, make much of the website content modifiable by the rest of the Committee, reducing the friction for keeping the website content fresh. Over the course of our campaign, the communications work grew in scope and scale of operation as new members joined the team and the demands of the campaign grew. Despite starting small, communications has proven to be a core component of our campaign to win Medicare for All. In myriad ways, the subcommittee ensures our messaging engages millions of people with a powerful democratic socialist demand. In under two years, our Twitter account has organically grown to nearly 20k followers and counting. In October we started a newsletter to communicate campaign news, events, opportunities to get involved and highlight chapter work across the country. The newsletter is now sent monthly and reaches nearly 3,000 subscribers with a 40% open rate. Our website has garnered 38k unique visitors and 63k page views, one third of which is “direct, ” meaning it comes from people searching the URL directly. Our videos have garnered over three million views collectively. We regularly issue press releases for national events (one of which was read aloud by Mitch McConnell on the Senate floor), and provide templates of these to chapters. Our five principles have permeated the discourse and continue to define the demands of our coalition as well as those co-sponsoring single-payer bills. We equip chapters across the country with beautiful and effective tools for their activism, and our communications infrastructure is being replicated in campaigns throughout DSA. Our style guide, best practices, website, and social media strategy are heavily informing DSA for Bernie 2020, making our campaign the model for national priorities going forward. In spite of our successes, two main communication challenges have been recurring over the course of our campaign. The first is that a campaign as large and sophisticated as this requires an increasing number of skilled volunteers who not only can commit a lot of time, but can do so with a high degree of reliability and responsibility. The second challenge is that coordinating with national DSA staff has been consistently uneven. During our coordination with national staff, we repeatedly ran into problems with access to social media and email channels that have made it difficult to effectively accomplish our goals. The extraneous steps we take to get our copy and materials out through national adds to the burden on volunteers already stretched thin. Therefore, the Medicare for All Communications Subcommittee makes the following recommendations: Communications Recommendations: 1. That the Medicare for All Campaign Committee shall be primarily responsible for creating political education, communication and social media content relating to DSA’ s Medicare for All campaign and shall have final approval of campaign communications sent through national channels; and, 6

[PDF page 7] 2. 3. That the Medicare for All Communications Subcommittee shall receive support from national staff when required to meet specifications for sending communications to the membership; and, That the campaign shall provide design and copy to staff for communications, but shall not duplicate administrative work, such as coding or otherwise formatting data, resizing images, or managing non-Medicare for All accounts; Tactics From its inception the Medicare for All campaign focused on supporting a diversity of tactics that allow DSA members to engage a maximum number of people to recognize their interest in Medicare for All and democratic socialism. Our initial organizing guide was written by 19 DSA members around the country and offered guidance in the execution of multiple mass tactics, including running canvasses, holding educational events, taking over town halls, and integrating Medicare for All into electoral work. The Medicare for All Campaign Committee has since released a second House pressure organizing guide , offering further guidance in coalition building, setting meetings with legislators, and escalating pressure on legislators. The Committee emphasizes the importance of canvassing as a mass tactic that provides DSA members with an opportunity to have face-to-face conversations with people about Medicare for All and democratic socialism. The importance of canvassing for a political organization like ours cannot be overstated. The only weapon we have against larger, better-funded and hostile political interests is a political and economic program that speaks to the needs, desires, and aspirations of working people in the United States. This program, however, does not automatically get broadcast onto the television screens and social media feeds of the mass of American workers. Instead, the labor-intensive and difficult task of bringing our ideas door-to-door is necessary. No level of media can replace the persuasive power of in-person conversations, and our conversations have been a fruitful demonstration of the socialist truism that class interest can generate a binding solidarity and a strong level of class political identification. Medicare for All is as much in the interest of our membership as it is in those potential supporters we meet, which means that conversations around its fruition are conversations about “ ” us versus the elite. These conversations have helped organizers learn how to translate their ideas into a common language, given canvassers the confidence to rebut corporate talking points, popularized the principles and ideas of a democratic socialist approach to health care, and attracted many into the organization itself. For these reasons, we believe that the mass-mobilization approach, with canvassing as a leading (though not exclusive) tactic is essential. Beyond these primary objectives, canvassing for Medicare for All has built up the electoral infrastructure of many chapters and enabled them to develop campaigns for 7

[PDF page 8] democratic socialist candidates across the country. The committee is proud that our canvassing program has been used in chapters to help organize and mobilize members for campaigns outside the scope of our Committee. Special thanks is owed to any member who serves as a Canvass Captain or who has organized and participated in our Medicare for All canvasses across the country. Beyond canvassing, the campaign also provided resources and trainings for DSA members on a variety of other tactics, including: ● Organizing and Leadership Development ● Holding Education Events ● Showing up at Elected Officials Town Halls ● Delivering a Political Speech ● Integrating your Medicare for All campaign with Electoral Work ● Passing a Medicare for All City Council Resolution The Committee has also encouraged chapters to set goals for their campaigns, and tie their Medicare for All work to local legislation. Many chapters have had great successes: ● Austin ’ s Paid Sick campaign is a model Medicare for All campaign, one that the Committee highlighted on our blog , on social media, in newsletters, on a Political Subcommittee call, and on a national organizing call . ● Ventura County , Long Beach , Bloomington-Normal , and many other chapters have launched canvassing programs through their Medicare for All work. ● Green Country supported teachers strikes, partnered with Oklahoma University Tulsa ' s School of Community Medicine for an educational event on universal healthcare, and made videos of members telling their personal healthcare stories and how Medicare for All would help them. ● Phoenix, Hudson Valley , Seattle , Northern Indiana and many other chapters have hosted Medicare for All Town Halls and used their canvassing operations to drive turnout. ● Boulder put on Medicaid sign-up events. ● Philadelphia passed the first city council resolution in support of Medicare for All. ● Santa Fe participated in the Health Security for New Mexicans Campaign, making it the chapter ’ s first chapter-wide campaign. Doña Ana County also made the HSA a top priority, and Albuquerque has agreed to help. ● In the summer of 2018 DSA members from West Virginia ’ s three main DSA chapters kicked off their first-ever joint campaign, focusing on the struggle to fund the Public Employees Insurance Agency (PEIA) and its connection to our larger national demand for Medicare for All. ● East Bay combined their campaign to elect Jovanka Beckles to State Assembly with their Medicare for All work. Similarly, Philadelphia combined their campaigns for Kristin Seale and Elizabeth Fiedler with Medicare for All canvassing and emphasis. Each 8

[PDF page 9] interaction at the door was a chance to talk to working people not just about their candidates, but about Medicare for All as a democratic socialist demand. ● Detroit demanded that Governor Gretchen Whitmer remove Blue Cross Blue Shield CEO Dan Loepp from her transition team. When Whitmer declined, DSAers marched on the Blues ’ Lansing headquarters to demand Loepp step down. ● Portland pressured Senator Wyden and Rep. Kurt Shrader to support Medicare for All through a series of public town halls. Bloomington-Normal pressured Rep. Rodney Davis. Many other DSA chapters are participating in the current campaign pressuring house reps to sign onto H.R. 1384. Austin successfully pressured Rep. Lloyd Doggett to co-sponsor the bill, and Louisville pressured Representative John Yarmuth to do as well. The Committee has also focused on planning major national events that chapters can use to organize around. These included three weekends of action— June 15th and 16th, 2019 , August 11th and 12th, 2018 , and April 21st and 22nd, 2018 and two regional speaking tours about Medicare for All, one across the South and the other through the Northeast . Despite the visibility of our successes, the campaign has not kept precise metrics on canvassing/outreach activity around the country, and we believe to DSA’ s detriment. The Committee attempted to roll out a national Action Network account, in order to create the necessary infrastructure for tracking this information, but was asked to abandon the project in late 2018. We have not thus far been in possession of the tools to keep metrics on the campaign, and we hope that DSA’ s national data situation improves so that every national priority campaign can do so. Tactical Recommendation: 1. 2. 3. 4. That participants in the DSA Medicare for All campaign pursue tactics tied to concrete activities that build organizing capacity and visibility for Medicare for All -- such as pressuring representatives, organizing town halls, canvassing, passing municipal resolutions et cetera; and, That participants in the DSA Medicare for All campaign pursue realizable short and medium term goals; and, That the DSA Medicare for All campaign committee shall offer guidance to locals upon request; and, That the DSA Medicare for All campaign committee shall promote tactical and strategic successes with the aim of building cross chapter communication and organization. Regional Organizers One of the campaign ’ s chief accomplishments was the organization and implementation of an all-volunteer Regional Organizer structure. Each Regional Organizer is responsible for a specific region of the country, communicating with chapters in that region about their Medicare 9

[PDF page 10] for All campaigns, offering support from the national campaign, and communicating national developments from within the campaign and the broader Medicare for All world. Throughout the campaign we have added Regional Organizers as needed and now have 14 Regional Organizers: WEST CA: James Dunn WA, OR, ID, MT, HI, AK: Paul Alexan der NV, AZ, UT, WY, CO, NM: Chris Diehn MIDWEST IL, IN, OH, MO: Brent O’Reilly ND, SD, MI, MN, IA, WI: Tim Johnson OK, KS, NE: Emily Betoma SOUTH TX: Kate Schneider LA, MS, AL, AR, TN: Allison Tebbe FL, GA, SC: Cris Carlson EAST NC, VA, KY, WV: Matthew Monteverde 10

[PDF page 11] PA, MD, DC, NJ, DE: Sean Mason NY State: Jamie Munro NYC: Christie Offenbacher ME, VT, NH, MA, CT, RI: Sheridan Aspinwall This structure has allowed us to exponentially increase our organizing capacity. Regional Organizers not only serve as guides to Medicare for All organizing; they also help relay important information from the chapter level to the national campaign and disseminate tactics and short-term campaign goals throughout the country. Finally, the Regional Organizer program has been key to developing a pipeline of organizers throughout the country who have a serious democratic socialist political vision and the skills needed to realize our collective aims. Organizational Challenges One difficulty in the campaign from the beginning, for both the Organizing and Communications Subcommittees, was communication with national staff. It was a struggle figuring out who to contact about what, and accomplishing basic tasks often proved to be challenging. In January 2019, Kaitlin Marone was assigned to be a part-time Medicare for All organizer, and though Kaitlin has been very helpful, the Committee recommends that a full-time Medicare for All director be hired to handle the many moving parts of the campaign. This is also important for maintaining coalition partners, as many are unsure how to relate to a volunteer-run campaign and would appreciate the stability of a staff contact. The largest intra-Committee challenge we ’ ve encountered has been the question of the role of the Political Subcommittee within the campaign. The Committee had hoped that the Political Subcommittee would be the policy research/agenda setting body, but it was clear from the beginning that engaged Political Subcommittee members wanted to have more of an organizing role within the campaign. This created confusion and disengagement. It was also difficult to coordinate meeting times with such a large body. By the summer of 2018, the Political Subcommittee was already a defunct body, with many members reporting that they considered it functionally dissolved. In the fall of 2018, the Policy Subcommittee was created to meet the need for policy research. In retrospect, the Committee should have attempted to incorporate Political Subcommittee members into other aspects of the campaign that were more directly tied to our day-to-day work. A large inter-Committee challenge we ’ ve encountered was knowing when and how to respond to suggestions or criticisms of the campaign. Most of the criticism of the campaign has taken place on social media, and the Committee was simply unsure of how to engage these online criticisms in a productive way. We believe there ought to be clear means of registering member suggestions and criticisms of the campaign, and clear mechanisms for holding the campaign accountable. 11

[PDF page 12] The greatest external challenge we ’ ve faced has been the campaign ’ s relationship to the larger Medicare for All coalition. Our first Medicare for All weekend of action in April 2018, which involved 45 chapters , was an exciting coming-out party for DSA and the Medicare for All campaign. Nothing similar had been organized in DSA’ s recent history. The idea was to channel that energy into the emerging campaign to win Medicare for All organized by NNU, of which DSA was a founding coalition partner. At the time, the Committee had every reason to believe plugging into a larger coalition was the best way to advance our work, and DSA eagerly participated in this initial formation. However, by the fall of 2018, this larger campaign had effectively disbanded, and DSA’ s Medicare for All campaign had to reorient without the hope of guidance from the larger coalition. The Committee built expansive field and sophisticated communications presences, but did not have the “inside the beltway ” knowledge to think through a national legislative strategy (as NNU did). The Committee had hoped to receive serious direction from the larger NNU campaign, which unfortunately never materialized. The NNU campaign has since reconvened as a coalition of groups, and while DSA has a seat at the table, the Committee is not as reliant on NNU for the overall strategy of our campaign, having learned our lesson the first time around. Thus, while the larger NNU coalition is also working on a House pressure campaign, DSA’ s own House pressure campaign, kicked off by the release of an addendum to our first organizing guide , is separately organized and executed. The Committee is nonetheless still working with the larger coalition to decide strategic House targets and to convene local tables. Organizational Recommendations: 1. 2. 3. That the DSA NPC shall, in consultation with the Medicare for All Campaign Committee, hire a full-time Medicare for All campaign director, familiar with the campaign and Committee; and, That said director will work in conjunction with the Medicare for All campaign and act as the point of contact for coalition partners; and, That the Political Subcommittee of the Medicare for All campaign shall be dissolved, and its members invited to join other Medicare for All campaign committees. Goals for 2019-2021 In retrospect, the Committee recognizes the demanding nature of the campaign ’ s initial goals. At the time of the campaign ’ s formation, viable single-payer legislation did not really exist: H.R. 676 was largely a messaging bill, and S. 1804 had just been introduced, seemed to need significant improvements, and in any event bore no path to victory in the Senate. Rather than winning something that was already in existence, our aim was to put something on the table, and this required a mass informational campaign wherein we had to set our own benchmarks. We believe our initial ambitious goals are worth pursuing: DSA should take advantage of the opportunity to shape the discourse around key proposals that currently lack a precise path to 12

[PDF page 13] victory—for instance, the Green New Deal. But since excellent Medicare for All bills exist in both the House and Senate now, and Bernie Sanders ’ s presidential candidacy puts the realization of socialized health insurance on the immediate horizon, DSA’ s Medicare for All campaign should have precise goals for the next two years. In addition to working for these two bills and to elect Bernie Sanders and other Medicare for All legislators, the Committee believes we should also begin organizing protests and demonstrations on insurance and pharmaceutical companies, bringing pressure to the source of our broken healthcare system. We also believe it strategic to join in the campaign to pass municipal resolutions in support of Medicare for All , as many of our chapters have already done. Recommendation : 1. DSA’ s Medicare for All campaign will continue to organize the movement for Medicare for All through a variety of tactics, but focus its efforts around the following five goals: a. Helping chapters tie their existing Medicare for All campaigns to work to elect Bernie Sanders as President. b. Getting as many U.S. Representatives as possible to sign on to H.R. 1384, the Medicare for All Act of 2019, by carrying out independent field operations as described in the House pressure organizing guide and in conjunction with the NNU coalition. Where strategic, this can also apply to getting U.S. Senators to sign on to S. 1129. c. d. Electing Medicare for All legislators. That the DSA Medicare for All campaign committee shall offer guidance to locals upon request; and, 11. That the DSA Medicare for All campaign committee shall promote tactical and strategic local successes with the aim of building cross chapter communication and organization. Appendix I. Campaign Accomplishments Timeline 14

[PDF page 15] Over the course of our campaign there have been two iterations of single-payer bills in the House and Senate, and we ’ ve seen polling for them climb from 49% to 70% . Over 100 chapters have become active participants in the campaign, organizing countless chapter actions ranging from canvasses to town halls to direct actions. 2017 (August to December) The campaign proposal was passed at DSA’ s 2017 National Convention. A month later, Bernie Sanders introduced S.1804, the Medicare for All Act of 2017. We commissioned and developed a design identity, including a style guide and logo. We launched the first pages of our website, as well as our Facebook and Twitter accounts. The first organizing guide was published for print and web. We hosted two national zoom calls with chapter leaders and organizers, one of which featured Carlos Rosa and Lee Carter. We published three videos to kick off our campaign featuring Meagan Day, Michael Lighty, and Tim Faust. 2018 In 2018 we held 12 national Zoom call trainings and webinars, published 15 videos, added 3 pages to our website, and placed 5 articles in Vox, Huffington Post, NBC, and Jacobin. The Political Subcommittee, composed of coalition partners, DSA working groups, and at-large members, convened. We recruited and trained seven Regional Organizers (ROs) to coordinate our organizing across the country. We joined a coalition with NNU, the Labor Campaign for Single Payer, Healthcare NOW, and Our Revolution. We organized watch parties for Bernie ’ s Medicare for All town hall. We held two national Weekends of Action, in April and July. We rallied support for the University of California statewide AFSCME strike with the DSLC. We coordinated large participation in the national Single-Payer Strategy Conference with panel speakers, a protest march contingent, and DSA Medicare for All breakouts. We organized the first leg of a national speaking tour, “All In, ” featuring Michael Lighty, with ten DSA chapters in Arizona, Texas, Louisiana, and Florida. Austin DSA helped win paid sick days. Philly DSA passed a Medicare for All city resolution. To get chapters started, our campaign kit launched at the start of the year. Priced at a sliding scale, it included political education brochures, organizing manuals, t-shirts, buttons and stickers for use in campaign activities (all of these were made available on the national DSA Store). We translated our online materials into Spanish and created accessible audio versions of our trifold. We created new materials, including a “Labor & Medicare for All” pamphlet for Labor Notes, and a Medicare for All issue of Democratic Left. We provided chapters with a communications best practices guide and piloted a program for print and traditional media initiatives. We launched our now monthly newsletter, All In. 15

[PDF page 16] Following the midterms, our House Pressure Campaign began in coordination with National Nurses United (NNU) and other coalition partners to move the new Medicare for All bill through the House of Representatives. 2019 (January to June) In 2019, new single-payer legislation was introduced in the House and the Senate. Our campaign endorsed both bills. HR 1384, the Medicare for All Act of 2019, was introduced in the House by Pramila Jayapal. SB 1129, the Medicare for All Act of 2019, was introduced in the Senate by Bernie Sanders, with legislation now including long-term care. The first Congressional hearing for Medicare for All featured DSA member Ady Barkan as a result of movement pressure. Austin DSA successfully helped push Lloyd Doggett to cosponsor HR 1384, and Louisville DSA successfully helped push John Yarmouth to cosponsor HR 1384. For our House Pressure Campaign we published a new organizing guide and hosted a national training. We organized the second leg of a national speaking tour, “Nothing Less ” in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Massachusetts. We also organized our third national Weekend of Action (June 15th & 16th). We created a “Nothing Less ” policy guide, comparing different competing healthcare plans. We published six videos and placed five articles in Jacobin. We called on DSA to endorse Bernie Sanders for president and following the endorsement we created a plan to include Bernie in our messaging and coordinate support for the DSA for Bernie campaign. 16

Proposed Resolutions to the DSA National Convention (Part I)

The Convention Resolutions Committee (Jared Abbott, Paul Garver, Jeremy Gong, Natalie Midiri and Chris Riddiough) has compiled the following list of resolutions for consideration by the National Convention. The list is now complete and additional resolutions will not be accepted.

The proposals following are listed in the order in which they were received. For each proposed amendment the number, timestamp, information about the sponsor(s)/proposer(s) of the resolution, their rationale for the amendment, old language, and proposed new language.

Amendments submitted to these constitutional and bylaw amendments are included in the packet of amendments to resolutions and constitutional amendments.

_____________________________________________________________

Resolutions

Number 2        Timestamp  6/21/17, 2:56 AM

Name(s) and Local(s) of those proposing the resolution who will serve as lead contact(s): Benjamin Arriaga & DSA, Sacramento

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

Given the difficulty of ensuring that what is communicated from any voice, individual or collective of any size, is in fact communicated as intended to the intended audience however large, this resolution would set forward an organizational and functional priority for establishing standards for internal social-movement-organizational communication.

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

Writing and theory-building.

Financial/Budgetary Implications for DSA:

No cost estimate, but anywhere from 1-5 years depending on how thorough standards are developed and how often they are revised. Three years would be likely, but one year is possible based on how soon communication about how to improve communication can yield results.

_________________________________________

Number 3        Timestamp  6/26/17, 12:30 AM

Name(s) and Local(s) of those proposing the resolution who will serve as lead contact(s): Collin Pucher, Seattle

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

While reforming prisons to improve the conditions of those currently incarcerated is a worthwhile goal, we must keep in mind our eventual goal is the abolition of prisons. This would be a symbolic resolution supporting prison abolition.

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

An acknowledgement of the eventual goal of prison abolition, not just reform.

Financial/Budgetary Implications for DSA:

$0.

______________________________________

Number 4        Timestamp 6/26/17, 3:46 PM

Name(s) and Local(s) of those proposing the resolution who will serve as lead contact(s): Molly Niedbala, Central Brooklyn DSA

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

To strip major private banks of significant funding, disabling investment in unjust projects like private prisons and fossil fuel infrastructure; to make the spending of public funds more transparent; and to make public funds significantly more available for investment in local projects that would benefit marginalized communities, such as community land trusts and infrastructure that would mitigate the effects of sea level rise

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

I propose a resolution to advocate for municipal banking in all 50 states, but particularly in NYC, as an alternative to cities' investment of public tax dollars in private banks (which invest that money in myriad unjust projects - e.g., private prisons, pipelines on indigenous lands, etc.) Public banking would give cities more transparent control over how their tax dollars are spent and would make funds available for investment in low- and medium-risk local projects (e.g., community land trusts, mini-grids compatible with renewable energy sources, etc.). Organizing would consist largely in 1) coalition-building with indigenous people and communities of color, who have the most to gain from a) stripping major private banks of significant funding and b) public investment in community projects, 2) public education via canvassing, 3) drafting, with significant input from marginalized communities, ordinances chartering public banks, 4) pressuring city council members to pass resolutions chartering public banks, and 5) GOTV efforts for city council candidates who have publicly pledged support for public banking.

Financial/Budgetary Implications for DSA:

$50/monthly in printing costs.

________________________________________

Number 9        Timestamp 7/7/17, 5:32 PM

Name(s) and Local(s) of those proposing the resolution who will serve as lead contact(s): Brad Voracek

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

Everyone should have the right to a decent job at a living wage. In order to reduce inequality and transition to more cooperative production it will require work. If we want an inclusive economy that work should be shared broadly. This means having some work 0 hours while others work 60 hours is completely ridiculous. A push for "Jobs for All" similar to our push for "Medicare for All" is a good way to move in this direction and is directly actionable like the actions we do around H.R. 676.

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

Support H.R. 1000 Rep. Conyers "Jobs for All" bill. Minimum organization is a vote and endorsement of support. Further organization could include lobbying representatives.

Financial/Budgetary Implications for DSA:

Sharing information through different connections and platforms. I do not know about cost and hours, but at a minimum making Jobs for All signs similar to our Medicare for All signs would be amazing.

_______________________________________

Number 10        Timestamp 7/8/17, 10:06 PM

Name(s) and Local(s) of those proposing the resolution who will serve as lead contact(s): Ben Johnson, Jarib Rahman, Eliza Mulcahy, Paul, Weisle, Stephanie Reis, Peter Morency, Annie Dellafera; Boston DSA

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

Whereas, the Democratic Socialists of America has been handed by fate the best opportunity to rebuild a fighting and effective socialist left in the United State in fifty years. All eyes on the left are fixed on the DSA and what it does next.

Whereas, the goal of the DSA is to win socialism in America by building a mass movement for democratic socialism that can struggle in the streets, the workplaces, and the halls of government.

Whereas, the most effective means to build a mass democratic socialist movement is through an independent political party. Such a mass, independent socialist party can offer an inspiring alternative to the rotten politics of the two-party system, unite all the lost tribes of the socialist and progressive left in the US, and galvanize the thousands of newly joined DSA members around a common political project. Such a party can do this all while winning real lasting reforms, winning hard fought union battles, and winning game changer elections.

Whereas, a cohort of DSA members elected to local offices can be the starting place we need to build a new mass democratic socialist political party.

Whereas, young people by the thousands are not joining the DSA to get more Democrats elected. If they wanted that they would have joined the Democrats. They are joining a socialist organization because they want to be part of building a future not hamstrung by the restraints of either the neoliberalism of Clinton or the neofascism of Trump. We have a responsibility to give that desire a political home and vehicle to be engaged in.

Whereas, running socialists as independents is both possible and necessary, either now or in the short-term future. Socialist Alternative, with a membership of somewhere around 1/20th to 1/30th of DSA’s present numbers, have successfully elected a fully independent socialist candidate to city council of a major city for multiple elections. Statement on Reproductive Justice

As socialists, we believe that the right to shape the conditions of your labor is a fundamental human right. This includes the conditions of reproductive labor: the work of bearing and rearing children, and any other unwaged care — cooking, cleaning, emotional support — that is necessary for society to function. This labor plays a key role in every economic system; only the advent of the wage makes it appear otherwise. Because reproductive labor is work, it can be exploited like any other form of work.

This establishes the need for reproductive justice: the human right to maintain personal bodily autonomy. Everyone has the right to have children or not have children, and to parent those children in safe and sustainable communities. Crucially, the intersection of class- and race-based oppressions has produced various systems of bodily control under capitalism. Historically, this involves both the ideological and legislative denial of access to abortion and contraception as well as the less widely-known history of compulsory sterilization, the latter of which has an undeniable tie to eugenics in this country. Thus, the reproductive justice we demand involves liberation from all forms of bodily control.

This introduces a crucial tenet of our demand: while reproductive justice is undoubtedly tied to economic justice, there is no need to derive it from an argument of economic expediency. That is, bodily freedom is central to socialism as a moral good in its own right. It is as fundamental as workers’ rights, or healthcare for all, or the abolition of poverty. A woman, trans man, or non-binary person’s right to control their body is not reducible solely to an issue of economic justice.

Thus, the socialist society we envision includes support for a full range of reproductive choices. We demand free and universal access to contraception and abortion, free and universal access to fertility support, and free and universal access to transgender healthcare. These programs allow individuals to determine the conditions of their own reproductive labor as well as their bodily freedom. Giving all people freedom to exercise their human capacities for parenting and gender expression must be part of any socialist program, for it resists the ideological naturalization of motherhood as a biological and cultural inevitability.

As socialists, we must also support the broad range of programs that are necessary to make it possible to have and raise children with dignity. These include decent holistic prenatal care, free and universal child care and public schools, and access to healthy food and clean water. These material necessities of reproductive labor should be shared by all of society. We must counter the ideology that women are the childbearing center of each individual family unit; by placing the bulk of the economic burden of raising the next generation on individual families, we reproduce the current system wherein families with disparate means simply pass on their wealth from generation to generation. If abortion is legal, but not free and accessible, only wealthy women can control their reproductive labor. Likewise, if some wealthy women are able to hire poorer women to perform household tasks at low wages, only wealthy women are in control of their domestic labor. Neither of these are wins for feminism or for socialism.

There is no time to lose. Our current political climate has provided a platform the bigotry that disciplines gender in every possible way — most recently, with a healthcare reform proposal that treats rape and pregnancy as pre-existing conditions. All socialists must raise the issue of reproductive justice — at work, on university campuses, in our local political domains and on the national level. As long as we live in a society that drastically restricts women’s reproductive freedom, we will continue to fight for reproductive and bodily liberation alongside all other forms of social liberation.

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

After the election of Donald Trump there has been a huge mobilization to resist the threats posed by his administration. We are inspired by the scale of the Resistance and by how open the average activist is to radical politics. There is consensus in DSA that we join the broad layers of people and organizations fighting against Donald Trump and the Republicans, understanding that as socialists our first task is to be part of and to build this movement. But we also understand that we must engage in a fight against the leadership of the Democratic Party and its neoliberal and austerity politics. These dual struggles will often put us in coalitions with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party and the social movement organizations connected to it. The activist members of these organizations correctly see them as a vehicle for the fight against Trump, but are often less clear about the need to fight the neoliberal Democratic Party leadership. The purpose of this proposal is to lay out a strategy to push for socialist politics while we work with progressive organizations electorally and in social movements.

While we join in coalition with these organizations we are ultimately in opposition to the current political and strategic perspectives of the leaderships of these progressive Democratic Party forces as well. Even in the short term, as we struggle side by side with progressive Democrats and their associated organizations against both Trump and the neoliberal Democrats, we must recognize that we are in competition with their organizations for influence among activists. This is especially important among the hundreds of thousands of mostly young and newly radicalized activists. In the medium term we aim to build independent working-class power while they tend to work to reform the Democratic Party apparatus, a set of institutions we see as fundamentally and permanently controlled by the capitalist class. In the long term we are fighting for socialism while they aim only to reform capitalism.

As we have seen with both the Wasserman-Shultz and Tom Perez experiences, the Democratic Party’s corporate leadership does ultimately control the Party. These corporate Party leaders will actively oppose efforts to pull the Party left, and they will not allow supposedly democratic internal process to be used for that purpose. Our assessment is that whatever the goals or intentions of groups attempting to do that —i.e. pull the Party left — they will not be successful because they will never be able to convince these corporate leaders to oppose their own interests. Instead, to the extent that they focus on pulling the Party left, these progressive Democratic Party groups will —intentionally or not — function to divert the energy of our resistance movements into battles within the Party that we cannot hope to win.

We see building working organizations independent of the Democratic Party as a more effective strategy. We are not talking here about third party of independent political campaigns for office. We are talking about movements that have their own sense of independent political identity, that maintain their organizational independence, and that do not subordinate their work to the Democratic Party. We must resist all efforts to pull newly-radicalized activists and social movement organizations into battles to reform the Democratic Party. Instead we should work to attract progressive organizations and their members toward our strategy.

Since the Democratic Party is not a party of the working class and never will be, we have little interest in its internal battles. The fight between Keith Ellison and Tom Perez for leadership of the Democratic National Committee was a fight we as DSA should have stayed out of. We should refrain from endorsing or supporting Democrats engaged in political struggles within the institutions of the Democratic Party, including inside local Democratic Party clubs. Taking part in such internal Democratic Party fights only disorients activists, leading them to believe that the Democratic Party can be a vehicle for the aspirations of working people. While we will support progressive Democrats running for office when it is strategic, we should resist the logic of these progressive Democratic Party organizations, which will lead activists to work for progressives in the primaries but then to support corporate Democrats or even Blue Dogs in general elections.

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

Therefore be it resolved that throughout the next two years, as the Democratic Socialists of America engage in struggles on the national and local levels that put us into coalition with progressive Democrats, we will formulate our strategy with the below points in mind.

Specifically, we will:
1.        Work to build the resistance movement alongside both radical and progressive organizations
2.        Focus on building working class organization with a political and structural identity independent from the Democratic Party and drawing progressives toward that strategy
3.        Carry out an educational campaign to point out the importance of independent working class organizations and the difference between the methods and goals of the progressive Democratic Party organizations and those of DSA.
4.        Be prepared to criticize progressive organizations when their strategies prioritize intra-Democratic Party battles and lobbying over social movements and mass disruption. Be prepared to put forward in anti-Trump coalitions our own socialist point of view.
5.        Refrain from working for the election of corporate Democrats in general elections whose campaigns are dependent upon the wealthy, corporations, and/or corporate PACs. While we will pursue electoral strategies that include running candidates on the Democratic Party line or supporting existing progressive Democratic Party candidates in the primaries, we will not follow these candidates in endorsing any corporate Democrat.

The Rationale: Statement of why this resolution is being proposed (Motivation for the Resolution)

Since the late 1970s and early 1980s the vast majority of the parties affiliated with the Socialist International (SI) have embraced neoliberalism and austerity policies. In many countries, they have helped to lead the attack on the welfare state and on the rights of workers and unions. As a result, many are in deep and potentially terminal crisis at the ballot box, as demonstrated by the recent implosion of France’s Socialist Party, the Dutch Labour Party, and PASOK in Greece, to name a few.

Many other SI affiliates have a long record of authoritarianism. For example, Mexico’s Institutional Revolutionary Party is still an SI member and Hosni Mubarak’s National Democratic Party — the ruling party of Egypt until 2011 — was a full member party right up until the Arab Spring rebellion.

Furthermore, the SI appears to be in its own organizational crisis. Its finances are in bad shape and many of its leading parties are leaving to join the recently formed Progressive Alliance, with the hopes of attracting the US Democratic Party and other centrist and center-left parties.

Our affiliation with the Socialist International hinders our ability to develop stronger relationships with parties and social movements that share our values and which, in many cases, are bitterly opposed to their country’s SI affiliate(s). By maintaining our SI membership, we create the impression that we either do not know or do not care about the real struggles against austerity and authoritarianism going on around the world.

DSA also has not paid its SI dues in years. If we were to continue our membership in any form, we would need to start again and pay part or all of our unpaid back dues. That money could be better spent sending representatives of DSA to meet and learn from other parties who hold more promise as international partners.

Leaving the SI is not a rejection of the original vision of democratic socialism that some of its affiliate parties once embraced. These parties may have given up on the fight for a new society. But the vision of democratic socialism that some of them advanced through the 1970s is championed today by new political forces — Podemos in Spain, Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL) in Brazil, MORENA in Mexico, Quebec Solidaire, Die Linke in Germany, Momentum in Britain, to name just a few. These formations, not the moribund parties of the SI, represent the possibility of a renewed international movement for popular power and socialism.

With this in mind, the 2017 DSA National Convention resolves to fully withdraw its SI membership effective immediately and instructs the newly elected National Political Committee to begin building relationships with parties and movements around the world committed to the work of building a new international socialist movement.

Statement of Action: Brief statement of the action mandated by the resolution

DSA will fully withdraw its membership in the Socialist International (SI) effective immediately. The National Office will then convey the convention’s decision to the appropriate representatives at the SI.

Further, the National Political Committee will initiate the formation of a committee tasked with building direct relationships with socialist and left parties and social movements around the world that we can learn from and which share our values.

Financial/Budgetary Implications for DSA:

There is no cost. It would save DSA $3,750 a year in SI membership dues; an estimated $3,000 a year from the cost of participating in SI events; plus $12,000-$18,000 in back dues that DSA has not paid to the SI and which the organization would likely need to pay if we wanted to continue to be an SI affiliate.

The resolution calls on the NPC to develop a strategy for developing new relations with socialist parties and movements around the world. This could involve spending organizational funds to send delegates to events. But those decisions would be made by the NPC and future conventions of DSA.
